compare.pay: Same base as M&A; bonus slightly lower (US product groups average US$66k vs M&A US$74k bonus, all levels, 2025). UK/Italy: as 3.1 (no ECM-specific data)

summary: Same base as M&A; bonus slightly lower (US product groups average US$66k vs M&A US$74k bonus, all levels, 2025). UK/Italy: as 3.1 (no ECM-specific data)

roles.part: Part 1: Investment banking and advisory
roles.title: Debt capital markets and leveraged finance (DCM/LevFin)

what.label: What you actually do
what.md: *DCM (investment grade):* you help large, highly rated borrowers issue bonds. An analyst prepares market updates for clients (where comparable companies have recently priced), builds debt capacity and credit-ratio analyses, drafts pitch books and "mandate" materials, tracks the new-issue calendar and spreads, prepares term sheets and supports documentation and rating agency processes. On pricing day you coordinate with the syndicate desk (the people who talk to investors and build the order book): initial price thoughts, order-book progress, final pricing and allocation. *LevFin:* you structure and sell financing for sub-investment-grade companies, especially private equity buyouts: analyse a target's cash flows and capital structure to find how much debt it can carry, build the debt side of an LBO model, negotiate terms (pricing, covenants) with the sponsor and with lenders, and manage a "marketing" process to place the loan and bond with investors (CLOs, credit funds, insurers). LevFin is slower and heavier than investment-grade work: LBO financings can take months of credit analysis, covenant negotiation and syndication, whereas IG DCM can move in days or weeks (interview-prep source; consistent with structural differences). Syndicate roles on the markets side (running the book, allocating, publishing price thoughts) are a related, trading-floor-oriented career.

day.label: A typical day and week
day.md: DCM: morning market update (rates, credit spreads, issuance calendar), client calls to flag windows, building comparable-bond tables and sizing analyses; a pricing day compresses everything: launch in the morning, book updates every hour, final pricing at midday or afternoon, then documentation and settlement. Quiet periods before and after holidays (August, Christmas) and around central bank decisions. LevFin: long sponsor-driven weeks, with periods of intense negotiation on documents and "marketing" (lender meetings, calls with investors), then quieter weeks between deals. Hours follow bond market hours and deal timetables; weekends are mostly free in IG DCM and more affected in LevFin.

hours.label: Hours, stress and lifestyle
hours.md: Hours: DCM typical 60-70, peaks 80-90 on pricing weeks; LevFin typical 70-80, peaks 95-100. Prep-site estimates for DCM run about 55-70 hours per week versus 70-90+ for M&A, and LevFin is described as "consistently among the longest in banking", comparable to M&A (one prep-site guide; all anecdotal). Stress: 4/5 (DCM: pricing days are high-stakes; LevFin: sponsor pressure and balance-sheet risk if debt cannot be sold). Lifestyle: DCM is usually described as the more lifestyle-friendly product group; LevFin is closer to M&A. Remote/travel: limited.

profile.label: Human vs. quantitative profile
profile.md: People/communication: 4/5. Quantitative/technical: 3/5 (DCM) to 4/5 (LevFin, because credit analysis and LBO debt modelling are central). Strong client and investor communication matters; credit judgement is the extra skill.

pay.label: Compensation (approximate)
pay.md: Same entry base as M&A at the same bank in each region (sources in 3.1); bonus typically somewhat lower than M&A (product groups average US$66,000 versus US$74,000 for M&A in Prospect Rock's August 2025 data; forum discussions say ECM/DCM bonuses are generally lower; anecdotal). A prep-site comparison estimated DCM analyst total comp at about US$230,000 for 60 hours versus M&A about US$250,000 for 80 hours; the numbers are unsourced and likely too high for the US median, but the direction (similar pay, fewer hours, higher per-hour pay) is what practitioners repeat. Senior: Prospect Rock's March 2026 report puts leveraged finance MDs with 4+ years at a median of about US$1.6 million, matching EB and BB medians. London, Milan, HK, Singapore, Dubai, Tokyo: no DCM/LevFin-specific data found; use 3.1 ranges as the ceiling.

path.label: Career path
path.md: Analyst (2-3 years) → Associate → VP → Director → MD, about the same pace as M&A. At the associate/VP level, cross-moves between DCM, LevFin and sponsor coverage are common. A bank may also place LevFin within a broader "Global Capital Markets" division.

exits.label: Exit opportunities
exits.md: After 2-3 years: private credit and direct lending funds (the most direct route; Ares, Blackstone Credit, Blue Owl, HPS, Oaktree and others hire from DCM, LevFin and restructuring - named as typical hirers in the project's Europe file, Oct 2026), credit hedge funds, CLO managers, fixed-income asset managers, corporate treasury, and private equity (possible from LevFin, less so from IG DCM). A forum-sourced observation: PE is atypical from DCM because modelling exposure is lighter. After 7-10 years: head of DCM/LevFin, credit fund partner or portfolio manager, corporate treasurer/CFO tracks, sponsor-side finance.

tiers.label: Tier list of employers
tiers.md:
Tier groupings reflect industry consensus and practitioner perception, not objective fact. Debt franchises depend on balance sheet and on distribution, so the biggest banks dominate.
- **Tier 1:** JPMorgan, Citi, Bank of America, Goldman Sachs, Morgan Stanley, Barclays, Deutsche Bank, BNP Paribas, HSBC, UBS (LevFin: JPMorgan, Goldman, Morgan Stanley, BofA, Citi, Barclays, Deutsche are the large players; ranking varies by year).
- **Tier 2:** Wells Fargo, RBC, Credit Agricole CIB, Société Générale, Natixis, Santander, ING, UniCredit, Intesa Sanpaolo IMI, Mizuho, MUFG, SMBC, Jefferies, Nomura. In Italy, UniCredit and Intesa are the natural domestic bond/loan franchises (they sit within the CIB divisions that run graduate programmes, for example Intesa's I'M IN programme includes roles from rates solutions to credit trading, 2026).
- **Tier 3:** Regional banks, private-credit-adjacent boutiques and independent debt advisers (Houlihan Lokey's capital markets group, Lincoln International, PJT's Park Hill is a fund-placement arm, not DCM). Smaller deals, mid-cap focus.
Elite M&A boutiques (Evercore, PJT, Perella, Moelis) have debt advisory groups, but debt underwriting needs balance sheet.

enter.label: How to enter
enter.md: Join through the general IBD analyst programmes (same calendar as 3.1) and specify capital markets/DCM/LevFin, or via a "Global Capital Markets" programme; at some banks, applying through corporate banking or markets and lateral-ing in is possible. *Degrees:* finance, economics, accounting, quantitative degrees. *Skills:* credit analysis (leverage, coverage ratios), bond maths (yield, spread, duration) and LBO modelling; awareness of credit markets (spreads, high-yield index, CLO demand). *Mistakes:* talking only about equity-style valuation in interviews, not knowing basic bond concepts, and treating DCM as "easy". *Non-target routes:* start in corporate banking, ratings agencies, credit risk, or a Big 4 debt advisory/restructuring team and move in at the associate level; mid-market debt advisory firms hire more broadly. *Certifications:* FINRA SIE and Series 79 in the US; the CFA is occasionally useful for credit (project earlier file notes it helps more in asset management/credit than M&A). Entry difficulty: 4/5 (smaller group than M&A, with the same selectivity at large banks).

downsides.label: Honest downsides and who it is NOT a good fit for
downsides.md: LevFin hours are close to M&A, and DCM can feel formulaic once you master the process. Exits to PE are narrower than from M&A, though credit funds are an excellent destination if you want them. Revenue depends on credit-market windows and on refinancing waves; during a credit squeeze, mandates dry up. Banks that take balance-sheet risk can suffer losses, and bonuses fall with them. Not a good fit if you want a creative, advisory role or deep business strategy exposure; also not good if you dislike repeated documentation and process work.

compare.name: DCM and leveraged finance
compare.pay: Same base as M&A; bonus slightly lower; no region-specific data found

summary: Same base as M&A; bonus slightly lower; no region-specific data found

roles.part: Part 1: Investment banking and advisory
roles.title: Restructuring

what.label: What you actually do
what.md: You advise companies in or near distress, or the creditors who hold their debt (section 2.5). Typical analyst work: building a 13-week cash-flow forecast and liquidity model (distressed companies run out of cash, so weekly cash is the central number), a "recovery waterfall" (who gets paid what, in order of priority, under different valuation outcomes), a capital-structure summary (every loan and bond, security, maturity, covenants), a business plan model, and comparisons of options: refinancing, an out-of-court amend-and-extend, an LME such as an uptier exchange, a sale of assets, or a court process (Chapter 11 in the US, UK restructuring plans or schemes of arrangement). You also prepare presentations for creditors and the board, support negotiations, and, in court cases, support expert-testimony materials. The work blends M&A (distressed sales), debt advice and legal/process knowledge. Because restructuring touches documents and law, you work with restructuring lawyers constantly.

day.label: A typical day and week
day.md: Highly situation-driven. In a live case: early morning call with the company's CFO and advisers about cash; mid-morning update of the liquidity model; afternoon meeting with creditors' advisers; evening work on a term sheet or court filing materials. Many cases run in sprints around bond payment dates, covenant tests, grace periods and court deadlines; weekends are common during a filing. When the cycle is slow, the team does pitches to companies approaching maturity "walls" and monitors credit markets. Travel to client sites and to court locations is more frequent than in M&A (UK/US/European cases). Hybrid working is limited in live cases.

hours.label: Hours, stress and lifestyle
hours.md: Hours: typical 70-85, peaks of 100+ around a filing or deadline; I found no 2025-26 survey isolating restructuring hours, so this is a practitioner estimate. Stress: 4-5/5 (high stakes, liquidity running out, emotionally charged negotiations, but fewer pitch-book revisions than in coverage). Lifestyle: lumpy; busy when credit is stressed. Restructuring groups are often said to have a more mature, less formatting-driven culture, and they are one of the places where analysts get early responsibility; this is practitioner perception, not measured.

profile.label: Human vs. quantitative profile
profile.md: People/communication: 4/5. Quantitative/technical: 4/5. You need strong accounting and credit logic (cash, covenants, priority of claims) and the ability to negotiate and manage tense meetings; it rewards people who like puzzles combining numbers, legal structure and people.

pay.label: Compensation (approximate)
pay.md: Entry pay follows the same bank/boutique analyst scales as M&A at the same employer; Prospect Rock (2023) states that restructuring analyst pay is "competitive with other IB roles" and gives no figures. The best proxies are analyst totals at restructuring-heavy firms in London: Houlihan Lokey about £115,000 (base £61-70k plus £30-80k bonus), PJT Partners about £110,000, Rothschild & Co about £104,000, Lazard about £90,000, Perella Weinberg about £119,000 (PrepLounge, 27 August 2026; aggregator). US figures as 3.1 (base US$105-110k for juniors; total around US$150-170k+ depending on year and bucket). Senior-level restructuring MD pay: no group-specific figure found. Italy: no reliable data found; Milan restructuring teams at Rothschild, Lazard, Houlihan Lokey, UniCredit/Intesa special situations and Big 4 pay on the local scales in 3.1 and 3.6. Hong Kong, Singapore, Dubai, Tokyo: no reliable data found.

path.label: Career path
path.md: Analyst → Associate → VP → Director → MD, with specialisation often starting at associate or VP level (Prospect Rock). Many teams are small, so promotion depends on revenue from a few mandates; lateral moves between restructuring and debt advisory or M&A are common. In Europe, restructuring bankers often sit within "financing solutions and restructuring" groups (Rothschild & Co's Global Financing Solutions & Restructuring group has over 200 bankers in 14 countries and advises on over US$200 billion of capital raises and restructurings each year, per its own programme page).

exits.label: Exit opportunities
exits.md: After 2-3 years: distressed credit and special-situations hedge funds, direct lending/private credit, distressed or special-situations PE, M&A or coverage groups, turnaround consulting, corporate development. Exit evidence is mostly from career guides and forums; the common claim is that credit funds are more typical than classic buyout PE, and that creditor-side experience helps for distressed funds (anecdotal). After 7-10 years: partner at a restructuring boutique, credit fund portfolio manager or head of a special-situations team, chief restructuring officer roles, or in-house at distressed investors.

tiers.label: Tier list of employers
tiers.md:
Tier groupings reflect industry consensus and practitioner perception, not objective fact.
- **Tier 1:** Houlihan Lokey, PJT Partners, Lazard, Rothschild & Co, Evercore, Perella Weinberg, Moelis. Houlihan Lokey topped LSEG's 2025 global distressed and restructuring tables by deal count (83 versus PJT 55, Lazard 50, Rothschild 44, Evercore 33; figures from Houlihan Lokey's own site, snippet-level). In Debtwire's Q2/H1 2026 Europe table, PJT led by number of mandates (8), ahead of Houlihan Lokey (7) and Rothschild (6).
- **Tier 2:** Large bulge-bracket restructuring/liability-management groups (Goldman Sachs, Morgan Stanley, JPMorgan, Citi, Barclays, Deutsche Bank, BNP Paribas, Lazard-like European teams), Ducera, Solomon Partners, Centerview (restructuring group), Greenhill (now part of Mizuho), Jefferies, Guggenheim, Gordian, GLC Advisors (recruiting for restructuring in its 2026 analyst class per a job-board posting, snippet-level).
- **Tier 3:** Operational restructuring and turnaround advisers (Alvarez & Marsal, FTI Consulting, Big 4 restructuring teams: they were among the Q2 2026 European leaders by mandates), mid-market and regional boutiques (Stephens, Raymond James, Oppenheimer, local Italian and German advisers). Different work: more operational and process-heavy, lower pay, shorter hours.

enter.label: How to enter
enter.md: Programmes and calendar as in 3.1: Rothschild's Global Financing Solutions & Restructuring summer analyst programme (London, 10 weeks from June 2027, requires an expected 2:1 and interest in corporate finance and debt markets; interns work on refinancings, acquisitions, LBOs, IPO financings and restructurings; applications opened 19 August 2026, rolling). Most boutiques hire into an "M&A or restructuring" pool and you choose a team after joining. *Skills:* accounting and credit, reading debt documents, cash-flow forecasting, knowledge of bankruptcy and restructuring processes (a plus), and recent case study knowledge (interviews reportedly ask about recent bankruptcies and recovery waterfalls; anecdotal). *Degrees:* finance, accounting, economics, law with finance, engineering. *Mistakes:* assuming restructuring is "losers' banking" (it is core at elite boutiques), not knowing basic bankruptcy mechanics, or not following current LME developments. *Alternative routes:* Big 4 restructuring or transaction services, credit rating agencies, or law/accountancy then lateral into advisory at associate level (post-grad restructuring talent is in demand: lateral hiring is strong amid LMEs and private credit, per a June 2026 trade article, snippet-level). Entry difficulty: 4/5 overall (5/5 at the best boutiques with few seats; 3/5 at Big 4 restructuring).

downsides.label: Honest downsides and who it is NOT a good fit for
downsides.md: Counter-cyclical demand means a long, unpredictable swing; the work can be emotionally heavy (job losses, creditor fights, litigation), with high-intensity periods; it is a narrower market than M&A, so transferability depends on the cycle. Hours rival M&A. Not a good fit if you dislike conflict, legal complexity, working with troubled clients, or very lumpy workloads; also not ideal if you want a classic private equity buyout exit as the main goal (exits to credit and special situations are the strongest).

compare.name: Restructuring
compare.pay: US: as 3.1. UK: boutiques about £90-119k total (aggregator). Italy: no reliable data found

summary: US: as 3.1. UK: boutiques about £90-119k total (aggregator). Italy: no reliable data found

roles.part: Part 1: Investment banking and advisory
roles.title: Corporate and transaction banking

what.label: What you actually do
what.md: *Corporate banking / relationship management:* you manage relationships with companies, from medium-sized firms to large multinationals, and sell them loans, credit lines, payment and cash management services, trade finance, currency and interest-rate hedging, and, through the investment bank, bond issues or M&A advice. As an analyst or graduate you prepare credit papers (the internal credit approval memos with financial analysis, covenants, risk grading), monitor client financials, price loans, support client meetings, and coordinate with product specialists, credit, risk and legal teams. Barclays describes its UK corporate bank graduates as working with clients from mid-sized businesses to FTSE 350 firms, rotating through support functions, and aiming for a career as a corporate banker or Relationship Director (Barclays careers, accessed October 2026); HSBC's two-year Corporate and Institutional Banking programme rotates through relationship banking and product teams, including trade finance, cash management and capital markets. *Transaction banking:* product specialists and sales who design and deliver cash management, payments, liquidity, supply-chain finance and trade finance solutions; at Citi it is called Treasury and Trade Solutions (TTS), at Deutsche Bank Global Transaction Banking. Work is more operational and client-service oriented, with technology and regulation (sanctions, anti-money-laundering) as important parts.

day.label: A typical day and week
day.md: Meetings with clients' finance teams (CFOs, treasurers) and internal credit teams; preparing credit approvals and annual reviews; responding to client requests (new facilities, covenant waivers, payment issues). Weeks follow client and credit-committee calendars with moderate peaks around large financings or year-end reviews. Travel is common for relationship managers (client visits), minimal for support analysts. Hybrid/remote work is more accepted than in IBD.

hours.label: Hours, stress and lifestyle
hours.md: Hours: typical 45-55 per week, peaks of 60-65 for large financings or reviews. I found no survey for these roles; this is a practitioner-based estimate consistent with the general view that corporate banking is "generally less intense" than IBD (no hard data found). Stress: 3/5 (credit risk, client expectations, regulation), lower than IBD. Lifestyle: more predictable, hybrid friendly, greater long-term stability. Flexibility: higher than banking at junior levels.

profile.label: Human vs. quantitative profile
profile.md: People/communication: 5/5 (this is a relationships job). Quantitative/technical: 3/5 (credit and financial statement analysis, not advanced maths; transaction banking adds product, payments and regulatory knowledge).

pay.label: Compensation (approximate)
pay.md: *United States:* JPMorgan's Global Corporate Banking summer analyst role in New York listed US$100,000 a year (2025 posting); an experienced analyst in the Consumer, Retail & Business Services group listed a US$105,000-110,000 base; Wells Fargo's Financial Institutions Group corporate banking analyst role listed US$100,000-110,000 base (February 2026 posting); bonus not disclosed. Self-reported bonuses are generally lower than IBD analysts (WSO data on middle-market and bulge-bracket analysts of US$65-75k are for IB, not corporate banking; the closest proxy, anecdotal). *United Kingdom:* HSBC's Commercial Banking graduate programme listed £35,000 plus a £5,000 welcome bonus (2025 intake, not London-based); Barclays does not publish a figure; Indeed's HSBC analyst average is about £43,700 (generic title; unreliable for this role). No reliable corporate-banking-specific London figure found; practitioner talk is that CIB-aligned corporate banking graduates in London earn below IBD analysts (unverified). *Italy:* Intesa Sanpaolo I'M IN CIB programme from EUR 40,000 gross a year (8 July 2026, secondary source); UniCredit Milan graduate analyst EUR 40,000 gross base (posting, undated). Both programmes also include non-corporate-banking roles (rates, credit trading, M&A). Bonuses are smaller than in IBD (unverified). *Hong Kong/Singapore/Dubai/Tokyo:* no reliable data found; a Michael Page Singapore guide shows a corporate banking relationship manager, executive director band of S$250,000-350,000 (2026; snippet-level), which indicates that senior relationship managers can earn comfortably but tells you nothing about entry pay. Seniors: Michael Page (Singapore 2026) as above; no reliable data for other regions.

path.label: Career path
path.md: Graduate/analyst (2-3 years rotation) → Associate/Assistant relationship manager (credit paper authorship) → Relationship Manager or Vice President (own a portfolio, 3-5 years) → Director/Senior RM (large corporates or sector heads) → Managing Director/Head of corporate banking. Transaction banking: analyst → sales/product specialist → head of region/product. Promotions are slower and more stable than IBD; many people stay in the same bank for long periods. A common internal move is into investment banking coverage or credit risk.

exits.label: Exit opportunities
exits.md: After 2-3 years: coverage or capital-markets roles in the same bank, credit risk, treasury or corporate finance at a corporate, private credit and direct lending (analyst/associate), leveraged finance at the same bank, fintech and payments companies (for transaction banking). After 7-10 years: head of a corporate banking team, corporate CFO/treasurer, direct lending portfolio manager, chief risk roles, or senior fintech roles. Moves into mega-fund private equity from corporate banking are unusual (my assessment; unverified).

tiers.label: Tier list of employers
tiers.md:
Tier groupings reflect industry consensus and practitioner perception, not objective fact.
- **Tier 1 (global corporate banking franchises):** JPMorgan, Citi (its TTS franchise), HSBC, Bank of America, Barclays, BNP Paribas, Deutsche Bank, Santander, Wells Fargo (US). Large-cap clients, global product range, integrated with investment banking.
- **Tier 2:** National champions: Intesa Sanpaolo, UniCredit (Italy), ING, ABN AMRO, Commerzbank, Société Générale, BBVA, Lloyds, NatWest, Mizuho/MUFG/SMBC (Japanese megabanks, global reach), FAB and Emirates NBD (Gulf). Mid and large domestic corporates, strong local relationships.
- **Tier 3:** Regional and savings banks, mid-sized domestic banks (Italy's Banco BPM, BPER, banche popolari, Germany's Landesbanken, US regional banks). Smaller corporates, lower pay, less international exposure, but often more local autonomy.

enter.label: How to enter
enter.md: Graduate programmes are the main route and are large and open to a wide range of degrees: Barclays UK Corporate Bank Graduate programme (rotations, 2027 intake listed), HSBC Corporate and Institutional Banking Graduate Programme (two years) and Commercial Banking Graduate Programme (UK; three six-month rotations), Citi corporate banking and TTS summer and graduate analyst programmes, Deutsche Bank Corporate Bank graduate programmes, and, in Italy, the CIB graduate schemes of Intesa and UniCredit (master's in economics, finance, maths or statistics, English B2). *Degrees:* any degree is common in the UK (business, economics, accounting, finance and others); Italian programmes expect an economics/finance/quantitative master's. *Calendar:* similar to UK graduate recruitment (applications from August-September for the following year; deadlines vary; I found no consolidated calendar for 2026-27). *Skills:* financial statement analysis, credit basics, communication and negotiation, sector knowledge, product knowledge for transaction banking (trade finance instruments, payments). *Certifications:* none required; a banking/credit certificate (such as the Chartered Banker or credit qualifications) can help in the UK (unverified); the CFA is of limited use. *Mistakes:* treating it as a fallback with no preparation, ignoring the importance of knowing clients' sectors, and not asking about rotation structure. *Alternative routes:* come from audit, credit risk or sector roles, or from a regional bank. Entry difficulty: 2/5 to 3/5 (many openings and large intakes, still competitive at global banks).

downsides.label: Honest downsides and who it is NOT a good fit for
downsides.md: Lower pay ceiling than IBD for equivalent seniority; more regulation, credit committee processes and paperwork; slower promotions; revenue depends on interest rates (margins fall when rates fall) and on credit losses. Roles are often tied to a portfolio or geography. Not a good fit if you want the intensity and deal exposure of M&A, are driven by the largest possible pay quickly, or dislike credit and compliance. Better fit if you want client relationships, stability, hybrid work, and a pathway into credit, treasury or corporate finance.

compare.name: Corporate and transaction banking
compare.pay: US: US$100-110k base (2025-26 postings), bonus undisclosed. UK: about £35k + £5k welcome bonus (HSBC commercial, 2025) to no published figure. Italy: from EUR 40k gross (CIB graduate schemes, 2026)

summary: US: US$100-110k base (2025-26 postings), bonus undisclosed. UK: about £35k + £5k welcome bonus (HSBC commercial, 2025) to no published figure. Italy: from EUR 40k gross (CIB graduate schemes, 2026)

roles.part: Part 1: Investment banking and advisory
roles.title: Transaction services / valuation / corporate finance advisory at Big 4 and boutiques
roles.shortName: Transaction services / valuation / CF advisory (Big 4 and boutiques)

what.label: What you actually do
what.md: *Transaction services (TS) / financial due diligence (FDD):* you test a company's numbers for a buyer (often private equity), a seller (vendor due diligence) or a lender. Typical tasks: reconciling management accounts to statutory accounts, adjusting EBITDA to "quality of earnings" (removing one-offs, normalising costs), analysing revenue by customer and product, working capital seasonality and "normal" level, net debt and "debt-like items" (pensions, leases, deferred payments), cash conversion, and the reasonableness of the business plan. You interview management, work in data rooms, produce a written report and workbooks, and present to the client. In the US, work is heavily historical; in Europe teams also review forecasts and do more modelling (Mergers & Inquisitions, article with 2022 figures). *Valuation:* purchase price allocation after an acquisition, impairment tests, valuations for tax, disputes and financial reporting. *Corporate finance advisory:* sell-side and buy-side advice for mid-market deals (Big 4 CF teams and independent boutiques), similar to a mid-market bank's M&A work but with accounting-led diligence and fixed-fee/time-based economics.

day.label: A typical day and week
day.md: FDD: a deal timeline drives the pace: 2-6 weeks of intense diligence, with daily calls with the deal team and the client, then a report deadline, then quieter weeks or the next project. Team structure is a pyramid (analyst/associate, senior associate, manager, director, partner). Weeks are more predictable than banking outside report deadlines; late nights cluster around report delivery and signing (Finbound UK guide, 27 June 2026, no numbers). Valuation teams have steadier schedules with peaks at year-end reporting. Client site visits and some travel, particularly for cross-border deals (KPMG describes a high volume of cross-border deals and looks for second European languages in its Deal Advisory pages, older 2019 PDF). Hybrid working is normal.

hours.label: Hours, stress and lifestyle
hours.md: Hours: typical 50-60 per week, peaks of 70-80 during report deadlines (Mergers & Inquisitions suggests 50-60 hours with occasional late nights and weekends; no recent survey found). Stress: 3/5 (regular deadlines, steady pressure). Lifestyle: noticeably more predictable than banking, more training and structure, hybrid and part-time options. The "Big 4 busy season" is audit-specific; TS follows deal flow.

profile.label: Human vs. quantitative profile
profile.md: People/communication: 3/5. Quantitative/technical: 3/5 (accounting is the main skill: strong understanding of financial statements, Excel, data analysis; valuation teams use more modelling).

pay.label: Compensation (approximate)
pay.md: *United Kingdom (London):* Big 4 graduate starting salaries around £30,000-36,000, with KPMG typically about £34,500, EY £30,000-36,000, PwC and Deloitte £30,000-35,000 (City AM, 29 September 2026; firm-wide, not TS-specific); Grant Thornton will pay £40,000 to London graduates from 2027 (same article). I found no published TS-specific graduate pay. Mid-tier firms pay about 10-20% less than the Big 4 (search summary, unverified). Bonuses are modest. *United States:* Mergers & Inquisitions (figures as of 2022, a dated source) quotes TS associate base US$80,000-100,000 (total US$100,000-130,000), senior associate US$115,000-145,000 base, manager US$150,000-190,000 base, and director US$220,000-300,000 base (total US$290,000-390,000); a Boston advisory-firm posting listed US$100,000-130,000 for a transaction services senior associate (job-board listing, undated). *Italy:* Big 4 entry-level gross pay of EUR 24,000-28,000 (Trend Online, 12 June 2024; across Big 4 service lines, no TS-specific figure); Indeed shows a Deloitte junior finance and accounting analyst in Milan at EUR 25,000-28,000; internships pay a reimbursement of EUR 400-800 a month. *Continental Europe, HK, Singapore, Dubai, Tokyo:* no reliable TS-specific data found. A Singapore Michael Page 2026 guide lists an M&A Associate band of S$105,000-175,000 (corporate finance role, snippet-level). Seniors: US director to partner figures above; UK partner pay: no reliable data found.

path.label: Career path
path.md: Analyst/associate (2-3 years; professional qualification study, for example ACA/ACCA in the UK or CPA in the US, often alongside) → senior associate/senior consultant → manager (4-6 years) → senior manager/director (7-10 years) → partner (12+ years, competitive). Lateral exits are common at manager level.

exits.label: Exit opportunities
exits.md: After 2-3 years: investment banking at middle-market or boutique banks (moderately plausible; the Mergers & Inquisitions article says it is possible at boutique and middle-market banks in the first one to three years and harder after four to six), corporate development, FP&A, other advisory roles, transaction advisory at PE-backed businesses. After 7-10 years: private equity in mid-market funds (moderate to strong plausibility per the Finbound guide, harder for mega-funds), corporate development head or CFO, or staying for partner. Evidence base for exits is career guides and coaching sites, not placement data; the claims that "TS is a springboard to IB" and "TS to PE is possible but harder than IB to PE" are consistent across them.

tiers.label: Tier list of employers
tiers.md:
Tier groupings reflect industry consensus and practitioner perception, not objective fact.
- **Tier 1:** Big 4 transaction/deal teams, ordered by practitioners variously: PwC Deals, EY-Parthenon Transaction Advisory (TAS), KPMG Deal Advisory, Deloitte Financial Advisory. Differences between them are small and vary by country; the major point is brand, deal flow with PE, and training. Also top corporate-finance boutiques and valuation specialists: Kroll (valuation), Houlihan Lokey's valuation arm, Duff & Phelps (now Kroll), Alvarez & Marsal (transaction advisory and restructuring), FTI Consulting, Lazard's financial advisory arm.
- **Tier 2:** Mid-tier accounting firms with strong deal teams: Grant Thornton, BDO, RSM, Mazars/Forvis Mazars, PKF (BDO and PKF list deal advisory graduate roles), Baker Tilly, plus independent corporate-finance houses such as Clearwater International and Cavendish in the UK (unverified list; Italian mid-market advisers are covered in section 2.6).
- **Tier 3:** Regional accountancies, local valuation shops and small corporate-finance boutiques; narrower deal flow, less brand recognition, more generalist work.

enter.label: How to enter
enter.md: Big 4 graduate schemes recruit autumn to winter for the following autumn start, with spring/summer internships and industrial placements as pipeline stages (Finbound UK guide, 27 June 2026). KPMG's Deal Advisory UK offers streams that include Transaction Services, Corporate Finance and Restructuring (KPMG careers pages; older programme PDFs). PwC Deals trainees and graduates are recruited in many countries (for example, a Finnish PwC FDD team of about 40 people and a 2-6 month trainee programme). In Italy the entry is via stage (internship) at Big 4 deal advisory practices followed by a fixed-term/permanent contract; EUR 400-800 monthly internship reimbursements are common (Trend Online, 2024). *Degrees:* accounting, finance, economics and business are best, but engineering, maths or law with strong Excel and accounting skills are accepted; many graduates start in audit and then move into TS after 12-24 months (an internal route that takes 2-3 years, per M&I). *Qualification:* ICAEW ACA or ACCA (UK), CPA (US), dottore commercialista/revisore legale (Italy, my understanding, unverified); a qualification is not mandatory for TS in all firms but strengthens your progression. *Skills:* accounting and Excel, data analysis (increasingly Alteryx/Power BI), concise report writing, commercial curiosity, and interviewing management. *Mistakes:* applying only to banks and ignoring the Big 4 as a route; assuming TS is "easy IB"; not understanding what a diligence report is. *Alternative routes:* start in audit and rotate; join a mid-tier firm and lateral to a Big 4 deals team; or join a corporate-finance boutique through direct graduate or internship applications. Entry difficulty: 3/5 (large intakes and open to many degrees, but a competitive assessment process and a push for strong academics and internships; 4/5 for EY-Parthenon or top boutique roles).

downsides.label: Honest downsides and who it is NOT a good fit for
downsides.md: Pay is materially lower than in banking at equivalent seniority (a forum poster estimates a 1.5-2x gap; anecdotal); the work is often retrospective ("what happened"), not strategic; you are an adviser to an adviser, as TS is often brought in late in a deal and can be dropped from the timeline; firms are pyramid-shaped and promotion to partner is highly competitive; conflicts of interest (audit independence rules) can restrict which clients you serve. Not a good fit if you want the prestige and pay of top investment banking and are unwilling to take the extra step later, or if you dislike detailed accounting work and reports. Better fit if you want deal exposure with more predictable hours and a stronger accounting grounding.

compare.name: Transaction services / valuation / CF advisory (Big 4 and boutiques)
compare.pay: US: about US$80-100k base for associates (2022 source, dated). UK: about £30-36k Big 4 London graduate (2026). Italy: about EUR 24-28k gross Big 4 entry (2024, all service lines)

summary: P1-3.6 Transaction services / valuation / CF advisory (Big 4 and boutiques)
US: about US$80-100k base for associates (2022 source, dated). UK: about £30-36k Big 4 London graduate (2026). Italy: about EUR 24-28k gross Big 4 entry (2024, all service lines)

roles.part: Part 2: Sales & trading, markets and research
roles.title: Trader at a bank (market-making)

what.label: What you actually do
what.md:
You price risk for clients and manage the book (the desk's inventory of positions). When a salesperson says a pension fund wants to sell GBP 200m of 10-year gilts, you decide the price, take the risk, then lay it off in the market or hold it. As a junior you build the daily P&L explanation, update pricing tools in Excel/Python, keep an eye on limits, execute small flows and shadow the senior trader; as a senior you set the quotes, size positions and deal with risk managers and regulators. Tools: Bloomberg terminals, bank pricing systems, trading platforms (e.g., MarketAxess, Tradeweb, Bloomberg), voice and chat; coding (Python, SQL, sometimes C++ or kdb+) is increasingly expected.

*Desk notes (what changes by desk):*
- **Rates:** high-volume, quantitative, driven by central banks and data releases; vanilla desks are electronic; options and exotics need strong maths. Typical start 6:30-7:00am London time.
- **Credit (IG/HY/distressed/securitised):** inventory-heavy and more analytical. IG is moving to electronic; HY and distressed need credit judgement and legal reading; securitised products need cash-flow modelling. Slower tempo but liquidity can vanish in stress.
- **FX:** the most electronic; spot traders manage a flow book with huge volume and tiny margins; options traders work on volatility. The day is long because FX runs around the clock; Asia-Pacific and London hubs start early.
- **Equities:** cash equities trading is increasingly algorithmic; derivatives traders ("vol traders") are the most quant; delta one traders work on baskets and ETFs. In practitioner opinion London cash equities has among the better hours (eFinancialCareers opinion piece, 10 June 2021).
- **Commodities:** fewer bank seats; hours follow the energy/metal exchanges; more hedging-oriented and weather/geopolitics-driven.

day.label: A typical day and week
day.md: (Practitioner consensus, not a survey.) 6:30-7:00am: read overnight news, check positions, prepare morning meeting; 7:30: desk meeting, view of the day; 8:00-4:30: quoting, hedging, talking to sales; after close: reconcile P&L, review risk, plan tomorrow. Weeks are structured around data releases (US payrolls, inflation), central-bank meetings, auctions, earnings and month/quarter-end. Evenings are generally free except in volatile markets; client entertainment is more a sales task.

hours.label: Hours, stress and lifestyle
hours.md: Hours: typically 50-65 per week, peak 70+ in crisis weeks or for juniors; an eFinancialCareers writer put S&T at 50-70 with a median nearer 50 (opinion piece, 10 June 2021) and another (15 May 2026) described the week as arriving a few hours before the open and staying a couple of hours after, roughly stable through the year with peaks around earnings and market shocks. The 2021 writer also claimed hours are longest in Hong Kong, then London, then New York (opinion). **Stress: 4/5** (5 in volatile markets: you are the person holding the risk and your P&L is posted daily). Lifestyle: office-based; the desk must sit together for compliance (recording of lines) so remote work is rare; travel is limited (some conferences and client visits); weekend work is rare except in crises.

profile.label: Human vs. quantitative profile
profile.md: People/communication: 3/5. Quantitative/technical: 4/5. Traders talk constantly (to sales, other traders, brokers) but the core skill is probabilistic thinking, mental arithmetic under pressure and risk discipline; coding is a growing differentiator.

pay.label: Compensation (approximate)
pay.md:
All figures are dated and from recruiters or press, not payroll data.
- **US (New York), 2025:** Selby Jennings' NYC guide (2025, based on placement data) shows trading base salary of US$125k for analysts, US$175k associates, US$200-275k VPs, US$300-350k directors, US$400-600k MDs. Total pay: analyst US$175-250k (equity derivatives up to US$275k); associate US$250-425k (credit US$250-425k, rates US$250-450k, FX US$250-400k, equity derivatives US$250-450k); VP US$400-850k; director US$600k-1.2m; MD US$800k to around US$2.5-2.75m (the PDF prints "2.5k" and "2.75MM"; I read the "2.5k" as 2.5MM). A different source, Wall Street Prep (updated December 2023, so older), shows a first-year analyst on US$85k base with US$50-75k bonus (all-in US$135-160k) and associates at US$150k base with US$90-130k bonus. The two disagree by roughly US$40-50k at analyst level; the difference reflects the year, the firms covered and the way the numbers were gathered (recruiter placements vs an educational site).
- **UK (London):** I found no recruiter guide that I could open for London S&T pay. A 2025 London/Europe guide seen only as a search-result summary (a page that returned 404 when opened; treat as unverified) gives first-year analyst base of about £60-65k, bonus 25-60% and total of £75-105k, with bulge-bracket analysts at £90-140k total and VPs £280-400k, and says European banks pay 10-15% less. The closest verified London sell-side bands are Selby Jennings' 2024 quant guide (so for quant-heavy desks, not typical traders): Associate/AVP base £75-120k, total £85-150k; VP base £115-180k, total £135-250k; Director £240-450k total; MD base £250-400k, total £600k-1.2m. Disclosure data from Pillar III filings for 2025 show London "material risk takers" (the most senior risk-taking staff, including traders and bankers) averaged US$1.46m (Citi) to US$2.2m (Morgan Stanley) total pay (eFinancialCareers, 8 July 2026); that is a senior-only average.
- **Hong Kong/Singapore:** Selby Jennings' 2024 guide (quant-heavy): sell-side Associate base US$85-100k, total US$120-140k; VP base US$150-170k, total US$220-250k; MD total US$550-700k. For banks' IB analysts in 2024, Bloomberg Intelligence/Michael Page data show Hong Kong analysts at about US$92k vs US$63k in Singapore (investment banking, not S&T). I found no reliable S&T-specific figure for Tokyo or Dubai.
- **Italy (Milan):** no reliable data found for trader pay. The only formal proxy is Michael Page Italy's 2026 salary study for "investment banking, capital markets, private equity": M&A analyst/associate <5 years €30-55k gross annual salary (RAL), bonus 50-100% of base; asset management analyst €30-55k, bonus 15-25% (Michael Page Italy, 2026). Because the EU bonus cap applies and Milan desks are smaller, expect lower total pay than London for the same title (inference).
- **Bonus outlook:** Johnson Associates projected 2026 year-end incentives for equity sales and trading at +10-15% and fixed income sales and trading at +5-10% (7 May 2026).

path.label: Career path
path.md: US-style ladder: Analyst (years 1-3) → Associate (years 3-6) → Vice President (about year 6-9) → Director/Executive Director → Managing Director, with promotion tied to P&L and risk ownership (practitioner consensus). Many bank trainees rotate through sales, trading and structuring during the internship and are placed on a desk at graduation. Only a minority of juniors become head-of-desk traders; many move into sales or structuring, or out. Bonuses are discretionary and depend on bank, desk and year performance, and a portion at senior level is deferred (typical).

exits.label: Exit opportunities
exits.md: After 2-3 years: another bank desk, a hedge fund analyst or junior-trader seat, an electronic market maker (uncommon from voice desks), buy-side trading, MBA or a master's in finance, a move into structuring, risk or strategy. After 7-10 years: portfolio manager at a hedge fund (eFinancialCareers found that about one-third of 15 star traders identified in 2016 had moved to hedge funds as senior PMs or unit heads by early 2026 (23 February 2026); a sample of 15 is anecdotal), head of desk, asset management, commodity house, fintech/electronic trading firm, or exit to corporate treasury.

tiers.label: Tier list of employers
tiers.md:
*Tier groupings reflect industry consensus and practitioner perception, not objective fact.*
- **Tier 1 (global franchises, the largest markets revenues):** Goldman Sachs, J.P. Morgan, Morgan Stanley, Citi, Bank of America (the five US "bulge brackets"). Coalition's 12-bank index (2025) also includes Barclays, BNP Paribas, Deutsche Bank, HSBC, Société Générale, UBS and Wells Fargo. Differences: scale, balance sheet, technology investment, the strongest client franchises, higher pay.
- **Tier 2 (strong in specific products or regions):** Barclays (rates/credit/FX), Deutsche Bank (rates, FX, flow), UBS, BNP Paribas (equity derivatives, rates), Société Générale (equity derivatives, structured products), Nomura (Japan/Asia), HSBC (Asia, FX), Jefferies, RBC, Macquarie (commodities), Mizuho/MUFG/SMBC.
- **Tier 3 (regional, smaller or boutique):** national champions and local players, e.g., in Italy Intesa Sanpaolo IMI CIB, UniCredit, Mediobanca (now within the Monte dei Paschi group) and Banca Akros (Banco BPM group), Equita and Intermonte in equities brokerage; mid-sized banks in Germany, Spain and Asia. Differences: narrower products, fewer graduate seats, lower pay, but often more responsibility early and strong local clients.

enter.label: How to enter
enter.md:
- *Degrees/backgrounds:* maths-heavy degrees (economics, finance, engineering, maths, physics, computer science) are favoured; recruiters in London and New York also take any strong student who can show market interest and numeracy. Nothing replaces strong exam results.
- *Internships and programmes:* the pipeline is the summer analyst programme, converted to a full-time offer. Morgan Stanley's Sales & Trading Summer Analyst Programme in London ran 10 weeks starting in June and rotated across institutional equities and fixed income, sales, trading and structuring; the 2027 London posting went live around 7 September 2026 (job-board listings, unverified). J.P. Morgan's 2027 "Markets" summer analyst track lists Sales, Trading, Structuring & Origination and Digital Markets (job boards, unverified); several J.P. Morgan 2027 Corporate & Investment Bank listings show deadlines around 1 November 2026, but the Markets deadline itself was not confirmed. Barclays' 2027 London graduate roles (Banking and Capital Markets) closed on 25 September 2026 according to Gradcracker; a third-party guide says Markets roles may stay open into January 2027 (unverified; Barclays page not confirmed). Goldman took about 2,500 interns in 2026 with a sub-1% acceptance rate for the third year (Fortune, 8 June 2026, via earlier project research). Asia: Morgan Stanley Japan's 2027 summer analyst deadlines were 16 August and 27 September 2026; Nomura's Asia Global Markets internship applications are expected to open around January 2027 (third-party guide, unverified). Italy: Intesa Sanpaolo's "I'M IN" international graduate programme has posted credit-trader and rates-solutions seats in Milan (mid-2026, listings only; details not readable).
- *Recruiting calendar (general pattern):* apply in the autumn (September-November) of the year before the summer internship (UK/Europe), or in the August-October window of junior year (US); spring weeks and early-insight programmes for first-years in the UK; off-cycle internships exist but are fewer for markets.
- *Certifications:* none required to start. Licences (e.g., US FINRA Series 7/63 or 57, UK FCA certification) are sponsored by the employer (general knowledge, unverified). CFA is of marginal value for trading; it is more useful for research and asset management (CFA Level I pass rates were 39-45% across 2025-26 windows, per the project's earlier research). Skills: Excel, Python, market knowledge (follow rates/FX daily), probability and mental arithmetic, a stock/market pitch, a view on what moved yesterday. Practise brainteasers and market-sense questions.
- *Common mistakes:* applying only to one product; not following markets; pitching "I like adrenaline" without a view; underestimating the numeracy test; applying late; ignoring Tier 2 and local banks.
- *Alternative routes:* lateral entry from middle office, trade support, operations, risk or control; a one-year finance master's (LSE, Imperial, Bocconi, HEC and similar) to earn an interview at off-cycle or graduate programmes; starting at a smaller bank or brokerage or in a regional hub and moving to a bigger bank; MFE/maths master's for derivatives. For non-target students, networking and demonstrable market projects (a trade journal, a tracked paper portfolio) matter more.
Entry difficulty: 4/5.

downsides.label: Honest downsides and who it is NOT a good fit for
downsides.md: P&L is visible every day and stressful; bonuses fall in bad years (and are discretionary); a quiet year can mean a desk closes (headcount in FICC at GSI fell 6% in 2025 despite higher revenue); electronic trading and AI will keep pressuring junior voice-trading seats; the work is repetitive on slow days; the first years are mostly support work; pay at Tier 3 and in Italy is much lower; and trading careers can end suddenly. Not a good fit if you dislike public mistakes, early hours or being measured in dollars daily, if you are uncomfortable with maths under time pressure, or if you want predictable job security.

roles.part: Part 2: Sales & trading, markets and research
roles.title: Institutional salesperson (by product)

what.label: What you actually do
what.md:
You cover a list of institutional clients (fund managers, pension funds, insurers, corporates, hedge funds), relay market colour and the desk's ideas, take orders and relay prices, set up trades, and sometimes arrange meetings with analysts and strategists. Deliverables: morning notes/calls, trade ideas, client lists, order tickets, "sales credits" (the revenue attributed to you). Tools: Bloomberg chat, phones, CRM, pricing screens, bank research.

*Desk notes:* 
- **Rates/credit sales:** relationship-driven but increasingly supported by electronic platforms; credit sales cover many mid-sized accounts and push bond inventory; rates sales include "solutions" to pension and insurance clients.
- **FX sales:** two models: institutional (asset managers, hedge funds) and corporate (hedging treasury flows), the latter more consultative. Electronic execution is the norm for small tickets.
- **Equities sales and sales trading:** cash equities salespeople cover long-only funds and hedge funds; sales traders execute orders and are on the phone/chat all day; derivatives sales covers vol and structured products with a heavier quant element.
- **Commodities sales:** hedging solutions for corporates (airlines, utilities, miners).

day.label: A typical day and week
day.md: (Practitioner consensus.) 7:00am start: morning call with the desk, a note to clients; 8:00-4:30 calls and chats, order handling; late afternoon: client meetings or calls; evenings: client dinners/entertainment 1-3 nights per week for senior people; Fridays are usually lighter. Travel: conferences, client roadshows, in-person visits are part of the job (Europe/Asia more than for traders).

hours.label: Hours, stress and lifestyle
hours.md: Hours: 55-65 per week typically, 70+ at peak; a 2021 reader comment on eFinancialCareers noted evening client entertainment should be counted in hours (opinion). **Stress: 3/5** (4 in volatile markets and on bonus days); the pressure is relationship-driven and revenue-driven; you are expected to be "always on" for key clients. Remote/hybrid: mostly office-based; some regulatory limits on working from home on a desk.

profile.label: Human vs. quantitative profile
profile.md: People/communication: 5/5. Quantitative/technical: 2/5 (3/5 for derivatives sales). You succeed by being trusted, accurate and fast in explaining products and moves; you need enough market maths to explain pricing.

pay.label: Compensation (approximate)
pay.md:
- **US (NY), 2025 (Selby Jennings):** sales base: analyst US$125k credit/rates/FX, US$100-125k cash equity and corporate FX/rates, associate US$150-175k, VP US$175-275k, director US$250-400k, MD US$350-600k. Total pay: analyst US$175-225k credit and FX, US$175-250k rates and equity derivatives, US$150-225k corporate FX/rates, US$120-170k cash equity; associate US$250-375k (cash equity US$225-350k); VP US$400-700k (rates and equity derivatives up to US$750k; cash equity US$300-450k); director US$575-900k (cash equity US$450-600k); MD US$775k-2m (cash equity US$650k-1.4m).
- **UK:** no reliable data found for sales specifically; use the trader ranges above as a rough guide, noting that sales pay is usually somewhat lower than trading pay at the same level in the same desk (inference from the NY table, where sales totals are usually a little below trading totals).
- **Hong Kong/Singapore and Tokyo/Dubai:** no reliable S&T-specific data found; see 3.1 for 2024 quant-heavy sell-side bands.
- **Italy:** no reliable data found. Proxy: Michael Page Italy 2026 "business development manager" in the banking section is €30-55k RAL for under five years with a 50-60% bonus (Michael Page Italy, 2026).

path.label: Career path
path.md: Analyst (years 1-3) → Associate → VP (a "coverage" role: you own accounts) → Director → MD (a senior franchise sales person). Equity sales and sales traders can also move to "head of sales" roles. Promotion depends on client revenue and relationships; star salespeople can be very well paid.

exits.label: Exit opportunities
exits.md: After 2-3 years: another bank, a sales role at an electronic platform or broker, buy-side relationship role, corporate treasury or fintech sales. After 7-10 years: head of sales, institutional sales at an asset manager or fund (capital-introduction/ investor relations at hedge funds), or a client-facing role at an exchange or data provider.

tiers.label: Tier list of employers
tiers.md:
*Tier groupings reflect industry consensus and practitioner perception, not objective fact.*
- **Tier 1:** Goldman Sachs, J.P. Morgan, Morgan Stanley, Citi, Bank of America: global clients and best products to sell.
- **Tier 2:** Barclays, Deutsche Bank, UBS, BNP Paribas, Société Générale, HSBC, Nomura, Jefferies, RBC, Macquarie, Mizuho.
- **Tier 3:** regional banks and brokers (Intesa Sanpaolo IMI CIB, UniCredit, Equita in Italy; Santander, ING, Natixis, Commerzbank, Banca Akros; Asian regional firms): narrower client base, local language and relationships matter.

enter.label: How to enter
enter.md: Same programmes as 3.1 (summer analyst programmes that rotate across sales, trading and structuring). Any degree works if you show numeracy and communication; languages are a real advantage in Europe and Asia (Tokyo: BNP Paribas's 2027 Global Markets graduate programme in Tokyo lists fluent Japanese and English as must-haves, per its posting, via search results). Skills: public speaking, concise market summaries, product knowledge, empathy for client needs. Alternative routes: junior roles in sales support/trade support, client service at a broker or fund administrator, or a regional bank. Certifications: none needed; employer sponsors licences. Mistakes: being all personality and no market knowledge; failing to track the news; poor listening. Entry difficulty: 4/5.

downsides.label: Honest downsides and who it is NOT a good fit for
downsides.md: Your revenue depends on client activity you do not control; sales is the first function to shrink when execution goes electronic; client entertainment and early starts can be exhausting; you are often the "face" blamed when the desk quotes badly; pay has less upside than trading at the top. Not a good fit if you dislike constant phone/chat contact, if you hate client entertainment, or if you want to be mostly analytical.

roles.part: Part 2: Sales & trading, markets and research
roles.title: Structurer

what.label: What you actually do
what.md: You design and price customised products and the supporting ideas for sales and clients. A typical equity derivatives structurer designs payoffs such as barrier options, worst-of structures, cliquets, digitals and autocallables (a note that redeems early if the underlying stays above a level), sometimes hybrids that mix equity, rates and FX, or quantitative investment strategies (QIS); then prices them with quants, checks they can be hedged, sizes capital and funding costs, and produces term sheets and pitch material (Citi, Selby Jennings and other postings, via search results). Compliance with product regulation (PRIIPs, MiFID II, benchmark rules) is part of the job. In rates, credit and FX, "solutions" or "origination" teams do similar work for liability management (helping issuers), hedging and structured notes. J.P. Morgan's markets programme includes "Structuring & Origination" as a distinct track (job-board listings, unverified).

day.label: A typical day and week
day.md: Morning: check volatility, correlation, dividend and funding levels; respond to sales requests (price this note for a private bank); build or adjust payoffs in a pricing tool (Python/Excel/internal libraries); coordinate with traders on hedge costs and with quants on model changes; prepare term sheets and pitches; afternoon calls with clients or private banks; review with legal/compliance. Multiple live requests at once; pitch deadlines.

hours.label: Hours, stress and lifestyle
hours.md: Hours: 50-60 per week typically, 65+ near product launches or pitch deadlines (practitioner consensus, unverified). **Stress: 3/5.** Hybrid arrangements and some remote work are more possible than on a trading floor because it is less tied to the market clock. Travel: client visits, particularly in Europe and Asia where the retail structured product market is large (France, Italy, Switzerland, Hong Kong, Singapore).

profile.label: Human vs. quantitative profile
profile.md: People/communication: 3/5. Quantitative/technical: 4/5. You need to explain complex payoffs simply and be rigorous in pricing and risk.

pay.label: Compensation (approximate)
pay.md: No recruiter table for structurers alone could be opened. Selby Jennings' 2025 NYC guide has no separate structuring row; equity derivatives (trading and sales) are the nearest: trading analysts US$175-275k total, associates US$250-450k, VPs US$400-850k (Selby Jennings, 2025). UK/Italy/Asia: no reliable data found. The Selby Jennings 2024 quant guide shows sell-side quant bands for London (Associate/AVP total £85-150k; VP total £135-250k) and Hong Kong/Singapore (associate US$120-140k total, VP US$220-250k), which sit near structurer/strat pay but are not the same job (2024).

path.label: Career path
path.md: Analyst (2-3 years) → Associate → VP (about 6-8 years, often hired laterally from a quant or structurer role) → Director → MD (head of structuring for a product or region). Many structurers start as quants/strats, graduates of mathematics and engineering programmes, and move into structuring; others rotate from sales or trading.

exits.label: Exit opportunities
exits.md: After 2-3 years: trading, sales, quant roles at banks, insurance product teams, private bank product teams. After 7-10 years: head of structuring, derivatives sales at a hedge fund, product control, fintech/robo-advice product design, or asset management product development.

tiers.label: Tier list of employers
tiers.md:
*Tier groupings reflect industry consensus and practitioner perception, not objective fact.*
- **Tier 1:** Goldman Sachs, J.P. Morgan, Morgan Stanley, Citi, Bank of America and the strongest European derivatives houses: BNP Paribas and Société Générale (known for equity derivatives and structured products), Barclays, Deutsche Bank, UBS.
- **Tier 2:** Nomura, HSBC, Natixis, Crédit Agricole CIB, other global banks on selected products, large Italian banks (Intesa Sanpaolo, UniCredit) and Mediobanca for Italian retail certificates.
- **Tier 3:** regional banks, brokers and small specialist houses.

enter.label: How to enter
enter.md: Strong maths/finance background (mathematics, engineering, physics, quantitative finance MSc such as Bocconi's MAFinRisk, whose placement page lists Mediobanca, Intesa Sanpaolo and UniCredit among recruiters in 2023-25 and says most graduates go into trading, risk, sales or structuring). Entry points: summer analyst programmes (structuring track), graduate programmes, strats/quant teams. Skills: derivatives pricing (Black-Scholes, volatility surfaces), Python, a clear way of explaining payoffs. CFA is not a signal; an MFE/quantitative master's is. Common mistakes: focusing on the maths with no communication; ignoring regulation; applying only to the biggest firms. Alternative routes: quant analyst/strat first, then structuring; ex-trader/associate moves; product control/valuation roles with strong derivatives knowledge. Entry difficulty: 4/5.

downsides.label: Honest downsides and who it is NOT a good fit for
downsides.md: The seats are few; structured product demand depends on volatility, rates and investor risk appetite; pressure to produce "something new" for pitches; the role is in the middle (sales wants cheaper, risk wants safer); regulators scrutinise retail products; and pay is typically below top traders. Not a good fit if you dislike repetitive pricing work, if you want direct P&L ownership, or if you are not comfortable with derivatives mathematics.

roles.part: Part 2: Sales & trading, markets and research
roles.title: Sell-side equity research analyst (and credit research)

what.label: What you actually do
what.md: You cover a sector (for example European banks, Italian utilities or US software), build and maintain financial models for 15-25 companies, write earnings notes, long reports (initiations) and thematic pieces, set a rating and target price, talk to company management, speak to clients and support the sales and trading desks. Credit research analysts cover bond issuers and focus on the ability to repay: leverage, cash flow, covenants, relative value between bonds, and recommendations for investment grade or high yield. They typically support the trading and sales desks and travel with sales to client meetings (sell-side postings, via search results). Associates (juniors) do the modelling and data gathering. Deliverables: models, notes, call notes, marketing presentations. Compliance and conflict-of-interest rules restrict what analysts can say and do, especially around investment banking deals.

day.label: A typical day and week
day.md: (Practitioner/secondary: ctacquisitions.com, 2026; undated.) Earnings season (about four two-week windows a year): review the results, update the model, write a short reaction note that goes through compliance, join the call, host client calls in the afternoon. Outside earnings: maintain models, publish one or two notes a week, run expert calls and channel checks, build initiation reports over weeks. Travel for client marketing: about 30% of the year at senior level (same source, unverified).

hours.label: Hours, stress and lifestyle
hours.md: Hours: typically 55-65, up to 70-80 in earnings season (ctacquisitions.com, 2026, a secondary source citing aggregated data; an eFinancialCareers opinion piece of 2021 claimed research has the longest hours of the S&T-type roles, also opinion). **Stress: 3/5.** Pressure peaks at earnings and in annual client rankings (Extel); you must be right in public. Hybrid is more possible than on trading floors, but analysts are on call during results.

profile.label: Human vs. quantitative profile
profile.md: People/communication: 3/5. Quantitative/technical: 3/5. Modelling and accounting skills are core; writing and the ability to build a clear investment view matter equally.

pay.label: Compensation (approximate)
pay.md:
- **US:** a 2026 secondary guide gives first-year analyst total pay of US$165-250k (2025 benchmarks), year 2-3 US$200-330k, senior associate US$275-550k, VP/sector head US$525k-1.2m, director US$0.9-2.2m, MD US$1.5-8m+ (ctacquisitions.com, 2026; cites recruiter sources; not independently verified). Bonuses depend on rankings, sector revenue and client votes. A different, older educational source (WallStreetMojo, undated) claims research bonuses are much smaller than IB (0-25% of base vs 50-100%); the two do not match, and I could not verify either.
- **UK, Italy, Asia:** no reliable data found. Michael Page Italy's 2026 study lists "asset management analyst/manager" at €30-55k RAL (<5 years) with a 15-25% bonus; equity research is not itemised (Michael Page Italy, 2026).
- Johnson Associates (May 2026) lists "Equities" (the traditional asset management category) up 5%, but gives no separate research figure.

path.label: Career path
path.md: Research associate (0-2 years) → senior associate (2-4) → analyst with own coverage (about 4-7) → senior analyst/sector head; ranking in the Extel survey drives pay and mobility. A common benchmark: analyst status takes about five years plus an MBA/finance degree or CFA (secondary guide). Research is a smaller industry than sales & trading, and the number of analysts has fallen (see 2.9).

exits.label: Exit opportunities
exits.md: After 2-3 years: the buy side (hedge fund analyst, long-only analyst), corporate development/investor relations, equity capital markets, consulting. After 7-10 years: portfolio manager, senior analyst at a long/short fund, head of research, CIO roles, or corporate IR/strategy. The ctacquisitions.com guide lists exits as: hedge funds about 45%, long-only 15%, corporate roles 10%, PE public-markets 8%, consulting 5%, operating companies 5%, staying in research 12% (its own estimates, unverified); a Euromoney poll reported that senior sell-side credit analysts were also leaving for the buy side. A 2024 academic study found high-quality analysts were more likely to leave the sell-side for the buy-side after MiFID II (as summarised in search results).

tiers.label: Tier list of employers
tiers.md:
*Tier groupings reflect industry consensus and practitioner perception, not objective fact.*
- **Tier 1 (top Extel/institutional rankings, global coverage):** J.P. Morgan (top the 2025 All-America research team table by number of positions), Morgan Stanley, Goldman Sachs, Bank of America, Citi; Evercore ISI (No. 1 by weighted analyst rank for four consecutive years to 2025), Bernstein.
- **Tier 2:** Barclays, UBS, Deutsche Bank, BNP Paribas Exane, Jefferies, Wells Fargo, RBC, Mizuho, Redburn Atlantic and strong independents.
- **Tier 3:** regional brokers and local research houses (in Italy Equita, Intermonte, Banca Akros, Intesa and Mediobanca's research teams); in credit, the research team may be small or merged into the strategy team.

enter.label: How to enter
enter.md: Degrees: finance, accounting, economics, engineering/science for sector specialists. Programmes: research summer internships (smaller than S&T), graduate programmes (e.g., Barclays' 2027 Capital Markets graduate listing mentions research and economic analysis among teams, per a job listing). Skills: building a three-statement model, valuation, writing a stock pitch (one or two prepared), accounting. Licences: in the US, Series 86/87 for research analysts are sponsored by the employer (ctacquisitions.com; unverified). CFA: the charter is not required but passing Level 2 is what most hiring managers look for, according to that guide; CFA Level I pass rates were 39-45% across the four windows from November 2025 to August 2026 (CFA Institute, via the project's earlier research). Common mistakes: writing generic pitches; weak accounting; ignoring industry knowledge; submitting too late. Alternative routes: junior analyst at a regional broker; buy-side research assistant; industry experience (engineer, doctor, lawyer) plus modelling skills for a sector team; equity research associate at an asset manager and later switch. Entry difficulty: 3/5.

downsides.label: Honest downsides and who it is NOT a good fit for
downsides.md: A shrinking, structurally challenged business: MiFID II cut budgets 20-30% and many banks cut analysts; pay is lower than trading and banking at the same level (US junior pay sources agree it is lower than trading but disagree on how much); the job is constrained by compliance and by banking conflicts; you are judged in public; and much of the work is repetitive earnings-season modelling. Bonuses depend on client votes and rankings. Not a good fit if you want dealmaking, trading or fast promotion; if you dislike writing and detailed models; or if you cannot accept being wrong in public.

compare.pay: US: total US$165-250k (secondary 2026, unverified). UK: no reliable data found. Italy: proxy only, AM analyst EUR 30-55k RAL + 15-25% bonus (Michael Page Italy 2026)

roles.part: Part 2: Sales & trading, markets and research
roles.title: Trader/analyst at a physical commodity trading house or energy trading arm
roles.shortName: Commodity trading house / energy trading arm

what.label: What you actually do
what.md:
Trading houses buy cargoes of crude oil, fuel, LNG, metals or grain, arrange shipping, storage, insurance and financing, hedge price risk with futures and swaps, and sell to refiners, utilities and manufacturers. A *trader* owns a book (e.g., naphtha in the Mediterranean, copper concentrate, Brent time spreads), negotiates deals, manages margin, and balances logistics. *Analysts* (junior) build position and P&L reports, curve and price analyses, fundamentals models, and support the trader; a Vitol-style "Commercial Analyst" maintains position and pricing reports, daily P&L, curve integrity and mark-to-market (search-result summary of Vitol's early careers page; unverified). Operators/logistics staff schedule ships and cargoes; risk and finance staff manage credit exposure and trade finance. Tools: Excel, Python, Bloomberg/Platts/Argus price assessments, internal trade systems, shipping platforms.

*Desk notes:* crude/products desks are the most senior and best paid; LNG/gas/power are growing; metals and agriculture have different supply chains and calendars; majors' trading arms (Shell, bp, TotalEnergies, Equinor) mix asset-backed trading with structured graduate rotations.

day.label: A typical day and week
day.md: Early morning review of overnight prices (Asia open) and shipping news; a morning meeting with the book; calls to brokers and counterparties through the London/Geneva day; nominations, credit-line checks, hedging; evenings or early mornings for time-zone overlap with Singapore or Houston. Week: bunker/loading windows and price benchmarks drive crunch points. Travel varies: junior analysts travel little, senior traders travel to counterparties, ports and conferences.

hours.label: Hours, stress and lifestyle
hours.md: Hours: 55-70 per week typical, 70+ in volatile markets (practitioner anecdote; I found no reliable survey). **Stress: 4/5** (large positions, 24-hour markets and operational risk). A forum thread said trading houses are much faster-paced than the majors, but that is hearsay. Lifestyle: office-based in Geneva, London, Singapore, Houston, Dubai; relocation between hubs is common; Singapore and Dubai attract people for lifestyle and tax (Dubai: zero personal income tax, general knowledge).

profile.label: Human vs. quantitative profile
profile.md: People/communication: 4/5. Quantitative/technical: 3/5. Trading is relational (counterparties, brokers, shipping, partners) and entrepreneurial, with solid numeracy and commercial judgement.

pay.label: Compensation (approximate)
pay.md:
- **Geneva/Switzerland:** a recruiter (Upreer, 2026, method undisclosed) says graduate traders start at CHF 90-130k and established traders earn CHF 150-300k base with bonuses that can double it; ERI SalaryExpert estimates the average Geneva securities and commodities trader at CHF 103,862 base plus CHF 16,878 bonus (updated October 2025). An older recruiter table (2018, outside the two-year window) put analysts at CHF 70-95k. I found no verified graduate survey.
- **London:** Upreer gives approximately £70-100k at entry level (same caveat).
- **Singapore:** Payscale (2026) shows a SGD 87k median base for commodities traders (25th-75th percentile SGD 63-112k; bonus S$9-48k).
- **Ownership pay is the real money:** Reuters reported (2024) that most traders at Vitol and Trafigura are paid a percentage of their book's profit and that partners receive large dividends; Vitol paid US$5.9bn to roughly 600 employee-owners for 2025 on US$4.2bn profit (Bloomberg in The Star, 27 July 2026), Vitol paid US$6.5bn to employee-owners in 2022 (about 450 owners, Bloomberg via Swissinfo), and Trafigura has more than 1,400 employee shareholders. These are averages for a small group of partners and cannot be read as graduate pay. Majors pay less cash and more deferred stock, and struggle to match independents' bonuses (Reuters 2024, as summarised in search results). Hedge funds also hired oil traders with seven-figure signing bonuses (Bloomberg, 2022; outside the two-year window).
- **US, Italy, Dubai:** no reliable data found. Eni's paid master's in Milan (Politecnico di Milano/Torino) pays €1,500 gross per month for STEM graduates (Eni, earlier project research).

path.label: Career path
path.md: Typical at independents: junior analyst/trading assistant (years 1-3) → trader or "senior analyst" (3-6) → trader with own book (5-10) → senior trader/desk head → partner (in some houses, with equity). Graduate programmes: Trafigura offers two-year Commercial (towards junior trading), Development (operations, deals desk, trade finance) and Technical (trading IT, data science, research analysis) tracks in Geneva, Singapore, Houston, Calgary, Montevideo and Shanghai; TotalEnergies offers a two-year programme with four six-month rotations; Gunvor/Centalion has a graduate programme with rotations through trading, risk, operations and analytics (company pages via earlier project research). Equinor has a two-year market analysis and trading graduate programme (search summary). Those programmes lead toward junior trading roles, not guaranteed trader seats; no house publishes how many graduates become traders.

exits.label: Exit opportunities
exits.md: After 2-3 years: move to another house, a major's trading arm, a bank's commodities desk, a commodity-focused hedge fund, a producer/refiner commercial role, or risk/finance roles. After 7-10 years: head a book or desk at a trading house, run a commodity fund, move to a producer or utility as commercial director, or start a trading business. Many exits are into trade finance, shipping and risk rather than trading seats.

tiers.label: Tier list of employers
tiers.md:
*Tier groupings reflect industry consensus and practitioner perception, not objective fact.*
- **Tier 1 (largest independents, highest upside):** Vitol, Trafigura, Glencore, Mercuria, Gunvor/Centalion (the "big five" by trading volume and reputation); in agriculture Cargill, ADM, Louis Dreyfus, Bunge, COFCO.
- **Tier 2:** energy majors' trading arms (Shell, bp, TotalEnergies, Equinor, ExxonMobil, Eni) with structured graduate programmes and better predictability; strong regional houses (Hartree, Freepoint, Castleton, Concord, Sucden, Aurubis in metals); bank commodities desks at a few banks (J.P. Morgan, Goldman, Macquarie).
- **Tier 3:** smaller independents, utilities' trading units (Uniper, Axpo, EDF Trading, Enel), regional brokers; they offer less pay but sometimes more breadth early.

enter.label: How to enter
enter.md: Backgrounds: commodities/energy economics, finance, engineering, logistics and supply chain, maths/data science. Graduate programmes are small and annual: Trafigura's page on 30 September 2026 showed most 2027 intakes closed, with the China programme open to 23 October 2026; Gunvor's programme asks for a 40-minute maths/logic/Python test (company page, per earlier research). The University of Geneva MSc in Commodity Trading is effectively a hiring funnel: in 2024, 170 applied, 100 were shortlisted and 33 were placed in paid company traineeships (UNIGE, 2024, via earlier research). Common mistakes: expecting a trading seat at graduation; ignoring operations/finance entry; applying to one house only; unfamiliarity with how oil/gas/metals markets work. Certifications: none required; shipping/trade finance courses and industry reading (Platts, Argus, Energy Intelligence, FT Commodities) help. Alternative entry: operations, trade finance, risk or analytics roles, then move to the desk; junior roles at brokers; energy-major graduate programmes; experience in a physical industry (shipping, refining, mining) then lateral. Entry difficulty: 4/5 (small intakes; no published acceptance rates; heavy referral/hiring through headhunters for experienced staff, Upreer 2026).

downsides.label: Honest downsides and who it is NOT a good fit for
downsides.md: Results are cyclical (Vitol's 2025 profit halved; Gunvor's fell 85%, then 2026 profits jumped with the Hormuz-related disruption, per Reuters/Kitco), so bonuses swing; the culture can be closed and politically complex; reputational and legal controversies exist (e.g., fines/pleas by Glencore, Trafigura and Vitol, per earlier research); you may be relocated, and hubs are small, expensive cities; opaque pay; and the best money is for partners. Not a good fit if you want transparency, regular hours, or a global brand name; if you dislike negotiation; or if you are uncomfortable working near fossil-fuel industries.
