roles.part: Part 2: Sales & trading, markets and research
roles.title: Discretionary trader/PM at a hedge fund or macro fund
roles.shortName: Discretionary trader/PM at a hedge fund

what.label: What you actually do
what.md: You take positions, using the fund's capital, based on your judgement of macro, rates, FX, credit, commodities or equities. A junior "analyst" or "associate trader" at a macro or multi-manager fund supports a PM by building trade ideas, running risk, doing data work and executing; a PM runs their own book with risk limits and a P&L target. A discretionary macro trader reads central banks, economic data, positioning and flows and then expresses views through futures, swaps, options and FX. Pod-shop PMs usually have strict stop-loss limits; macro funds (Brevan Howard, Rokos, Caxton, Soros-type) allow larger views. Tools: Bloomberg, in-house risk tools, Python, execution through banks.

day.label: A typical day and week
day.md: Early start tracking Asia and Europe; reviewing positions and risk; research on themes; calls with sell-side salespeople and strategists; trades around data releases and central bank meetings; end-of-day risk review. Weeks revolve around data, central bank meetings and position management.

hours.label: Hours, stress and lifestyle
hours.md: Hours: 55-70 typical; 70+ in stress periods (practitioner consensus; no survey). **Stress: 5/5**: your P&L is your livelihood and hitting a drawdown limit can end the seat quickly. Pay is variable. Lifestyle: office-based (funds are hybrid for analysts, but PMs sit near risk), London, New York, Greenwich, Hong Kong, Singapore, Dubai and Geneva hubs.

profile.label: Human vs. quantitative profile
profile.md: People/communication: 2/5. Quantitative/technical: 4/5. The job is mostly decision-making under uncertainty and risk management; the network (to sell-side and to talk to) matters, but it is a solo-ish performance role.

pay.label: Compensation (approximate)
pay.md:
- **US:** Selby Jennings (2024): fund PM base US$200-300k, payout 10-20% of P&L; quant trader at a prop/HFT firm base US$150-200k and 30-50% of P&L. Top hedge fund quant PhD hires US$300-750k total. Johnson Associates (May 2026) projects hedge fund incentives +2.5% to 10%+ in 2026 with wide variation; macro, commodities, prop and quant "outperforming," event-driven under; a "talent war for star PMs" and growing pass-through fees pushing pay up.
- **UK:** Selby Jennings (2024): fund PM base £120-250k, payout 5-20% of P&L.
- **Asia, Italy:** no reliable data found (Italy has few discretionary macro funds). Hong Kong/Singapore quant researcher bands in the 2024 guide are US$120-240k total for top hedge funds with PhDs, not typical for discretionary roles.
- **Entry level:** junior analyst seats at hedge funds are usually filled by people with 1-4 years at a bank, so there is no "entry" salary table; a London buy-side execution role was advertised at £70-90k and mid-to-senior traders at hedge funds at £150-250k in job ads (search results; unverified).

path.label: Career path
path.md: Typical path: bank analyst/associate (2-5 years in sales, trading or research) → hedge fund analyst or junior trader (2-4 years) → PM (with risk capital) → senior PM / CIO. Others start in prop trading or at a pod shop. Many do not make PM: seats are scarce and the attrition rate is high. eFinancialCareers' 2026 analysis of 15 star traders from 2016 found about a third had moved to hedge funds as senior PMs or unit heads; only four of the 15 still worked in banking (23 February 2026; small sample). In credit and distressed, bank MDs have moved to Verition and Schonfeld (same source).

exits.label: Exit opportunities
exits.md: After 2-3 years: another fund, a different strategy, the sell side, a prop firm or long-only manager. After 7-10 years: run your own fund (rare), family office CIO, senior PM at larger multi-manager, asset management or advisory, or leave finance. Non-competes in Europe can force 6-12 months (or up to three years in extreme cases) of gardening leave, according to Selby Jennings (2024).

tiers.label: Tier list of employers
tiers.md:
*Tier groupings reflect industry consensus and practitioner perception, not objective fact.*
- **Tier 1 (multi-manager and top macro funds):** Millennium, Citadel, Point72, Balyasny, Brevan Howard, Rokos, Caxton, Bridgewater (systematic-macro hybrid), Soros Fund Management. Differences: capital, risk infrastructure, pay upside, strict limits.
- **Tier 2:** Schonfeld, Verition, ExodusPoint, Marshall Wace (macro and equity), Haidar, Qube (systematic), regional macro funds.
- **Tier 3:** smaller funds, family offices, emerging managers in Dubai, Hong Kong, Singapore, London.

enter.label: How to enter
enter.md: There is almost no direct graduate entry into discretionary PM roles. The route is: a strong sell-side desk seat (Tier 1 or Tier 2), strong P&L or an idea-generating track record, relationships with funds (via sales), and a headhunter. Some funds hire graduates as analysts (smaller intake; often via referral) or from investment banking/research. Skills: market view, risk discipline, scenario thinking, Python for analysis, and the ability to run a track record. Certifications: none required; CFA is helpful for fundamental equity. Mistakes: leaving a bank desk too early; building no P&L record; ignoring risk management. Alternative routes: prop trading, personal-account track record (rare), starting at a multi-manager as an analyst after a research or quant background. Entry difficulty: 5/5.

downsides.label: Honest downsides and who it is NOT a good fit for
downsides.md: High attrition; careers hinge on performance and capital allocators' patience; the 2025-26 pod-shop market has strict drawdown limits and long non-competes; compensation concentrates in a few stars; moves cost months on gardening leave; and Johnson Associates flags that AI firms and proprietary trading firms are competing for quantitative talent. Not a good fit if you want stable pay, work-life balance, or if you are uncomfortable with a personal P&L; also not a fit if you want a team environment or have little tolerance for losses.

roles.part: Part 3: The buy side
roles.title: Asset management investment roles (research analyst to portfolio manager), long-only

what.label: What you actually do
what.md: Analysts cover a sector (e.g. European banks, US healthcare) and decide whether stocks or bonds in it are worth owning. You build and update financial models, read filings, listen to earnings calls, visit companies, talk to management and industry experts, write recommendations (often a 2-10 page note or a pitch to the PM) and defend them. Tools: Bloomberg, FactSet, Excel, increasingly Python and alternative data. Fixed-income analysts do credit work (covenants, leverage, recovery) and macro analysts follow rates. Portfolio managers (PMs) decide position sizes, manage risk limits and client mandates, and answer to investment committees.

day.label: A typical day and week
day.md: 7:00 read overnight news and broker notes; morning team meeting; results days mean updating models within hours; afternoons on company meetings or sector deep dives; Friday on a pitch or portfolio review. Quarterly reporting seasons are the busy phase. PMs spend more time on risk, client meetings (as the "investment specialist" in 3.2) and trade sizing.

hours.label: Hours, stress and lifestyle
hours.md: 45-55 hours typical; 55-60 in earnings season or market selloffs (practitioner estimate; the earlier project file also puts asset management at 50-55). Stress 3/5. Hybrid working (2-3 office days) is common at large firms (unverified). Travel: company visits and conferences, a few trips a quarter. Lifestyle is the best of the investing roles, but performance reviews against benchmarks are public and constant.

profile.label: Human vs. quantitative profile
profile.md: People/communication: 3/5. Quantitative/technical: 3/5. You need clear writing and persuasion to convince a PM, and solid modelling, but few firms require advanced maths outside fixed income and quant-driven houses.

pay.label: Compensation (approximate)
pay.md: Entry: London graduate analysts in investment banking and investment management £32-52k base, average about £41k (TargetJobs, May 2025); Italy: portfolio/fund managers ("gestori") from about €35k gross annual salary below five years' experience (PageGroup survey via We Wealth, December 2024); US: no reliable entry figure found. ~5 years: US financial and investment analysts at investment-pool and fund firms had a median wage of $146,640 in May 2023 (BLS via search summary; wages only, all experience levels, older than two years); Italy 5-10 years: no AM-specific figure. Senior: Italy portfolio managers from €70k and above (PageGroup 2024); US mutual fund PMs expected $251k base and $1.12 million variable on average in 2018 (Institutional Investor, stale). Incentives: Johnson projected 2025 asset-management incentives +7-12% (equity-focused +9-12%, fixed income +6-9%) (via AI-CIO, 10 November 2025). Hong Kong, Singapore, Tokyo, Gulf: no reliable data found.

path.label: Career path
path.md: Analyst/associate analyst (0-3 years), analyst/senior analyst (3-7), assistant PM or sector head (6-10), PM (8-15 years, fewer than one in five analysts get there in practice, practitioner view, unverified). At bank-owned managers titles follow bank grades (Analyst, Associate, VP, Director).

exits.label: Exit opportunities
exits.md: After 2-3 years: another asset manager, hedge fund analyst (with a strong track record), equity research at a bank, MBA, corporate strategy/IR. After 7-10 years: PM or CIO elsewhere, hedge fund PM, family office or allocator CIO, investor relations at listed companies, start your own fund.

tiers.label: Tier list of employers
tiers.md: Tier groupings reflect industry consensus and practitioner perception, not objective fact. *Tier 1 (research-driven, selective, strong training):* Capital Group, Fidelity, Wellington, T. Rowe Price, PIMCO (fixed income), BlackRock (active), J.P. Morgan Asset Management, Schroders, Amundi. *Tier 2 (large bank- or insurer-owned, solid brand, more bureaucratic):* DWS, UBS Asset Management, Allianz Global Investors, Generali Investments, Eurizon, Mediolanum. *Tier 3 (boutiques and regional/Italian independents):* Anima, Azimut, Algebris, local SGRs, regional UK/Nordic houses; smaller and more varied, can offer earlier responsibility.

enter.label: How to enter
enter.md: Degrees: finance, economics, accounting, engineering; strong quantitative skills are rewarded. Graduate programmes: Capital Group's Capital Associates Program (CAP) targets final-year undergraduates or non-MBA master's students with up to one year of experience; the Asia round has a 1 November 2026 deadline with Super Day interviews October to December 2026, the US round opened mid-January and closed early February 2026 (per third-party guides; confirm on the firm site). Fidelity (Equity Research Associate internship, 10 weeks, researches three stocks and pitches to funds; Summer 2027 listings in Tokyo and Hong Kong), T. Rowe Price (Associate Analyst internship) and Wellington (applications expected September to late October per a third-party guide) hire mainly through summer internships, usually with a few places and heavy competition. In Europe, graduate schemes at Amundi, Schroders and Generali exist, and many Italian firms hire through 6-month internships. CFA: widely valued here; Level I pass rates were 39-45% across the four windows from November 2025 to August 2026, and all three levels cost US$3,520-4,570 plus about 300 study hours each (CFA Institute figures in the project career file, 2026; secondary guides quote slightly different fees). The charter needs 4,000 hours of relevant work over at least 36 months (secondary guides). Build: a stock-pitch portfolio, a written equity research sample, modelling skills, and investing club or student fund experience. Common mistakes: generic "I love markets" pitches without a view on a real stock; applying only in the final year. Alternative routes: start in equity research or credit at a bank or rating agency, in performance/risk or operations at an asset manager, or in a boutique, and move to investing after 2-3 years. Entry difficulty: 4/5.

downsides.label: Honest downsides and who it is NOT a good fit for
downsides.md: Fee pressure from passive limits headcount and pay growth in traditional active management; PM seats are scarce; investment style can go out of favour for years. Not for you if you want deal excitement or very high early pay, dislike public performance comparison, or are not curious about reading industry detail. Not a good fit if you want to avoid being measured against an index for a decade.

roles.part: Part 3: The buy side
roles.title: Asset management client and distribution roles (sales, client portfolio manager/investment specialist, product)

what.label: What you actually do
what.md: Sales/relationship managers sell funds and mandates to pension funds, insurers, banks' distribution networks and wealth advisers; investment specialists or client portfolio managers (CPMs) explain the portfolio managers' views and performance to clients; product managers design funds, set fees and manage launches. Deliverables: pitch books, RFP (request for proposal) responses, due-diligence questionnaires, performance commentary, market updates, client reviews. Tools: CRM systems, Excel/PowerPoint, Bloomberg, increasingly data dashboards.

day.label: A typical day and week
day.md: Morning market call, then client emails and calls; two or three meetings a day (in person or video); writing RFP answers; liaising with PMs. Travel to clients and conferences; month-end and quarter-end reporting cycles. Sales teams are measured on flows (net new money).

hours.label: Hours, stress and lifestyle
hours.md: 45-55 hours; 60 around pitches and travel (practitioner estimate). Stress 3/5, driven by sales targets and fund redemptions. Travel 20-40% for institutional sales (unverified). Hybrid common.

profile.label: Human vs. quantitative profile
profile.md: People/communication: 5/5. Quantitative/technical: 2/5. You must understand portfolios well enough to explain performance, but the job is trust, storytelling and responsiveness.

pay.label: Compensation (approximate)
pay.md: Hardly any public entry data. Averages across all seniorities (54% of respondents were managing directors) in a Heidrick survey of 186 alternatives marketing and IR professionals (spring 2025): US$416k base for private equity and private credit sales/IR, US$419k for product specialists, US$287k for individual hedge fund sales producers and US$272k for hedge fund sales/IR (Heidrick via Funds Society); this is not entry pay. Italy: relationship managers from about €35k, up to more than €90k with 10+ years (PageGroup 2024). UK/US entry: no reliable data found. Bonus and incentives follow sales: Johnson projected 2025 incentives +7-12% in traditional asset management (AI-CIO).

path.label: Career path
path.md: Sales/product analyst or associate (0-3 years), VP/senior sales (4-7), director/head of a region or client segment (8-12), managing director/head of distribution (12+). Investment specialists often come from the investment side after a few years.

exits.label: Exit opportunities
exits.md: After 2-3 years: product or sales at another manager, fund selector roles at banks, wealth management, fintech sales. After 7-10 years: head of distribution, chief commercial officer, move into alternatives fundraising (investor relations at PE, credit and hedge funds), consulting to managers.

tiers.label: Tier list of employers
tiers.md: Tier groupings reflect industry consensus and practitioner perception, not objective fact. *Tier 1 (global distribution machines with best training):* BlackRock, J.P. Morgan AM, Fidelity, Amundi, Schroders. *Tier 2:* DWS, UBS AM, Allianz GI, Eurizon, Generali Investments. *Tier 3:* boutiques, local SGRs, bank wealth distributors. Alternatives fundraising (IR) at big PE and private credit firms (Blackstone, KKR, Apollo, Ares, EQT) pays more but hires mostly experienced people.

enter.label: How to enter
enter.md: Business, finance, marketing, economics and languages all work; fluency in the local language matters (Italian for Italian institutional clients, German for DACH, Japanese for Tokyo). Graduate schemes at large managers (BlackRock, Amundi, DWS, UBS AM, Schroders) include distribution tracks; internships in sales support/marketing at managers are a common start. Certifications: CFA is helpful, not required; in the EU, local registration (e.g., EFPA/MiFID II knowledge requirements) matters for advice roles. Show: client-facing work (summer jobs in sales, wealth, consulting), strong writing, and some product knowledge. Common mistake: dismissing sales as "less prestigious" in the interview. Alternative routes: start in operations, client service or performance reporting and move into sales support. Entry difficulty: 3/5.

downsides.label: Honest downsides and who it is NOT a good fit for
downsides.md: Targets are partly out of your control (flows follow performance and markets); the job can feel like you are selling someone else's product; senior jobs are scarce. Not for you if you dislike travel, repetitive questionnaires or being measured on flows, or if you want to make investment decisions.

roles.part: Part 3: The buy side
roles.title: Hedge fund analyst / portfolio manager (with strategy notes, especially pod platforms)

what.label: What you actually do
what.md: Analysts generate long and short ideas, build earnings models, track "what the market expects" versus what is happening, meet companies and experts, and size trades with the PM; in pods, analysts run a sector for a PM and can get their own capital after proving themselves. PMs set the risk budget, trade daily and are measured on profit and loss (P&L), often daily. Event-driven analysts read legal documents; macro people follow central banks and flows; credit analysts model recoveries.

day.label: A typical day and week
day.md: Start around 6:00-7:00 with news and overnight positions; market open, constant trading and risk checks; earnings calls after close; evenings on models. Friday: weekly P&L review. A bad month tightens the PM and trims analysts' allocation. Strategy notes: fundamental long/short is the slower, research-heavy end; macro and RV are market-driven and episodic; merger arbitrage involves reading deal documents and monitoring regulators; distressed involves months-long legal processes and negotiation.

hours.label: Hours, stress and lifestyle
hours.md: 55-70 hours typical; 70-80+ in earnings season and market crises (practitioner estimate; no survey found). Stress 5/5 at pods (daily P&L, strict loss limits, quick firing), 4/5 at slower fundamental funds. Mostly in the office. Travel is modest, except for company or expert meetings. The risk is job insecurity rather than raw hours.

profile.label: Human vs. quantitative profile
profile.md: People/communication: 3/5. Quantitative/technical: 4/5. You need conviction and the ability to argue with a PM, but numbers, probabilities and risk dominate.

pay.label: Compensation (approximate)
pay.md: Survey (almost 3,000 respondents across financial services, 2025 pay, eFinancialCareers Compensation & Lifestyle Report 2026, reported 25 August 2026): hedge fund junior (analyst and associate) average total US$227k; seniors (VP/director) more than three times that; managing directors US$2.2 million; base salaries rarely above US$300k; no breakdown by city. Entry programmes: Millennium's Equities Analyst Program (run with UBS: a first year in UBS equity research, then a Millennium PM team) listed a New York base of US$125,000 in May 2025 (job listing via MIT CDO; I could not open the live page); Point72 Academy summer internship base of US$120-140k prorated (Point72 posting) and a New York Academy listing at about US$125,000 (Indeed, unverified). Mid-career: pod-level estimates of US$300-700k for a New York analyst and US$500k-1.5 million+ for a senior analyst (Quantt Millennium guide, 2026; estimates from public and anecdotal sources); a former Balyasny analyst says senior analysts on a good pod make US$1-3 million in a normal year (X post as relayed by eFinancialCareers; anecdote). PMs commonly receive 12-25% of their P&L; top PMs earn tens of millions; one report says offers above US$100 million have been made to star PMs (Hedgeweek/WSJ, relayed by search; unverified details). Johnson projected hedge fund bonuses +2.5% to 10%+ for 2025 (AI-CIO). Europe, Asia, Gulf: no reliable breakdown found; the pay surveys exist but are paywalled.

path.label: Career path
path.md: Analyst (0-3 years), senior analyst (3-6), PM or junior PM with own capital (5-10, if at all), senior PM. At single-manager funds the path is analyst, senior analyst, sector head, partner. Most pods work on a "up or out" basis.

exits.label: Exit opportunities
exits.md: After 2-3 years: move between funds, go to long-only asset managers (often for lifestyle), PE/growth equity, a corporate role, or business school. After 7-10 years: start your own fund (rarely with outside money now), family-office CIO, allocator, operating roles, or a long-only PM role.

tiers.label: Tier list of employers
tiers.md: Tier groupings reflect industry consensus and practitioner perception, not objective fact. *Tier 1:* multi-manager platforms (Millennium, Citadel, Balyasny, Point72, ExodusPoint, Schonfeld) and elite single managers (Bridgewater, D. E. Shaw, Elliott, Viking, Marshall Wace, Brevan Howard in Europe). *Tier 2:* well-known mid-sized fundamental or macro funds, such as Lansdowne, Egerton, Capula, Pharo, Hillhouse in Asia. *Tier 3:* small, specialist and emerging managers (often under US$1 billion), where resources are thinner and survival risk is higher. Italian hedge fund jobs are few: Milan has some boutiques, but London and Switzerland are the main European hubs (practitioner view; unverified).

enter.label: How to enter
enter.md: Graduate programmes are rare but growing at platforms: Point72 Academy is a paid ten-month programme (eight months of training, two of rotations with teams) for students graduating between December 2026 and July 2027, with more than 230 graduates placed as of March 2026 (Point72 posting, via search); Millennium's analyst programme and 2027 summer internships (applications opened 3 August 2026, closed 3 September 2026) asked for a GPA of 3.5+ (listing); Citadel and Citadel Securities took about 350 interns out of more than 115,900 applicants, an acceptance rate of about 0.36% (Fortune via AlphaMaven, undated); Balyasny received over 40,000 applications for about 100 intern places (Pensions & Investments, undated). Most hires still come from sell-side research, investment banking, consulting or long-only funds after two to four years. Degrees: finance, economics, maths, engineering, accounting; STEM is valued at systematic or data-heavy pods. Certifications: CFA is optional; track record matters more. Build: a documented stock-picking record, a published pitch, or a student fund. Common mistakes: pitching only large caps with consensus views, no short idea, ignoring risk. Alternative routes: sell-side research, a credit or restructuring job, or an internal move from a bank's markets desk. Entry difficulty: 5/5.

downsides.label: Honest downsides and who it is NOT a good fit for
downsides.md: Pay is extreme in the best cases and zero in the worst: pods cut people quickly after drawdowns; bonuses depend on a PM you do not control; there are few seats for graduates. March 2026 shows the model can lose money for the largest names. Not for you if you need stability, dislike public daily scoreboards or are not comfortable being wrong in front of colleagues several times a week.

roles.part: Part 3: The buy side
roles.title: Private equity associate to partner

what.label: What you actually do
what.md: Associates build LBO (leveraged buyout) models, review confidential information memoranda, run due diligence calls with consultants, accountants and lawyers, manage data rooms, write investment committee memos (often 30-40 pages), and work with banks on financing. After the deal, you monitor portfolio companies (monthly KPI packs, board materials). VPs and principals source deals and lead execution; partners decide on the investment and raise funds.

day.label: A typical day and week
day.md: Morning: model updates and calls with management or advisers; afternoon: diligence sessions or lender discussions; evenings and weekends: IC memo and model. Weeks differ: a "live deal" can mean 80-100 hours near signing, while portfolio monitoring and sourcing weeks are calmer.

hours.label: Hours, stress and lifestyle
hours.md: 55-70 hours typical, 80-100 during live deals (a recruiter's guide says 60-80 regularly with longer stretches at closing, Wall Street Careers, 2026; lower mid-market is often 50-60, practitioner estimate). Stress 4/5. Travel to portfolio companies and targets. Hybrid is partly possible, but most junior work is in the office.

profile.label: Human vs. quantitative profile
profile.md: People/communication: 4/5. Quantitative/technical: 3/5. Modelling must be solid, but the job at VP level is judgment, negotiating with sellers, managing management teams and winning deals.

pay.label: Compensation (approximate)
pay.md: US: Associates (typically hired after 2-3 years in banking) earn base US$140-175k and first-year total US$250-400k+ (Leland, July 2025); Glassdoor averages US$246,462 total with a 25th-75th percentile range of US$186,657-332,138 (February 2026, via Wall Street Careers); one third-party estimate puts mega-funds at US$325-425k and middle-market at US$250-340k (Refonte Learning, 2026, an estimate). Carry is rare at associate level and begins around senior associate/VP (Wall Street Prep, via Wall Street Careers; recruiter material). Heidrick's 2025 North America survey (656 respondents, 19 November 2025) found half of respondents had base increases of 10% or less and three-quarters said bonuses are discretionary; the public page gives no dollar tables. UK: associates total £170-300k in London (Jobrise, 2026; low-reliability estimate; an older Emolument survey from March 2020 gave £100k+ base, bonus up to £36k, and carry up to £300k, stale). Italy: the PageGroup survey puts "M&A analyst/associate/manager (investment banking, private equity cluster)" at €27-60k gross below five years, up to about €100k at 5-10 years and above €100k beyond, with bonus 50-100% (via We Wealth, December 2024); this mixes banking and PE, so treat as a floor. Continental Europe: Heidrick's Europe survey (302 participants, 11 December 2025) shows managing partners with an average base of €339k and bonus of €459k (finews); other levels not public. Hong Kong/Singapore: managing partners average US$891k, up 14% (Heidrick 2025 APAC/Middle East survey via Gulf News, 6 April 2026), with average carry allocations of US$5.487 million; Middle East managing partners average US$750k total cash (up from US$624k); associate-level 2025 data: no reliable data found (older Heidrick data is stale). Tokyo: one recruiter listing for an associate to senior associate at a global PE fund quoted ¥14-17 million (Morgan McKinley, undated listing).

path.label: Career path
path.md: Analyst (pre-MBA, at some funds 0-2 years), associate (2-3 years), senior associate or VP (3-6 years), principal/director (6-10), partner/managing director (10-15+). Promotion timelines have widened as holding periods lengthened to about seven years (Bain, 2026).

exits.label: Exit opportunities
exits.md: After 2-3 years: MBA, move to a bigger or different fund, growth equity, venture, corporate development, portfolio company operating roles. After 7-10 years: partner at the same or another fund, start a fund or independent sponsor, CFO or CEO of a portfolio company, family office.

tiers.label: Tier list of employers
tiers.md: Tier groupings reflect industry consensus and practitioner perception, not objective fact. *Mega-fund (largest funds, global, biggest deals, most structured):* Blackstone, KKR, Apollo, Carlyle, TPG, CVC, EQT, Bain Capital, Advent, Warburg Pincus, Permira, Hellman & Friedman, Thoma Bravo, Silver Lake. *Upper-middle-market / large mid-market:* Leonard Green, Veritas, Francisco Partners, Apax, Ardian, PAI Partners, Bridgepoint, Cinven. *Middle-market:* regional and sector funds such as Riverside, HIG, Audax; in Italy Investindustrial, Clessidra, Wise Equity, Xenon, Ambienta, and the state-backed Fondo Italiano d'Investimento. *Lower middle-market / independent sponsors:* small funds with fewer resources and more operational involvement, where hiring is less structured.

enter.label: How to enter
enter.md: Almost all associate hires at top funds come from top-tier banks' M&A or leveraged-finance analyst classes, strategy consulting (especially in Europe), or occasionally other funds. US "on-cycle" recruiting means that large funds interview junior bankers very early (historically within months of starting as an analyst) for jobs 18-24 months ahead, through headhunters such as Henkel, Amity, CPI and Oxbridge, in processes that can go from call to offer in days. This was disrupted in 2025: JPMorgan warned that analysts accepting future-dated PE jobs in their first 18 months could be fired; on 11-12 June 2025 Apollo and General Atlantic announced they would not formally interview for the class of 2027 (Banking Dive, 12 June 2025); recruiting resumed on 5 January 2026 with Blackstone, Apollo, KKR and Thoma Bravo among a dozen-plus firms interviewing (reporting via PE Insights/Business Insider summaries); Apollo says it fills under half of its associate class on-cycle. Several firms now allocate about half their classes to off-cycle hiring (Prospect Rock Partners). The 2028-class calendar has not been reported; an undated forum post says it had not started (anecdote). In Europe and Asia, I found no source documenting a fixed on-cycle calendar; listings from European mid-market funds look rolling and year-round and ask for 1-3 years in investment banking, strategy consulting or M&A boutiques (job listings via CFA Institute career centre, Munich/Frankfurt/Zurich). That suggests continental mid-market PE is off-cycle, but this is my inference, not documented. Certifications: CFA is not required; some value a Master's. Skills: LBO modelling tests, case studies, a view on industries. Common mistakes: applying without any transaction experience, weak understanding of leverage, thinking MBA alone is a route (the earlier project file notes that post-MBA PE seats go almost exclusively to people with prior PE or elite M&A experience). Alternative routes: transaction services (Big 4), strategy consulting (Bain, BCG, McKinsey), credit funds, restructuring, or joining a smaller or independent sponsor and moving up. Entry difficulty: 5/5.

downsides.label: Honest downsides and who it is NOT a good fit for
downsides.md: Pay is very high but bonuses are discretionary; realised carry depends on exits that are now slow (distributions under 15% of NAV for four years, Bain 2026). Junior work is repetitive modelling and diligence. Partnership seats are few: many associates exit. Not for you if you want predictable hours, hate negotiating, or want to run operations rather than make bets.

roles.part: Part 3: The buy side
roles.title: Venture capital analyst/associate to partner

what.label: What you actually do
what.md: Source start-ups (cold outreach, events, founder referrals, data tools), screen decks, take first calls, write investment memos, run reference calls with customers and former colleagues, track portfolio KPIs and help with follow-on rounds. At seed stage there is little modelling; at growth stage you build revenue-cohort models. Partners decide on investments and sit on boards.

day.label: A typical day and week
day.md: Founder meetings in the morning, internal pipeline meeting, evenings at events or calls with founders in other time zones. Mondays: partner meeting; the rest is sourcing and diligence. Rhythm is irregular but less intense than PE.

hours.label: Hours, stress and lifestyle
hours.md: 45-60 hours; peaks around a deal. Stress 3/5; the pressure is long-term (fund performance, fundraising) not daily. Flexible and often hybrid; travel to hubs (San Francisco, London, Berlin, Milan). Many firms are small, so culture varies widely.

profile.label: Human vs. quantitative profile
profile.md: People/communication: 5/5. Quantitative/technical: 2/5. Relationships, taste and speed to a decision count more than modelling; technical depth in your sector is a big advantage.

pay.label: Compensation (approximate)
pay.md: Data are weak. A 2025 survey run by Gannon/Venture5 (700+ respondents, as relayed by a search summary, unverified) reports average base of about US$78k (analyst), US$126k (associate), US$154k (senior associate), US$206k (VP/principal) and US$317k (partner), with total cash of roughly US$90-170k (analyst), US$130-300k (associate), US$250-700k (principal) and US$400k-1.8 million (partner). Another table (VCBeast, 2026) lists carry as rare for associates, meaningful for principals and the main reward for partners. Because many VC funds have no preferred-return hurdle, carry is paid on all profit (VCBeast). Johnson projected flat VC bonuses for 2025 (AI-CIO). A reported "median total cash of about US$125k for a VC analyst in 2025" attributed to Carta could not be verified. UK, Italy, Singapore, Hong Kong, Tokyo, Gulf: no reliable data found. Carry in venture pays out only after 7-10 years and depends on rare outliers (power law, 2.5).

path.label: Career path
path.md: Analyst (0-2 years), associate (2-4), senior associate/principal (4-7), partner (7-12; often by bringing in a winning investment or raising a fund). Many people also start their own fund ("scout" or angel route) or become operators.

exits.label: Exit opportunities
exits.md: After 2-3 years: start-up operating roles (strategy, business development, product), growth equity, PE, a founder role. After 7-10 years: partner or GP at another fund, founder, CVC head, family office.

tiers.label: Tier list of employers
tiers.md: Tier groupings reflect industry consensus and practitioner perception, not objective fact. *Tier 1 (brand and deal access; extremely selective, very few hires per year):* Sequoia, Andreessen Horowitz, Accel, Benchmark, Founders Fund, Lightspeed, General Catalyst; in Europe Index Ventures, Atomico, Balderton, Lakestar; in Asia Peak XV and HongShan. *Tier 2:* strong specialist or regional funds (e.g., in Italy P101, United Ventures, Primo Ventures, and the state-backed CDP Venture Capital). *Tier 3:* emerging managers, angel syndicates, accelerators and university funds. CVCs (Intel Capital, Salesforce Ventures, bank and utility ventures) form a separate group where jobs are more stable but investment mandates are strategic.

enter.label: How to enter
enter.md: There is no standard path. Typical hires come from start-ups (operators), investment banking or consulting (especially tech M&A and strategy), PE and growth equity, or from founding a company. Some funds run analyst programmes (e.g., through Kauffman Fellows or fellowships, often with part-time roles for students). Recruiting is year-round and unstructured: you pitch yourself via cold emails, a portfolio of writing (a market map, a newsletter, a deep dive on a sector), and a record of building (side projects, hackathons, student venture funds). Certifications: none matter; the CFA is rarely relevant. Skills: sourcing, sector knowledge (AI, climate, fintech, defence), clear memos. Common mistakes: applying with no sourcing evidence; pitching "I like start-ups"; ignoring that most funds hire one or two people a year. Alternative routes: join a start-up and become a "platform" or scout; join a student venture fund; work in a university tech-transfer office. Entry difficulty: 5/5.

downsides.label: Honest downsides and who it is NOT a good fit for
downsides.md: Very few seats; low base for junior roles compared with PE or hedge funds; the reward is carry, which takes a decade and may be zero; many funds under-deliver (power law). Not for you if you need quick, measurable feedback, financial security early on, or dislike constant networking.

roles.part: Part 3: The buy side
roles.title: Private credit analyst/associate

what.label: What you actually do
what.md: Analyse borrowers (usually PE-owned mid-sized companies): model cash flows and leverage, study covenants and legal documents, speak with sponsors and management, write credit memos for the investment committee, negotiate terms with other lenders and lawyers, and monitor the portfolio after funding (quarterly compliance and amendment requests). Special-situations teams do restructuring, rescue financing and distressed purchases; asset-based finance teams analyse pools of receivables or consumer loans and value collateral.

day.label: A typical day and week
day.md: Review new deals from sponsors, build a model, speak to lawyers about the term sheet, and prepare an IC memo. During a closing, 14-hour days; in monitoring weeks, updating covenants, calling borrowers, and approving amendments. In stressed periods (2026 software loans) much time goes on "watch-list" names.

hours.label: Hours, stress and lifestyle
hours.md: 50-65 hours; 70-80 around closings (practitioner estimate). Stress 4/5, higher in 2026 with valuation and redemption pressure. Mostly in-office; some travel to sponsors.

profile.label: Human vs. quantitative profile
profile.md: People/communication: 3/5. Quantitative/technical: 3/5. Downside analysis, documentation and sponsor relationships matter more than complex maths.

pay.label: Compensation (approximate)
pay.md: US: a posted direct lending associate role lists base US$125-150k excluding bonus (Marathon Fund, listing); a recruiter guide gives entry-level base US$90-130k with 30-80% bonus (Wall Street Careers, 2026); a Wall Street Oasis benchmark summary (forum, unverified) puts Tier-1-city associates at about US$300k total (US$150k base plus US$150k bonus) and VPs at about US$505k. Heidrick's first North American private credit survey (297 respondents, 10 June 2025) says carry commonly vests over five years, clawbacks are rare, and deferral is common above the most junior levels (20-30% of bonus). One recruiter blog says a direct-lending principal averages about US$2.9 million of carry over a five-year fund cycle (attributed to Heidrick; not verified). UK/Europe: Dartmouth Partners' 2025 guide has London figures for analyst to director (paywalled) and says Paris and Frankfurt pay is "typically 10-20% lower"; actual numbers: no reliable data found. Italy: no reliable data found (Milan private credit teams are small; Tikehau Capital, for example, advertises a private equity internship in Italy without pay). Johnson projected 2025 private credit bonuses +5-10% (AI-CIO), and a secondary report says -2.5% to -7.5% for 2026 (unverified). Asia/Gulf: no reliable data found.

path.label: Career path
path.md: Analyst (0-2), associate (2-4), VP (4-7), principal/director (7-10), partner/MD (10+). Carry usually starts around VP/principal.

exits.label: Exit opportunities
exits.md: After 2-3 years: another credit fund, PE, restructuring advisory, bank leveraged finance, hedge fund credit. After 7-10 years: partner, head of a strategy, CIO of an insurer's credit book, CFO/treasury roles, start own lending platform.

tiers.label: Tier list of employers
tiers.md: Tier groupings reflect industry consensus and practitioner perception, not objective fact. *Tier 1 (large platforms with proprietary origination and insurance capital):* Apollo, Ares, Blackstone Credit & Insurance, HPS (now part of BlackRock), Blue Owl, Oaktree, Sixth Street, Golub, Goldman Sachs Asset Management; in Europe ICG, Hayfin, Arcmont, Tikehau, Pemberton. *Tier 2:* mid-sized specialist lenders and the credit arms of PE and asset managers (Barings, Churchill, Muzinich, Marathon). *Tier 3:* small, regional and BDC-style lenders, where deal flow is less proprietary.

enter.label: How to enter
enter.md: Hired mainly from leveraged finance, DCM (debt capital markets), restructuring and credit research at banks, and from Big 4 transaction services; some firms hire analysts directly from undergraduate programmes (e.g., Ares and large platforms' analyst classes, check each firm's site). In Europe, internships at Tikehau or Muzinich in Milan, Paris and London are a way in. Certifications: CFA is respected for credit; the CAIA is a secondary signal for alternatives. Skills: credit analysis, loan documents, covenant logic, financial modelling. Common mistakes: treating credit like equity (upside) rather than downside protection; ignoring legal documents. Alternative routes: bank credit risk, rating agencies, restructuring and insolvency practice. Entry difficulty: 4/5.

downsides.label: Honest downsides and who it is NOT a good fit for
downsides.md: The asset class is in its first major test since scale; if defaults rise, the junior staff of weaker platforms are the first to be cut (headhunter: jobs down up to 25% in 2024). Upside is capped by the loan's interest rate, so pay depends on fees and scale. Not for you if you dislike legal documents, prefer fast-moving equity stories, or dislike the monitoring of problem loans.

roles.part: Part 3: The buy side
roles.title: Investment professional at an institutional allocator (pension, insurer, sovereign wealth fund, endowment, fund of funds)

what.label: What you actually do
what.md: Allocators manage large asset pools. Roles include asset allocation and portfolio construction, manager selection and monitoring (due diligence meetings with funds, performance and risk analysis, ESG and governance checks), co-investments and direct deals (at SWFs and large Canadian pensions), liability matching (pensions and insurers) and reporting to boards. Consultants and fund-of-funds analysts do the same for many clients. Deliverables: manager due-diligence reports, investment committee papers, allocation models, reports for trustees.

day.label: A typical day and week
day.md: Calls and meetings with fund managers, internal committee preparation, risk and performance reviews, writing papers. Cycles follow board and committee calendars. Direct teams at SWFs behave like PE teams on live deals.

hours.label: Hours, stress and lifestyle
hours.md: 40-50 hours; up to 55 during committee cycles or deals (practitioner estimate). Stress 2/5 (3 on direct investing teams). Hybrid is common (Cambridge Associates requires 12-16 office days a month for analysts, per listings). Travel: manager visits and conferences; larger SWFs have international offices.

profile.label: Human vs. quantitative profile
profile.md: People/communication: 3/5. Quantitative/technical: 3/5. You evaluate other people's decisions: you need judgment on people and process, solid statistics and writing.

pay.label: Compensation (approximate)
pay.md: Public-sector pay is lower than hedge funds and PE and published only in some places. CalPERS Investment Officer I: US$4,238-8,049 per month (about US$51-97k a year), Investment Officer II US$7,760-9,713 per month (about US$93-117k), a 5% differential for the CFA, incentives of 0-10% of salary, and a 3% pay reduction through the Personal Leave Program from July 2025 (CalPERS postings; annualised by me). CalPERS commissioned a March 2025 McLagan benchmark review (percentile tables not retrieved). Cambridge Associates (consultant) Investment Analyst Program: base US$80,000 (Boston, Dallas, Arlington) or US$88,000 (San Francisco), four-year programme, any major with GPA 3.3+, US work authorisation without sponsorship (listings via TheLadders, Class of January 2027). Canadian pensions publish senior pay in annual reports (not retrieved). GIC, Temasek, NBIM, ADIA, Mubadala, PIF: no reliable data found. UK and Italy: no reliable data found. Johnson Associates reporting does not cover allocators in the public material I found.

path.label: Career path
path.md: Analyst/associate (0-3 years), senior associate or investment officer (3-6), principal/portfolio manager/director (6-12), head of an asset class or CIO. Consultants: analyst (2-4 years), senior analyst, investment director/consultant.

exits.label: Exit opportunities
exits.md: After 2-3 years: PE/VC fund investor-relations or fund-of-funds roles, asset-manager distribution, private markets managers (as the "other side of the table"), MBA. After 7-10 years: CIO roles at endowments, family offices, insurers, or senior roles at managers; moving to a PE firm's fundraising team.

tiers.label: Tier list of employers
tiers.md: Tier groupings reflect industry consensus and practitioner perception, not objective fact. *Tier 1 (prestige, scale, direct investing):* NBIM, GIC, Temasek, ADIA, Mubadala, CPP Investments, Ontario Teachers', Yale and other large endowments. *Tier 2:* large public pensions and insurers (CalPERS, APG, PGGM, USS, GPIF, Allianz, AXA, Generali), and top consultants (Cambridge Associates, Mercer, WTW). *Tier 3:* smaller pension funds, regional foundations (Italy's Cassa Depositi e Prestiti, bank foundations, professional pension funds such as Cassa Forense or Enpam), and regional consultants, which offer stability and a narrower investment scope.

enter.label: How to enter
enter.md: SWFs run graduate programmes: NBIM's graduate programme lasts 12 months (nine on projects with the AI team, then three in a business area) for final-year students or graduates with up to two years' experience, in Oslo, London or New York; applications for the 2027 programme ran 1-15 August 2026 (NBIM). Temasek's Associate Programme in Singapore runs 20 months from 3 August 2026 to 31 March 2028; applications opened 2 March 2026 and closed 27 March 2026, with a video interview and a half-day case-study assessment (Temasek listing); summer 2027 internship information was due in July 2026. GIC's Professionals Programme takes final-year students from any discipline with less than a year of work experience on a rolling basis, and its 12-week internship targets penultimate-year students (GIC, via a mirror page; verify on the official site). PIF's Graduate Development Program is for Saudi nationals only (PIF). Japan's GPIF is expanding a small team (187 staff, Bloomberg, 11 August 2025). Gulf SWFs often prioritise nationals for graduate schemes (I found no eligibility page for ADIA or Mubadala graduate programmes; treat as unverified). For consultants, Cambridge Associates and Mercer hire graduates directly. CFA and CAIA are valued here; CFA is explicitly rewarded at CalPERS. Skills: statistics, portfolio theory, private markets knowledge, writing. Common mistakes: expecting the same pay as hedge funds; applying without a view on asset allocation. Alternative routes: asset-manager client roles, performance/risk teams, auditing of funds. Entry difficulty: 4/5 (very high at SWFs, moderate at consultants).

downsides.label: Honest downsides and who it is NOT a good fit for
downsides.md: Slower progression, public-sector pay, committee decision-making and political constraints; at SWFs, nationality and visa rules can restrict access; you rarely own the investment decision. Not for you if you want to be a stockpicker with a big bonus, or want to move fast.

roles.part: Part 3: The buy side
roles.title: Private banker / wealth manager

what.label: What you actually do
what.md: A private banker (relationship manager) is the single point of contact for wealthy clients: understand their goals, propose portfolios, advisory or discretionary mandates, lending (Lombard loans, mortgages), and coordinate specialists (tax, estate planning, family governance). Juniors work as assistants/analysts: prepare reviews, execute trades, KYC (know-your-customer) and AML (anti-money laundering) paperwork, and learn the client book. Real income depends on bringing in new money.

day.label: A typical day and week
day.md: Market review, client calls, portfolio reviews, documentation, client meetings or dinners; time on compliance. Business development (prospecting new clients) grows with seniority. Month-end reports.

hours.label: Hours, stress and lifestyle
hours.md: 45-55 hours plus client events (practitioner estimate). Stress 3/5, with spikes in market falls and under asset-gathering targets and compliance scrutiny. Travel depends on client geography (Swiss bankers cover clients abroad). Hybrid possible, but client contact is in-person.

profile.label: Human vs. quantitative profile
profile.md: People/communication: 5/5. Quantitative/technical: 2/5. Trust, discretion and sales skills dominate; you need enough finance to explain portfolios.

pay.label: Compensation (approximate)
pay.md: Italy (best data): Magstat (updated January 2026, via We Wealth): junior private bankers (under five years, no fully consolidated book) earn €50-68k gross a year in total, with variable pay up to 50% of fixed; senior bankers (10+ years) have fixed pay of €55-100k and total pay that can roughly double; top performers with ultra-high-net-worth portfolios exceed €500k. Another Magstat-based report puts junior fixed pay at €45-60k (Citywire). PageGroup (via We Wealth, December 2024): private banker €35-55k (under five years), €55-110k (5-10 years), above €110k (10+ years). Glassdoor (January 2026) averages about €68k in Italy and warns it underestimates variable pay. UK: entry private bankers about £50.4k (range £41,000-60,800, Salary.com) and Glassdoor average of about £73,900 (City Wealth, 2025 update; aggregator data). US: wirehouse trainees (Merrill, Morgan Stanley) are paid a salary for training, then a mix of salary and commissions; Payscale estimates about US$47k (modelled, 2026), older reporting says Merrill trainee pay was raised by US$10k in 2019 to about US$65k; the failure rate of rookie advisors was reported above 72% (Cerulli, older), though Merrill says about three-quarters of its roughly 2,400 trainees are on track (American Banker, undated). Switzerland: the only figure I found is a recruiter advertisement of CHF 200-300k for an experienced private banker with a book in Geneva or Zurich (Selby Jennings listing); entry pay: no reliable data found. Hong Kong, Singapore, Tokyo, Gulf: no reliable data found. Johnson projected wealth-management bonuses +8-10% for 2025 (AI-CIO).

path.label: Career path
path.md: Assistant/analyst (0-3 years; 12-24 months to exams and licences in Italy at Fideuram: 12 months assistant, 12 months specialist, 24 months partner stage), junior RM (3-6), RM/senior RM (6-12), team head or area manager (12+). In Italy, networks (reti) of financial advisers (consulenti) may work as self-employed agents; area managers can earn €160-400k (Citywire/Magstat).

exits.label: Exit opportunities
exits.md: After 2-3 years: another private bank, family office, asset management client roles, wealth tech. After 7-10 years: head of a desk or region, independent wealth manager (often taking clients), family office head, move to fund distribution.

tiers.label: Tier list of employers
tiers.md: Tier groupings reflect industry consensus and practitioner perception, not objective fact. *Tier 1 (global brands with large platforms):* UBS Global Wealth Management, Julius Baer, Pictet, Lombard Odier, J.P. Morgan Private Bank, Goldman Sachs Private Wealth, Morgan Stanley Wealth Management; in Italy Fideuram-Intesa Sanpaolo Private Banking, Mediobanca Private Banking. *Tier 2:* UniCredit Private Banking, Banca Generali, Azimut, Fineco, EFG, DBS and HSBC Private Banks in Asia, wirehouses outside the top. *Tier 3:* regional banks, independent wealth firms and multi-family offices (smaller platforms, entrepreneurial but fewer resources). In Italy, change at Mediobanca after its absorption into Monte dei Paschi: wealth management lost €1.1 billion in the final quarter of 2025 after banker exits, with 28 net departures from the distribution network in the half (Teleborsa, 9 February 2026; via project file).

enter.label: How to enter
enter.md: Business, economics, finance or law; languages and cultural fluency are major assets. Programmes: UBS and Julius Baer run graduate and trainee schemes; Fideuram's "Private Wealth Assistant" programme pairs young graduates with senior consultants and prepares them for professional registration exams (bluerating/We Wealth reporting); US wirehouses run advisor training programmes of 18 months to several years (Merrill reduced its to 18 months in 2021). Italian roles typically need the albo (financial adviser register) exam and IVASS (insurance) registration for advisers. Certifications: CFA helpful; in Switzerland, local private-banking and advisory certifications that vary by employer (not researched), and in the UK the CISI qualifications; US advisers need Series 7 and 66. Build: client-facing experience, language skills, a network, and a credible personal story. Common mistakes: expecting a salary regardless of new money; ignoring licensing requirements. Alternative routes: bank branch, financial planning, insurance, family business networks. Entry difficulty: 3/5 (higher at Swiss top-tier banks, where banks prefer experienced bankers with a client book).

downsides.label: Honest downsides and who it is NOT a good fit for
downsides.md: Income depends on winning and keeping clients; very high attrition in US wirehouse training; compliance and AML burdens; layoffs and consolidation after mergers (UBS-Credit Suisse). Not for you if you dislike sales or networking, or want purely analytical work.

roles.part: Part 4: Corporate finance, risk, quant and fintech
roles.title: FP&A / corporate finance analyst (to CFO track)

what.label: What you actually do
what.md: Build and maintain the annual budget and monthly/quarterly forecast; compare actuals to plan and write the "variance commentary" (why revenue, margin or cost differed); model pricing, headcount and capex scenarios; prepare management and board packs; support the monthly close with accounting. Tools: Excel (advanced), a planning system (Anaplan, Oracle EPM, SAP BPC, Adaptive), BI tools such as Power BI or Tableau, increasingly SQL and Python. Deliverables: forecast files, a business review deck, a one-page "bridge" explaining year-on-year profit.

day.label: A typical day and week
day.md: Early week, pull the latest sales and cost data and refresh the forecast; midweek, meet your business partner (for example the sales director) to challenge assumptions; Thursday-Friday, prepare commentary for the monthly review. Week 1 of a month is close-heavy (late evenings); the budget season (typically September-December for calendar-year companies) and quarter-end are the crunch periods. Between peaks, the rhythm is steady.

hours.label: Hours, stress and lifestyle
hours.md: Typical 42-50 hours per week; peaks of 55-65 at quarter-end, year-end or during a restructuring (practitioner consensus; not systematically surveyed). Stress: 3/5 (regular deadlines, steady pressure; 2 in quiet mature companies). Flexibility is among the best in finance; hybrid is normal at most large corporates. Travel is low (some site visits).

profile.label: Human vs. quantitative profile
profile.md: People/communication: 4/5. Quantitative/technical: 3/5. You need to translate numbers into a story for non-finance managers; the modelling is spreadsheet-level, not advanced mathematics.

pay.label: Compensation (approximate)
pay.md:
- US: Robert Half's listing for FP&A analyst shows about US$71k-88k base (2026 guide as shown in search snippet; the page itself did not display the table when I fetched it, so treat as unverified). BLS median for all financial and investment analysts US$101,350 (May 2024). Financial managers (controllers, FP&A heads, finance directors) US$161,700 median (BLS, May 2024; top 10% above US$239,200).
- UK: no reliable data found for FP&A analyst entry pay. Robert Half UK 2026: Finance Business Partner 25th/50th/75th percentile GBP 54,500 / 59,750 / 66,250 base (mid-career).
- Italy (Milan): aggregator estimates for controller roles: median about EUR 37k-43k, range EUR 30k-51k (Jooble, data to 29 July 2026; low-quality sample); France FP&A analyst EUR 55k-75k (Robert Half France, 2026, shown for comparison only).
- Senior (CFO): no reliable data found by region; listed-company CFO pay is disclosed in annual reports and varies enormously.

path.label: Career path
path.md: Analyst (0-3 years) -> Senior analyst/finance business partner (3-6) -> FP&A manager (5-9) -> Director of FP&A / divisional finance director (9-14) -> VP Finance / CFO (15+). Many CFOs come from FP&A, controllership or banking; a CPA/ACA/CIMA or MBA is common at the step to director in some markets (practitioner consensus). Rotational finance programmes at large corporates accelerate this.

exits.label: Exit opportunities
exits.md: After 2-3 years: another corporate (bigger brand or strategy role), FP&A at a tech company, MBA, a move into corp dev or consulting. After 7-10 years: head of FP&A, divisional CFO, private equity portfolio-company CFO, or investor relations. Moving to investment banking or PE is unusual from here.

tiers.label: Tier list of employers
tiers.md: Tier 1 (industry perception): global brand groups with structured finance programmes (large tech such as Microsoft and Google; consumer goods such as P&G, Unilever, Nestle; pharma; LVMH in luxury; Siemens in industrials). Tier 2: large listed domestic groups (in Italy for example Eni, Enel, Stellantis, Generali on the finance side, Luxottica/EssilorLuxottica, Ferrero; in the UK FTSE 100 firms; in the US Fortune 500). Tier 3: mid-sized and family-owned companies, private-equity-backed companies (faster growth, thinner support), and smaller listed companies. Tier groupings reflect industry consensus and practitioner perception, not objective fact. Differences: Tier 1 gives structure, training, rotations and brand value; Tier 3 gives earlier responsibility.

enter.label: How to enter
enter.md: Degrees: finance, accounting, economics, business, engineering with strong Excel; a few arrive from audit (Big Four) after qualifying. Programmes: corporate graduate/rotational finance programmes (applications typically open in autumn and close between October and January for September starts in the UK and Europe; US programmes recruit September-November for summer internships and conversion). Certifications: CPA (US), ACA/ACCA/CIMA (UK), CMA (US management accounting) help for controller track; CFA is not needed. Skills: advanced Excel, financial statements, a planning tool, SQL/Power BI, concise communication. Interview formats: case or modelling exercise, "walk me through a variance", behavioural stories; no probability puzzles. Common mistakes: presenting numbers without a recommendation; underestimating accounting knowledge. Alternative routes: Big Four audit then move in-house (the most common non-target route), accounting graduate roles, an internal move from operations or sales. Entry difficulty: 2/5.

downsides.label: Honest downsides and who it is NOT a good fit for
downsides.md: Pay growth is slower than in banking and the career is tied to one company's fortunes; the work can feel repetitive (forecast cycles) and "cost centre" status limits influence; budget season can be bureaucratic. Not a good fit for people who want high pay, deal excitement or a purely technical/quant role. Early-career AI/automation of reporting is reducing pure number-crunching, pushing roles towards interpretation.

roles.part: Part 4: Corporate finance, risk, quant and fintech
roles.title: Corporate treasury analyst

what.label: What you actually do
what.md: Forecast daily and weekly cash positions across bank accounts and entities; decide where surplus cash is invested and where shortfalls are funded; execute or monitor FX and interest-rate hedges against exposures reported by the business; maintain bank relationships and facility documentation; administer bank accounts and payment systems (treasury management systems such as Kyriba, SAP Treasury, Coupa); handle covenant compliance and support bond or loan issuance; increasingly work on payments, working-capital finance and cash-pooling structures.

day.label: A typical day and week
day.md: Morning, check the previous day's cash balances and forecast against the treasury management system; midday, check hedging positions and discuss a quote with a bank FX dealer; afternoon, update the 13-week cash forecast and answer subsidiaries' questions. Weekly: liquidity report to the CFO. Periodic: a bond issue or refinancing, which means weeks of documentation with banks and lawyers.

hours.label: Hours, stress and lifestyle
hours.md: Typical 40-48 hours; peaks of 50-60 around a financing or a market shock (practitioner consensus). Stress: 3/5 (a missed payment or breached covenant is serious, but most days are routine). Hybrid common; travel modest (bank meetings, subsidiaries). Treasury teams are small, so a junior gets exposure quickly.

profile.label: Human vs. quantitative profile
profile.md: People/communication: 3/5. Quantitative/technical: 3/5. Banks and business units are your counterparties, but the work is mostly systems and spreadsheets.

pay.label: Compensation (approximate)
pay.md:
- US: Treasury Analyst I median about US$68.8k-70.7k (Salary.com, 2024, aggregator; two pages disagree). AFP's 2025 compensation survey reports average base pay rise of 3.9% for 2024, but the detailed title tables are paywalled (AFP press release).
- UK: no reliable data found for treasury analyst in London.
- Italy: no reliable data found.
- Asia (comparison): Singapore treasury analyst S$80k-100k gross base, median S$90k; Treasury Manager S$125k-180k, Treasury Director S$215k-300k (Robert Half Singapore 2026 guide, excludes bonus and CPF); Hong Kong treasury analyst HK$290k-420k, median HK$360k (Robert Half HK 2026 guide, per search snippet).

path.label: Career path
path.md: Treasury analyst (0-3 years) -> Senior analyst / assistant treasury manager (3-6) -> Treasury manager (6-10) -> Head of treasury / group treasurer (10-15) -> CFO or regional finance director. Small field; moves between companies are the main route to promotion.

exits.label: Exit opportunities
exits.md: After 2-3 years: bank roles (corporate banking, transaction banking, FX/rates sales), FP&A, treasury at a bigger company, or consulting. After 7-10 years: group treasurer, CFO of a mid-sized company, or treasury advisory/technology (Kyriba, SAP, banks' corporate-client coverage).

tiers.label: Tier list of employers
tiers.md: Tier 1: global multinationals and large tech/pharma treasuries with in-house FX trading and capital-markets activity (e.g. Apple, Microsoft, Shell, Nestle, Unilever). Tier 2: large national groups and utilities/industrials. Tier 3: small and mid-cap companies where treasury is one or two people. Banks' transaction-banking and corporate-sales teams are the adjacent route. Tier groupings reflect industry consensus and practitioner perception, not objective fact. Tier 1 treasuries do more complex hedging and issuance and offer bigger teams; Tier 3 gives breadth.

enter.label: How to enter
enter.md: Finance, accounting, economics or business degrees; treasury analyst roles are rarely open to complete beginners, so common routes are corporate graduate finance programmes with a treasury rotation, bank transaction-banking graduate schemes, or an audit/accounting start. Certifications: CTP (AFP, US; exam of 170 questions, normally needs about two years of qualifying full-time work, with a student route to the CTPA title) and the ACT (Association of Corporate Treasurers, UK) ladder from Certificate in Treasury Fundamentals through Certificate in Treasury (about 250 study hours) to Diploma, per AFP and ACT. They help a career but are not required to enter; I found no independent salary-premium data. Skills: cash-flow forecasting, FX forwards and swaps basics, Excel, treasury systems, basic banking knowledge. Interviews: technical questions on hedging a currency exposure, working capital, and the bond/loan market. Alternative routes: payments/operations roles at a bank or a fintech; accounts-payable/cash-management roles. Entry difficulty: 3/5 (few roles, but little competition from the quant crowd).

downsides.label: Honest downsides and who it is NOT a good fit for
downsides.md: Few graduate openings and small teams, so promotion depends on who leaves; low bonuses; the market feel of banking is absent. Not suited to those wanting trading adrenaline, large bonuses or a broad choice of employers.

roles.part: Part 4: Corporate finance, risk, quant and fintech
roles.title: Corporate development (in-house M&A)

what.label: What you actually do
what.md: Screen and track acquisition targets and partnerships; build valuation models (DCF, comparables, precedent transactions) and merger models; prepare investment-committee papers for the CEO/board; run due diligence with legal, tax and operational teams and outside advisers; coordinate with investment banks on sell-side and buy-side processes; after closing, support the integration. Also does divestments and strategy projects. Tools: Excel/PowerPoint, data providers (CapIQ, FactSet, PitchBook).

day.label: A typical day and week
day.md: Quiet periods: market mapping, updating target lists, discussing strategy with business-unit heads. Active deal: daily calls with advisers and diligence teams, evenings on models and board materials, weekends before signing. Typically one to three live deals a year per person at a large corporate.

hours.label: Hours, stress and lifestyle
hours.md: Typical 45-55 hours; peaks of 65-80 in live deals (practitioner consensus). Stress: 3/5 on average, 4 during live deals. Considerably more flexible than banking. Travel for due diligence and site visits, higher in global groups.

profile.label: Human vs. quantitative profile
profile.md: People/communication: 4/5. Quantitative/technical: 3/5. Success depends on influence with executives and operating managers more than model complexity.

pay.label: Compensation (approximate)
pay.md:
- US: corp dev associate posting (Houston, PE-backed services company, 2025): base US$100k-120k, total US$150k-175k+ (expired posting, single data point). Aggregator averages (ZipRecruiter via Wallstreetmojo, Aug 2026): M&A analyst about US$92k, associate about US$175k (low-quality, unverified definitions).
- UK: no reliable data found.
- Italy: no reliable data found.
- France (comparison): analyst 0-3 years base EUR 45k-55k, total EUR 60k-75k; associate base EUR 50k-80k (Paris 2025-26 market summary via search).
- Senior: no reliable data found; typical ladder runs to Director/Head of Corporate Development and CFO.

path.label: Career path
path.md: Rarely a first job. Typical: 2-4 years in investment banking, transaction services (Big Four), consulting or PE -> corp dev analyst/associate -> manager (2-4 years) -> director/VP -> head of corp dev (10+ years) -> CFO/strategy head/GM. Corp dev ladders are less standardised than banking.

exits.label: Exit opportunities
exits.md: After 2-3 years: another corporate, PE or growth-equity roles (less common than from banking), strategy consulting, MBA. After 7-10 years: head of corp dev, CFO, general management, or business-unit head.

tiers.label: Tier list of employers
tiers.md: Tier 1: big tech and acquisitive large caps with dedicated, deal-active teams (e.g. Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, Salesforce; health and pharma acquirers such as Roche, Novartis, Pfizer; industrial consolidators). Tier 2: other large listed corporates and conglomerates. Tier 3: PE-backed platform companies (more deals, leaner support) and mid-caps with occasional deals. Tier groupings reflect industry consensus and practitioner perception, not objective fact. Tier 1 teams are small, selective and hire almost only experienced bankers; Tier 3 will take less-credentialed hires and offer bigger responsibility.

enter.label: How to enter
enter.md: Backgrounds: finance, economics, accounting, engineering or science (for industry-specific groups) combined with two to four years of banking, transaction services, consulting or PE. Few direct graduate programmes; a handful of large acquirers run finance rotations that include corp dev. Certifications: CFA is a modest plus; none required. Skills: valuation, merger modelling, memo writing, structured interviews with modelling tests. Recruiting calendar: lateral hiring all year; bankers move after the bonus season (March-June). Common mistakes: applying straight from university; expecting banker-style analytics without the operating story. Alternative routes: internal transfer from FP&A or strategy in an acquisitive company; Big Four transaction services. Entry difficulty: 4/5 (small teams; competes with bankers).

downsides.label: Honest downsides and who it is NOT a good fit for
downsides.md: Deals come in waves and may stop in a downturn (teams are cut); few roles; the work depends on the CEO's appetite; compensation below banking. Not for people who want a graduate job directly or who dislike politics and internal persuasion.

roles.part: Part 4: Corporate finance, risk, quant and fintech
roles.title: Risk management (market, credit, operational, liquidity) at banks, insurers and asset managers

what.label: What you actually do
what.md: Examples by sub-area. *Market risk analyst:* produce the daily VaR and sensitivity report for a desk, investigate a breach, explain risk to traders, run stress scenarios. *Credit risk analyst / underwriter (commercial bank):* analyse a borrower's accounts, build a credit memo, set a rating and limit, monitor covenants. *Operational risk:* run risk-and-control self-assessments, review incidents and track remediation. *Liquidity/ALM:* project cash flows and run liquidity-coverage and interest-rate-risk reports. *Model risk/validation:* review model documentation, replicate and test models (see 3.6). *Regulatory reporting and stress-test teams:* populate templates for the Fed, EBA and PRA. Tools: Excel, SQL, Python/R, SAS, risk engines (Murex, Calypso, internal systems), Tableau/Power BI.

day.label: A typical day and week
day.md: Market risk: early-morning review of the overnight P&L and risk numbers before the desk opens, explain moves, escalate limit breaches, meetings with desk heads; afternoon on methodology or reporting projects. Credit: reading financial statements, writing memos, meeting relationship managers, quarterly reviews. Stress-test season (US: Q1-Q2; EU: when the EBA exercise runs) brings weeks of intense reporting and reconciliation.

hours.label: Hours, stress and lifestyle
hours.md: Typical 42-50 hours; peaks of 55-65 (stress tests, regulatory deadlines, market events) (practitioner consensus). Stress: 3/5 (market risk on volatile days: 4). Hybrid works widely; travel low. Hours in risk are generally more predictable than in front-office roles.

profile.label: Human vs. quantitative profile
profile.md: People/communication: 3/5. Quantitative/technical: 3/5 (4 in market risk and model-heavy teams, 2-3 in operational and credit underwriting). You must argue with powerful front-office people politely and with evidence.

pay.label: Compensation (approximate)
pay.md:
- US: BLS median for financial risk specialists about US$106,000 (OOH comparison table, 2024 data; all experience levels, not graduate). Entry range by employer: no reliable data found.
- UK (London base salary, FD Capital recruiter placements to March 2026): operational risk analyst (2-5 yrs) GBP 42k-65k; credit risk analyst (2-5 yrs) GBP 45k-68k; operational risk manager (5-10 yrs) GBP 70k-105k; market risk manager (5-9 yrs) GBP 80k-120k; enterprise risk manager (8-14 yrs) GBP 95k-140k; CRO GBP 130k-250k+ (GBP 200k-350k+ total package at large banks and insurers). Bonuses 15-30% of base at larger FCA-regulated firms (FD Capital, Q1 2026).
- Italy: junior risk specialist EUR 28k-35k RAL, mid-level (3-7 yrs) EUR 38k-50k, senior (8+) EUR 55k-80k (Masterin, undated guide; low-medium reliability).
- Asia: no reliable data found on a like-for-like basis.

path.label: Career path
path.md: Analyst (0-3) -> Associate/senior analyst (3-6) -> VP/risk manager (6-10) -> Director / head of a risk area (10-15) -> Chief Risk Officer or deputy (15+). Specialists move between banks and regulators as the regulatory cycle changes.

exits.label: Exit opportunities
exits.md: After 2-3 years: front-office roles are possible but hard (market risk to trading support/structuring), other risk functions, regulators, consulting (risk advisory), fintech risk teams. After 7-10 years: head of risk at a smaller bank, insurer or asset manager, regulator, or business-embedded risk roles.

tiers.label: Tier list of employers
tiers.md: Tier 1 (industry perception): bulge-bracket and large global banks' second-line risk and the largest asset managers/insurers, plus risk functions at the top hedge funds, with the strongest technical teams and desk proximity (JPMorgan, Goldman Sachs, Morgan Stanley, Citi, BlackRock; in Europe Deutsche Bank, BNP Paribas, Barclays, UBS, HSBC). Tier 2: other universal banks and large insurers (UniCredit, Intesa Sanpaolo, Generali, Allianz, AXA). Tier 3: smaller banks, regional lenders, specialist lenders, fund administrators. Regulators (ECB, Bank of England, Fed, PRA, Banca d'Italia) are a separate prestigious track. Tier groupings reflect industry consensus and practitioner perception, not objective fact. Tier 1 offers desk proximity, more modelling and higher pay; Tier 3 offers broader responsibility.

enter.label: How to enter
enter.md: Degrees: finance, economics, mathematics, statistics, engineering, physics; credit analysis also takes accounting graduates. Graduate programmes in risk at the larger banks (applications typically open in September-October and close between November and January for summer-after-graduation starts; early applications recommended); internships are a conversion route. Certifications: FRM (GARP) is the main risk credential: two exam parts (windows in May, August and November), a one-time US$400 enrolment fee and about US$600-900 per part depending on timing (third-party prep sites; check GARP), pass rates reported around 44-58% for Part 1 and 50-63% for Part 2 over recent years (300Hours, third party), and two years of relevant work for the designation (GARP). PRM (PRMIA) is an alternative; CFA is a modest plus for credit; CQF for quantitative market risk. They help in risk but rarely decide the first hire. Skills: SQL, Python, statistics, understanding of derivatives and financial statements. Interviews: technical (VaR, duration, credit ratios), market awareness, case or modelling test. Common mistakes: not following markets; treating risk as a "backup" for a failed trading application (interviewers hear it). Alternative routes: audit/Big Four financial services risk, operations or credit-analyst entry at a bank, and internal transfers from middle office. Entry difficulty: 3/5 (2 for credit/operational risk, 4 for quantitative market-risk at top banks).

downsides.label: Honest downsides and who it is NOT a good fit for
downsides.md: Seen as a cost centre and a "No" function; limited bonuses; regulation-driven projects can be paperwork-heavy; headcount has shrunk during bank cost cuts and offshoring (Barclay Simpson, 2026). Not suited to those who want to take risk and own P&L, or who dislike being the person who stops a deal.
