roles.part: Part 1: Building AI systems
roles.title: Computer vision / robotics / edge AI engineer

what.label: What you actually do
what.md: You build models and software that interpret and act on sensor data. Tasks include training detection, segmentation or tracking models (for cars, factory defects, tumours on scans), building data collection and labelling pipelines, compressing models to run on small chips (quantisation, pruning, TensorRT/ONNX conversion), writing real-time code in C++ and Python, calibrating cameras and lidar, running simulation, and, in robotics, integrating perception with planning and control (ROS, learned policies, imitation or reinforcement learning). Deliverables: a model that hits, say, 99.5% recall on defect detection at 30 frames per second on a specific device, plus the test evidence safety and quality teams require.

day.label: A typical day and week
day.md: Look at failure cases from the last test drive or production line; retrain or adjust the model; profile latency on target hardware; code review (often C++); sync with hardware, mechanical or safety engineers. Weekly: a field or lab test session (a test track, a factory floor, a robot cell), a data-labelling quality review, a safety-case or validation meeting. You spend more time with physical hardware, test benches and labelling vendors than in a pure software role.

hours.label: Hours, stress and lifestyle
hours.md: 40-50 hours typical; 55-60 near field tests, demos or product launches (practitioner consensus). Stress 3/5, higher (4/5) in safety-critical automotive, medical and defence settings or in robotics startups racing to demos. Mostly in-person or hybrid because hardware is involved; travel to test sites is common; remote work is harder than in pure software.

profile.label: Human vs. quantitative profile
profile.md: People/communication: 3/5. Quantitative/technical: 5/5. You work with hardware, safety and operations teams, but the core is mathematics (geometry, probability), programming and engineering judgement about the physical world.

pay.label: Compensation (approximate)
pay.md: No dedicated Levels.fyi or BLS figure for computer vision or robotics was retrievable (the specific pages returned errors), so I use the ML engineer proxy and flag the gap. Levels.fyi, 9 Oct 2026, ML engineer: US median US$280K; Meta E3 US$187K; NVIDIA IC1 US$205K; Google L3 US$208K; these are internet and chip companies, and pay at automotive, industrial and medical-device firms is generally lower (my expectation based on practitioner consensus; no dataset found). UK: ML engineer median GBP 103,596 (Levels.fyi) or GBP 67,500 (ITJobsWatch ads); computer vision specific: no reliable data found. Italy: Levels.fyi ML engineer median EUR 32,471; automotive/industrial entry likely at the lower end of that (unverified). Germany ML engineer median EUR 88,465; Zurich CHF 152,282; France EUR 75,949; Singapore S$141,805. Robotics startups often pay lower base and more equity.

path.label: Career path
path.md: Junior perception/CV engineer (0-2) -> CV or robotics engineer (2-4) -> Senior (4-7) -> Staff/principal, tech lead, or perception manager (7-12). Master's graduates often enter at the same level as bachelor's with 1-2 years' experience; PhDs enter at a higher level in research-heavy teams.

exits.label: Exit opportunities
exits.md: After 2-3 years: general ML engineer, embedded/robotics software, autonomy and simulation, drone/defence tech, medical-imaging AI. After 7-10 years: perception lead, head of autonomy/robotics, CTO at a robotics or vision startup, technical roles in industrial AI.

tiers.label: Tier list of employers
tiers.md: Tier 1: autonomy and physical-AI leaders (Waymo, Tesla Autopilot, NVIDIA robotics/Drive, Wayve in London, Mobileye, Boston Dynamics, well-funded humanoid and robot-foundation-model startups, Google DeepMind robotics) and defence-tech (Anduril, Skydio). Tier 2: large automotive and industrial companies' AI/autonomy groups (BMW, Mercedes, Bosch, Siemens, ABB, Siemens Healthineers, GE HealthCare, Philips), medical-imaging startups, drone makers. Tier 3: system integrators and consultancies, smaller industrial suppliers, inspection and vision-systems vendors (in Italy, for example, groups such as Leonardo, Comau or university/IIT-linked labs are examples I did not verify as hiring now). Tier groupings reflect industry consensus and practitioner perception, not objective fact. Tier 1 offers frontier problems and big budgets with intense schedules; Tier 3 offers stability and domain knowledge with slower tools and lower pay.

enter.label: How to enter
enter.md: *Degrees and backgrounds.* Computer science, electrical/electronic, mechatronics, robotics, physics, maths or aerospace. A master's is common in Europe, and many perception roles at serious teams prefer an MSc or PhD with a computer vision thesis; strong bachelor's graduates enter via internships. *Programs.* NVIDIA internships and New College Grad (the program lists "edge computing" and "autonomous machines" as areas), carmaker graduate programmes, EU research projects, Anthropic Fellows are not relevant here. Hiring calendar: carmakers and industrials recruit on a university cycle (autumn), startups year-round. *Interviews.* Coding (often C++), ML/vision fundamentals (convolutions, transformers for vision, detection metrics), geometry questions, a project deep-dive, sometimes a take-home on a dataset. *Certifications.* Mostly irrelevant; NVIDIA Deep Learning Institute courses and Jetson projects are mild positives. *Portfolio.* A project on a real device (Jetson, Raspberry Pi with accelerator, a small robot or drone), participation in competitions (Kaggle vision, robotics challenges, F1TENTH, RoboCup, formula-student driverless teams), a model deployed with measured latency and accuracy, open-source contributions (OpenCV, ROS, PyTorch). *Common mistakes:* working only on benchmark datasets and never on messy real data or hardware; ignoring C++ and real-time constraints; underestimating data collection and labelling. *Alternative routes:* embedded or robotics software engineers adding ML; ML engineers moving to a vision team; mechatronics/electrical engineers learning ML. Entry difficulty: 4/5

downsides.label: Honest downsides and who it is NOT a good fit for
downsides.md: Smaller job market than general ML; relevant employers cluster in a few cities (Bay Area, Munich/Stuttgart, London, Zurich, Tokyo, Shenzhen), so in Italy the options are fewer; safety certification and testing slow progress; the physical world (weather, hardware faults) makes failures hard to reproduce. Many robotics and self-driving ventures have burned cash for years, so job security at startups is weak. Not a fit if you want pure remote software work, avoid C++ and hardware, or dislike slow, validation-heavy engineering.

roles.part: Part 1: Building AI systems
roles.title: AI data specialist / AI trainer / annotation and human-feedback work

what.label: What you actually do
what.md: You produce and judge the data models learn from. The work ranges from drawing boxes on images and transcribing audio (micro-tasks), to ranking pairs of model answers (RLHF: reinforcement learning from human feedback, where human preferences steer the model), writing ideal responses, grading chain-of-thought reasoning, red-teaming (trying to make a model fail), and, at the expert end, writing hard problems in medicine, law, finance, coding or mathematics that models should be tested on. Salaried versions exist inside labs and data vendors: data operations, quality assurance, data-pipeline and annotation-tooling roles. The Scale AI job board in October 2026 shows data-adjacent salaried roles such as data acquisition lead (frontier environments), data engineers and field engineers, alongside the "Human Frontier Collective" programme for advanced contributors.

day.label: A typical day and week
day.md: Contractors pick tasks from a platform queue, follow a long guideline document, complete assignments in a browser tool, and are scored on quality; many work on irregular schedules in the evenings. Salaried staff manage vendor quality, write guidelines, audit samples, build tooling and report accuracy metrics. A week may involve a sudden project start or a sudden stop when a client pauses (see below).

hours.label: Hours, stress and lifestyle
hours.md: Contractors set their own hours, often 10-40 per week, with pressure from task quality scores and uncertain volume; salaried data-ops staff typically 40-50 hours. Stress 2/5 for task work in routine conditions but income uncertainty and account-deactivation risk are real stressors; 3/5 for managers under project deadlines. Fully remote for contractors; salaried roles at labs are hybrid or office-based.

profile.label: Human vs. quantitative profile
profile.md: People/communication: 2/5 for individual contributors (mostly solo, written guidelines), 4/5 for vendor/quality managers. Quantitative/technical: 2/5 for general annotation; 3-4/5 for coding, maths or domain-expert tasks. The value is in domain judgement and care, not in programming.

pay.label: Compensation (approximate)
pay.md: This is the least regulated segment. DataAnnotation's own site (accessed Oct 2026) advertises US$25-50 per hour for generalists, US$40-125+ for professional/STEM roles (finance, law, medicine, maths) and US$40-150+ for coding, ML and data-science tasks, language specialists US$25-40; these are advertised ranges, pay is tied to output quality, there is no commitment, and testimonials on the page are self-reported and unverified. Reports about Mercor (Wikipedia citing The Verge, New York Magazine and Wired) mention a "stressful work environment" and "declining pay" among contractors. Micro-task platforms such as Remotasks have historically paid far less (the Scale AI Wikipedia page notes critics saying pay can be late or very low); I found no reliable per-hour figure for those. Salaried data-operations staff at US data vendors and labs: Levels.fyi lists Scale AI software engineer entry total of US$227K but that is engineering pay, not annotation. For Italy, Europe, Asia and the Gulf: no reliable data found; in lower-income countries micro-task pay is much lower and lawfulness of contractor status varies.

path.label: Career path
path.md: Annotator / AI trainer (contract) -> senior or expert reviewer / quality lead -> project manager, data operations specialist or guideline writer -> data-quality manager or evaluation lead at a lab or vendor. For people with a technical background, movement into evaluation engineering, ML data engineering or tooling is a realistic step; from pure micro-task work it is rare.

exits.label: Exit opportunities
exits.md: After 2-3 years: data operations or quality roles, evaluation specialist, content/domain jobs, a return to one's original profession (many contractors are doctors, lawyers or academics doing this part-time). After 7-10 years: head of data operations at a vendor, data-quality or evaluation lead, product roles in data platforms, or entry to an engineering path if technical skills were developed meanwhile. Honest note: the base of the pyramid is shrinking as platforms move from volume to experts only, so long-term paths from entry-level labelling are narrow.

tiers.label: Tier list of employers
tiers.md:
Tier 1: data teams inside frontier labs and the specialist expert-data vendors with the biggest clients (Scale AI, Surge AI, Mercor), which pay best for experts. Tier 2: Turing, Invisible, Handshake-type expert marketplaces, enterprise data-services arms (TELUS Digital, Appen), and corporate data teams. Tier 3: crowd micro-task platforms and outsourced annotation firms in Southeast Asia, Africa and South Asia (Remotasks, Toloka-type marketplaces). Tier groupings reflect industry consensus and practitioner perception, not objective fact. Tier 1 pays more per hour for scarce expertise but is concentrated in a few clients; Tier 3 pays least and is most precarious.

Concrete context on precarity (all from the Wikipedia pages on these firms, secondary): Scale AI faced lawsuits in December 2024 and January 2025 over wage theft, worker misclassification and psychological harm from disturbing content, and Meta bought a 49% non-voting stake for about US$14.8 billion in June 2025. Surge AI (DataAnnotation) reportedly worked with about 1 million annotators in 2025, had revenue reported at US$1.2 billion in 2024 with about 110 employees, and faced a May 2025 class action alleging misclassification of annotators; the platform has drawn criticism for unexplained account cancellations. Mercor reportedly managed 30,000 contractors in October 2025 at a US$10 billion valuation, and a reported March 2026 supply-chain data breach led to lawsuits and a temporary work pause by major clients such as Meta. The takeaway for a student: the industry's headline revenues are large; the people doing the work are mostly independent contractors without benefits or guaranteed hours.

enter.label: How to enter
enter.md: *Degrees and backgrounds.* No fixed degree; platforms screen with qualification tests, and expert tracks want a degree or professional credentials in the subject (law, medicine, finance, maths, coding). Languages other than English are in demand. *Programs.* No graduate schemes; sign up to platforms, pass assessments, and expect a waiting list or irregular projects. Internal data-ops roles at labs and vendors are advertised on their career pages. *Hiring calendar.* Continuous; project-driven bursts. *Interviews.* Skills tests, writing and reasoning tests; for salaried roles, structured interviews and a quality-audit exercise. *Certifications.* Not relevant. *Skills and portfolio.* Precision, reading long guidelines, domain expertise, strong writing; for the career-building route, learn Python and basic data analysis, spreadsheets/SQL and evaluation concepts, and document any quality-assurance or tooling work. *Common mistakes:* treating it as stable income; accepting unclear classification or unpaid training time; ignoring tax and legal status as a contractor; assuming the work leads automatically to an AI engineering job (it usually does not). *Alternative routes:* professionals and graduate students use it as a side income; people with technical skills move into evaluation or data engineering. Entry difficulty: 2/5 for contract task work (platform screening rejects many, but volume is high); 4/5 for salaried data-operations, evaluation or tooling roles at top labs.

downsides.label: Honest downsides and who it is NOT a good fit for
downsides.md: Pay can fall without notice, work can vanish when a client pauses, accounts can be deactivated, and contractors often lack benefits, a job title or career ladder. Content can be disturbing (the Scale lawsuits cite psychological harm). It may build little transferable experience unless you actively add technical skills. Not a fit as a primary career if you need predictable income, health coverage or progression; fine as a short-term, flexible bridge or side income for someone who understands the trade-offs.

roles.part: Part 2: Research, frontier and governance roles
roles.title: AI research scientist (industry and academia)

what.label: What you actually do
what.md: You pick a research question (for example, how to make a model reason more reliably over long tasks), design experiments, run them on clusters, analyse results, and turn them into methods that go into the next model or into papers. Typical tools: PyTorch or JAX, internal training stacks, experiment trackers, Slurm or Kubernetes clusters. Deliverables: internal write-ups, ablation studies (removing components to see what matters), code that ships into training runs, and for academic and some industry roles, papers at NeurIPS, ICML, ICLR or ACL. Postings differ by subfield: Anthropic's interpretability scientist role is about reverse-engineering algorithms inside models; a Databricks principal scientist role is about scaling; Scale AI's research scientists cover post-training, evaluations and agents; OpenAI's researcher titles span alignment, safety training, reasoning and multimodal work. Academic scientists add grant writing, teaching and supervising PhD students.

day.label: A typical day and week
day.md: Industry: morning reading experiment results and dashboards from overnight runs; a few hours of coding or analysis; a team research meeting; a call with an engineer about a training bug; writing notes. A week often includes a research review where you present, plus chat-heavy collaboration on shared training runs. Academia: split between supervising students, writing papers and grants, teaching and committees; much less access to compute. Hours below are my estimates.

hours.label: Hours, stress and lifestyle
hours.md: Typical 45-55 hours a week at frontier labs, peaks of 60-80 around model releases and conference deadlines (estimate; no survey exists). Stress 3-4/5: no client deadlines but competitive pressure, release timelines and a publish-or-be-scooped dynamic. Academia: 45-60 hours, stress 3/5 (grant and tenure pressure). Most frontier-research postings I read name an office city (San Francisco, London, New York, Seattle, Zurich, Paris, Palo Alto); Anthropic's say staff should be in the office at least 25% of the time. Remote work is rare for frontier research. Travel: conferences.

profile.label: Human vs. quantitative profile
profile.md: People/communication: 2/5. Quantitative/technical: 5/5. You mostly work with a small team and communicate through write-ups and code review; the core of the job is mathematics, statistics and programming.

pay.label: Compensation (approximate)
pay.md:
- US, industry, total compensation including stock (Levels.fyi, 9 October 2026, self-reported): research scientist median across companies US$305,000 (25th percentile $180,000; 75th $403,000; 90th $520,000). By company: Google median $472,000 (L3 $246,000 to L6 $729,000); Meta median $482,000 (E3 $233,000 to E6 $656,000; 584 submissions); Microsoft median $282,000 (176 submissions); OpenAI median $800,000 (only 16 submissions; mostly stock); Anthropic software engineers $367,000 at entry to $1.13 million at staff level. So entry for a PhD graduate at big tech is roughly $190,000-$430,000 total; about five years in, $430,000-$520,000; senior $650,000+. Equity at private companies is paper value.
- Employer postings, US base salary ranges (October 2026; levels differ, so do not read them as a ranking): OpenAI Research Scientist/Engineer (San Francisco) $250,000-$445,000 and named researcher roles (interpretability, safety training, multimodal safety) $380,000-$500,000; Anthropic Research Scientist, Interpretability $350,000-$850,000; xAI "Member of Technical Staff" $180,000-$440,000, up to $600,000 for post-training (the pay text names the company SpaceXAI; equity extra); Databricks Principal Research Scientist, Scaling $280,000-$350,000; Scale AI ML Research Scientist $165,600-$207,000, senior/staff agents roles $302,400-$378,000; Google DeepMind Research Scientist (US) $174,000-$252,000 and Frontier AI Research Scientist $147,000-$211,000 (mirrors of 2026 postings); Meta Superintelligence Labs AI Research Scientist $122,000-$181,000, technical-leadership role $219,000-$301,000 (mirrors, May 2026). Cohere prints one band, CA$250,000-535,000, for Member of Technical Staff roles in London, Paris, Toronto and San Francisco (about US$175,000-$375,000 at roughly US$0.70 per C$, my assumption).
- Mega-offers: 2025 press reports said Meta offered some researchers packages worth $1 million to $100 million to join Meta Superintelligence Labs (as summarised on Wikipedia, read October 2026). A signal about a handful of people, not a benchmark.
- UK (Levels.fyi, 9 October 2026): research scientist median GBP 116,501 total (25th GBP 50,100; 75th GBP 165,000; 90th GBP 245,000); the wide spread shows non-lab employers pay far less than lab postings. Lab postings in London: Anthropic alignment GBP 260,000-370,000 base, Cohere CA$250,000-535,000 (see above). The UK AI Security Institute pays a total of GBP 65,000-145,000 including a technical allowance (see 3.3).
- Switzerland (Levels.fyi, 9 October 2026): research scientist median CHF 119,153 (25th CHF 74,500; 75th CHF 220,000; 90th CHF 264,000).
- Italy: no Italian frontier-lab research roles found. Software engineer median EUR 39,258 total (Levels.fyi, 9 October 2026, 384 submissions; 90th percentile EUR 65,600). Public research: PhD scholarship about EUR 18,433 a year gross at Brescia for 2026/27 and a Bocconi PhD fellowship of EUR 27,000 in year 1 and EUR 23,000 in years 2-4 (both via the project's earlier research file). Postdoc and tenure-track pay in Italy: no reliable data found.
- Asia and Gulf (Levels.fyi, 9 October 2026, self-reported, small samples): Singapore research scientist median SGD 90,299 total (25th SGD 74,200; 90th SGD 150,000); Japan research scientist median JPY 10.46 million (percentiles look inconsistent, so treat loosely); Abu Dhabi G42 research scientist median AED 429,653 (range AED 396,000-700,000+, tax-free in the UAE, sample size not stated); Technology Innovation Institute (TII, Abu Dhabi) software engineer median US$121,154. MBZUAI postings promise "competitive tax-free" pay with housing and flights but print no figure; Sakana AI lists Tokyo research roles with no pay. Hong Kong: no reliable data found.
- Academia elsewhere: UKRI minimum PhD stipend GBP 21,805 from 1 October 2026 (London GBP 23,805); Swiss SNSF floor about CHF 50,000 (both via the project's earlier research file, which read the primary pages on 2 October 2026). US academic pay: no reliable data found.

path.label: Career path
path.md: Typical (industry): PhD (4-6 years) -> research scientist / member of technical staff (years 0-3) -> senior (years 3-7) -> staff/principal or research lead (years 7-12) -> director of a research area. Lab titles vary ("Member of Technical Staff" at several labs). Academic: PhD -> postdoc (2-4 years; one to three postings) -> assistant professor (tenure track, 5-7 years to tenure) -> associate/full professor. In Italy: dottorato -> assegno di ricerca / RTD-A -> RTD-B -> associate professor through national qualification (abilitazione); the path is long and slow (general knowledge, unverified in detail).

exits.label: Exit opportunities
exits.md: After 2-3 years: another lab, a startup (many researchers co-found companies), applied-research roles at big tech, or quantitative finance (hedge funds and trading firms hire ML researchers; general knowledge). After 7-10 years: research director, chief scientist or founder at an AI startup, professor, government advisor (AI safety institutes), venture capital technical partner.

tiers.label: Tier list of employers (alphabetical within each tier; no ranking implied inside a tier)
tiers.md:
- Tier 1 (the frontier): Anthropic, Google DeepMind (offices in London, Bay Area, Zurich, Paris, Tokyo, Toronto, Montreal and others per its careers page), Meta (Superintelligence Labs, including the TBD Lab and FAIR group, reorganised since 2025), OpenAI, plus the strongest academic groups (Stanford, Berkeley, MIT, CMU, Oxford, Cambridge, ETH Zurich/EPFL, Mila/Toronto). Distinguishing feature: access to the largest compute budgets, top pay, and the right to work on the frontier.
- Tier 2: Amazon's AGI/science groups, Apple machine learning research, Cohere, Databricks, Microsoft Research, Mistral AI (Paris), NVIDIA Research, Scale AI, xAI, newer well-funded labs, and leading Chinese groups (ByteDance, Alibaba, DeepSeek; general knowledge). Strong research and good pay, but either less compute, less publishing freedom, or a narrower mission.
- Tier 3: corporate research groups at banks, pharma and industrials; national and regional institutes (IIT, FBK, FAIR network spokes, Fraunhofer, INRIA, and in Asia and the Gulf MBZUAI, TII, Sakana AI and similar; I could not verify their standing, so placement is a judgement); mid-ranked universities. Good for applied work, lower pay and compute.
- Reorganisations (for example the reported cut of about 600 roles at Meta's AI unit in October 2025) show that even Tier 1 job security is volatile.

Tier groupings reflect industry consensus and practitioner perception, not objective fact.

enter.label: How to enter
enter.md: A PhD is still the default for research scientist roles; DeepMind's careers page states that research scientists normally hold one. But several lab postings (Anthropic's interpretability and research engineer roles, for example) ask for a bachelor's degree or equivalent experience plus evidence of research ability, so the door has widened. The strongest signals: first-author papers at top venues, strong open-source or replication work, and a mentor's recommendation. Routes: a PhD at a top group (ideally with a lab internship: DeepMind runs a Student Researcher Program); external safety fellowships open to people from outside the field (Anthropic Fellows, MATS, the OpenAI Safety Fellowship and others, compared in 3.3); the ELLIS PhD programme in Europe (I could not verify details). In Italy: a master's in AI/data science/mathematics (Politecnico di Milano, Sapienza, Bocconi, Trento, Pisa, SNS) then a PhD in the FAIR network or abroad. Calendar: European PhD applications close roughly October-January, US ones in December; lab internships recruit mostly September-January (general pattern, unverified per lab). Interviews: at DeepMind, a recruiter call, two or three skills interviews, then leadership interviews (careers page); other labs test coding and research discussion (Anthropic's alignment posting says Python). Certifications do not matter. Common mistakes: applying with only coursework and no research output; chasing every trend instead of going deep; treating Kaggle as a research record. Alternative routes: physics, maths or neuroscience career changers; non-target-school candidates can win with replications, open-source work and fellowships; 80,000 Hours notes some people moved into safety research from other quantitative fields in under a year. Entry difficulty: 5/5.

downsides.label: Honest downsides and who it is NOT a good fit for
downsides.md: The work is concentrated in a few cities and companies, hours can be punishing around launches, and pay is tied to equity in private companies whose value is uncertain. Most experiments fail, and projects get cancelled when strategy changes. Academia pays far less than industry and gives limited compute, and competition for posts is rising. In Europe the pay gap versus San Francisco is large (section 4). Not a fit for people who need predictable hours, want to work mainly with people and clients, will not relocate, or want guaranteed outcomes.

roles.part: Part 2: Research, frontier and governance roles
roles.title: Research engineer

what.label: What you actually do
what.md: You make the research possible and fast. Typical work across labs: designing RL environments and coding tasks, building reward signals and verifiers, running training experiments on frontier models and diagnosing why models do or do not improve, and building the pipelines that let research iterate quickly. October 2026 examples: Anthropic's Research Engineer, Code RL and Interpretability roles; OpenAI Research Engineer roles in retrieval and search, frontier evals and environments, Codex and privacy; Scale AI's ML Research Engineer, ML Systems; xAI and Cohere "Member of Technical Staff" roles in training infrastructure, RL frameworks and inference. Other work: distributed training across GPU clusters, profiling and CUDA kernels, data platforms for RL, evaluation tooling.

day.label: A typical day and week
day.md: Debugging a failed training run or a slow job; reviewing a colleague's pull request; pairing with a researcher on a new experiment; writing infrastructure code; on some teams an on-call rotation (one Anthropic cybersecurity RL posting mentions a possible on-call rotation). A week mixes coding (60-70%), meetings with researchers, and diagnosing experiments.

hours.label: Hours, stress and lifestyle
hours.md: Typical 45-55 hours; peaks 60-70 near launches or when a big run breaks (estimate). Stress 3-4/5: expensive runs make failures costly and on-call can interrupt evenings. On-site or hybrid: postings I read name an office city (San Francisco, Palo Alto, New York, London, Paris, Toronto, Zurich). Travel: low.

profile.label: Human vs. quantitative profile
profile.md: People/communication: 3/5. Quantitative/technical: 5/5. Collaboration with researchers is constant, but the hard part is distributed systems, performance and ML engineering.

pay.label: Compensation (approximate)
pay.md:
- US employer postings, base ranges (October 2026): OpenAI Research Engineer (San Francisco) $250,000-$445,000, Frontier Evals & Environments $295,000-$380,000, Retrieval & Search $293,000-$585,000, Codex $380,000-$500,000; Anthropic Code RL $500,000-$850,000, Interpretability $315,000-$560,000 (5-10+ years' experience), Applied AI Research Engineer $300,000-$400,000; Scale AI ML Research Engineer, ML Systems $189,600-$237,000, senior/staff $290,400-$363,000; Databricks Staff ML Engineer $190,000-$285,000; xAI Member of Technical Staff $180,000-$440,000; Cohere Lead MTS, Inference Infrastructure $235,000-$325,000. The spread is wide because titles map to different levels.
- London and Europe: Anthropic Research Engineer (RL) GBP 260,000-630,000; Cohere Senior ML Systems Engineer, London CA$250,000-535,000 (about US$175,000-$375,000, my conversion); OpenAI research roles in London and Paris: no pay printed.
- Levels.fyi (9 October 2026): research engineers across companies, median US$240,000 total (25th $115,000; 75th $369,000; 90th $660,000); Google research engineer shows one level, L5 at $620,000 (base $233,000). Anthropic software engineers: entry $367,000 total (base $250,000), senior $598,000, staff $1.13 million; OpenAI software engineer L2 $249,000, L3 $346,000, L5 $960,000; Palantir software engineer median $230,000 (711 submissions).
- Big tech entry: a new-graduate or junior ML engineer at Google/Meta earns roughly $190,000-$310,000 total (derived from the research scientist ladders above at L3/E3-E4 levels; this is an upper-ish proxy).
- Switzerland: research scientist median CHF 119,153 (proxy). Italy: software engineer median EUR 39,258; no data for research engineers. UAE software engineer median AED 337,547 (282 submissions; 90th AED 540,000; Levels.fyi). Mistral (Paris): software engineer median US$104,124 (small sample, Levels.fyi).

path.label: Career path
path.md: Software or ML engineer (0-3 years) -> research engineer (2-5) -> senior/staff research engineer (5-10) -> research engineering manager or technical lead. Many labs also convert strong research engineers into researchers; postings for "Staff+ Research Engineer", "Research Manager" and (at OpenAI) "Research Engineer / Research Scientist" shared titles show the ladder.

exits.label: Exit opportunities
exits.md: After 2-3 years: ML infrastructure roles at big tech, AI startups (often at higher equity), HPC/quant firms. After 7-10 years: head of infrastructure, founding engineer, CTO at an AI startup, or staff engineer at a cloud/GPU company.

tiers.label: Tier list of employers (alphabetical within each tier)
tiers.md:
- Tier 1: Anthropic, Google DeepMind, Meta Superintelligence Labs, NVIDIA (for performance engineering), OpenAI. Distinguishing: frontier-scale clusters and the hardest infrastructure problems.
- Tier 2: Amazon, Apple, Cohere, Databricks/MosaicML-style training companies, Microsoft, Mistral, Scale AI, xAI, strong AI startups.
- Tier 3: research engineering at universities, institutes and corporate labs (smaller clusters), national supercomputing centres (for example CINECA in Italy; general knowledge).

Tier groupings reflect industry consensus and practitioner perception, not objective fact.

enter.label: How to enter
enter.md: A bachelor's or master's in computer science, maths or physics works; Anthropic's postings require a bachelor's or equivalent experience and say publications are not necessary (I did not verify the same wording elsewhere). PhD not required but helpful. The practical filter is evidence of strong engineering plus familiarity with LLMs: shipping projects with PyTorch/JAX, reproducing a paper, contributing to open-source training libraries (reimplementing a small transformer, writing a fast attention kernel). Experience is usually required: postings call for 5-10+ years (Anthropic Interpretability) or "depends on level"; entry-level research engineer roles exist mainly at big tech and through fellowships (see 3.3) and internships. Interviews: Python coding, ML-infrastructure system design, take-home or pair programming on experiments, research discussion. Certifications: not valued. Common mistakes: notebook-level ML projects, ignoring systems fundamentals (networking, GPUs), underestimating coding-interview preparation. Alternative routes: backend or HPC software engineers; cybersecurity engineers moving into RL environments for security (Anthropic's cyber RL postings); non-target-school candidates through open source. Entry difficulty: 4/5.

downsides.label: Honest downsides and who it is NOT a good fit for
downsides.md: You are a support function for researchers: credit goes to the papers' authors and priorities can change quickly. On-call and launch crunches exist. Pay at the top is very high but concentrated in equity of private firms. Not a fit for people who want to set the research agenda, dislike infrastructure work, or cannot live in a few expensive cities. Not a fit for those wanting a standard regulated-industry career with predictable hours.

compare.pay: US: base $190k-237k (Scale AI), $250k-445k (OpenAI), $300k-850k (Anthropic); Levels.fyi median $240k total / UK: GBP 260k-630k base (Anthropic London), CA$250k-535k (Cohere London) / Italy: no reliable data found (software engineer median EUR 39k total)

summary: US: base $190k-237k (Scale AI), $250k-445k (OpenAI), $300k-850k (Anthropic); Levels.fyi median $240k total / UK: GBP 260k-630k base (Anthropic London), CA$250k-535k (Cohere London) / Italy: no reliable data found (software engineer median EUR 39k total)

roles.part: Part 2: Research, frontier and governance roles
roles.title: AI safety, alignment, interpretability and evaluations / red-teaming researcher
roles.shortName: AI safety, alignment, interpretability, evals/red teaming

what.label: What you actually do
what.md: Alignment researchers run experiments on whether models behave as intended (October 2026 examples: Anthropic's London role testing safety techniques by training models to subvert them; OpenAI's "Researcher, Alignment CoT Monitorability" and "Researcher, Safety Oversight"; Scale AI's "Research Scientist, AI Controls and Monitoring"). Interpretability researchers analyse model internals (features and circuits). Evaluations researchers design tasks that measure capabilities and risks: METR's roles include "evaluation execution" and "task development engineer" with a roughly two-day paid work trial; Scale AI lists "Frontier Risk Evaluations" and OpenAI "Data Scientist, Preparedness". Red teamers attack products: Anthropic's Red Team Engineer, Safeguards role asks for penetration-testing and jailbreak experience and a public body of work; OpenAI lists a "Red Team Specialist - Cyber"; AISI has alignment, control and misuse red teams. Government evaluators (UK AISI, US CAISI) test models before and after release; AISI open-sources its evaluation tool Inspect.

day.label: A typical day and week
day.md: Running and analysing experiments; writing evaluation tasks and scoring rubrics; reviewing transcripts of model behaviour; discussing findings with policy or product teams; writing up a safety case or a blog post. In evaluations roles, deadlines come from model release dates: pre-deployment testing windows can be short. Red teamers spend time crafting attacks, building automation, and reporting.

hours.label: Hours, stress and lifestyle
hours.md: Typical 45-55 hours, peaks 60-70 before model releases (estimate). Stress 3-4/5: high-stakes releases and the sense that errors matter. Government institutes are closer to 40-45 hours with hybrid working (AISI offers hybrid, with offices in London and other UK government sites). METR and Apollo are mostly office-based in Berkeley, London or San Francisco; Apollo offers flexible hours and visa sponsorship.

profile.label: Human vs. quantitative profile
profile.md: People/communication: 3/5. Quantitative/technical: 4/5. Strong written communication is needed because the output is arguments and evidence; interpretability and theory roles are heavily mathematical; red teaming leans on security skills.

pay.label: Compensation (approximate)
pay.md:
- US labs and AI companies, base ranges (October 2026): OpenAI Researcher, Interpretability $380,000-$500,000, Alignment $295,000-$500,000, Frontier Cybersecurity Risks $380,000-$500,000, Data Scientist, Safety $265,000-$380,000, Red Team Specialist - Cyber $198,000-$320,000; Anthropic Research Scientist, Interpretability $350,000-$850,000, Red Team Engineer, Safeguards $320,000-$405,000, London alignment GBP 260,000-370,000; Google DeepMind Research Engineer, AGI Safety and Alignment (US) $174,000-$253,000 (mirror; no range seen for London); Scale AI Research Scientist, Frontier Risk Evaluations / Agent Robustness / AI Controls and Monitoring $216,000-$270,000; xAI MTS, Imagine Safety $180,000-$440,000; Cohere Senior MTS, Safety and Security for Agents (London) CA$250,000-535,000.
- US nonprofits: METR salary ranges (October 2026): Member of Technical Staff, Evaluation Execution $328,000-$578,000; Embedded Assessments $402,000-$687,000; Task Development Engineer $260,000-$385,000. Apollo Research: no ranges listed in the page I read.
- UK AI Security Institute (Greenhouse job board, October 2026; 13 postings open, including Misuse, Control and Alignment Red Team roles and a Research Director): base plus a "technical allowance", outside the civil-service DDaT framework. Total package by level: Level 3 GBP 65,000-75,000 (base 39,850); Level 4 GBP 85,000-95,000 (base 47,355); Level 5 GBP 105,000-115,000 (base 61,620); Level 6 GBP 125,000-135,000 (base 74,605); Level 7 GBP 145,000. A further 28.97% employer pension is paid on base. Older adverts printed slightly different base splits, so check the live advert. Far below US lab bases, high for UK public service.
- US government: CAISI sits inside NIST; no CAISI-specific range found. NIST Information Technology Laboratory AI postings (USAJOBS, September 2026, closed) show the scale: AI Computer Scientist ZP-III $85,447-$133,142 and ZP-IV $121,785-$187,093; Applied AI Technical Lead ZP-5 $169,279-$197,200.
- EU: the AI Office's 2026 call for expressions of interest (CNECT RL AI/2026, closed 8 September 2026) sought about 40 contract agents for 2027 in Brussels, including Technology Specialist and Legal Officer profiles at function group IV (one-year contracts extendable to six; from the EU Careers listing summary, call PDF not opened). EU agency (AMLA) pay examples, monthly: contract agent FG IV grade 13 basic EUR 4,449 (about EUR 3,856 net without allowances), grade 14 EUR 5,034 (about EUR 4,051 net); temporary agent AD6 EUR 6,961-7,254 basic.
- Fellowships (often the entry route; stipends differ): MATS US$1,250 a week plus about $2,000 a week compute for 12 weeks; Anthropic Fellows (economics and policy track) $3,850, GBP 2,310 or C$4,300 a week for 4 months, safety track about $15,000 a month compute; Constellation Astra $8,400 a month for 5 months in Berkeley plus about $15,000 a month compute; Pivotal GBP 6,000-8,000 for 15 weeks in London (next cohort 18 January 2027); LASR Labs GBP 15,000 for 13 weeks in London (next cohort June-September 2027); OpenAI Safety Fellowship (14 September 2026-5 February 2027; stipend amount not stated; applications closed 3 May 2026). Unverified (aggregators): ERA, Cambridge, GBP 10,000 for 10 weeks; PIBBSS $3,000 a month.
- Europe/Italy: no frontier-lab safety research roles found in Italy; Italian-based researchers typically work remotely for non-Italian groups or move. No reliable data found.
- Asia/Gulf: no reliable data found for safety-specific roles (see 3.1 for research proxies).

path.label: Career path
path.md: Fellowship or master's (0-1 year) -> junior researcher/engineer, research contributor (1-3 years) -> senior researcher, research lead (3-7 years) -> team lead or head of a safety area (7+). 80,000 Hours describes the same split: contributor versus research lead, with a PhD "practically the default" for leads. Government path: technical staff -> research scientist -> workstream lead (AISI's levels above).

exits.label: Exit opportunities
exits.md: After 2-3 years: mainstream ML research, safeguards or trust-and-safety roles at labs, AI security startups, government institutes. After 7-10 years: head of safety/evaluations at a lab or institute, founder of an evaluation or security startup, senior government advisor, policy leadership.

tiers.label: Tier list of employers (alphabetical within each group)
tiers.md:
- Tier 1: Google DeepMind, OpenAI and Anthropic (lab safety teams); UK AI Security Institute and US CAISI (state evaluators with pre-release access to models: AISI has access agreements with Anthropic, Google and OpenAI); METR, Apollo Research and Redwood Research (specialist nonprofits).
- Tier 2: Academic groups (Berkeley/CHAI, Oxford, Cambridge, MIT, NYU), the EU AI Office's AI Safety unit, other national institutes (Japan, Canada, Singapore; general knowledge), big-tech safeguards and trust-and-safety teams, safety research teams at Scale AI, xAI and Cohere.
- Tier 3: corporate red teams in banks and cybersecurity firms with an AI practice, small startups and consultancies.

Tier groupings reflect industry consensus and practitioner perception, not objective fact.

enter.label: How to enter
enter.md: Backgrounds: ML, software engineering, security, physics, maths. Several fellowships say a PhD, prior ML experience or papers are not required (Anthropic Fellows and Astra say no prior AI safety experience is needed; the OpenAI Safety Fellowship asks for no specific credentials but requires reference letters). MATS (631 researchers since late 2021; 75% of alumni work in alignment, transparency or security; alumni at Anthropic, DeepMind, OpenAI, UK AISI, METR; per its own site) is the best-known pipeline; Anthropic reports that over 35% of past Fellows joined it full-time (employer-reported). Cohorts: Anthropic Fellows (4 months; apply by 18 October for January); MATS Winter 2027 applications closed in October 2026; Astra's have run late August to late September; Pivotal and LASR open rounds ahead of each cohort. Horizon covers policy-oriented tech talent in the US (3.5). Portfolio: replicate a safety paper, run evaluations with an open framework such as Inspect, write a public post analysing model behaviour, produce a red-team report, hold CVEs or bug-bounty credit. Interviews: Apollo's process is short application questions, a 30-minute screen, a 2-2.5 hour take-home, three 60-minute interviews and a leadership interview; METR uses a code screen, take-home, interviews and a roughly two-day paid work trial; UK AISI uses a CV, short written statement, skills assessment and 2-4 interviews, sponsors visas for technical roles, and requires civil-service nationality for non-technical roles. Certifications: none valued. Common mistakes: reading only the discourse and never producing empirical work; applying with no artefact; applying to one organization only. Alternative routes: security professionals (red teaming), physicists and mathematicians (interpretability and theory), lawyers and policy people into evaluation policy; fellowships open the door for non-target schools. Entry difficulty: 5/5.

downsides.label: Honest downsides and who it is NOT a good fit for
downsides.md: The field is small and jobs are few; funding and strategy shift with politics (the UK institute was renamed from "Safety" to "Security" in February 2025). Nonprofit and government roles can be insecure or capped in pay (AISI's top published total is GBP 145,000); lab safety teams depend on company priorities. Reviewing harmful outputs (for enforcement and safeguards roles) can be distressing. Not a fit for people who need a standardised career ladder, who are mainly drawn by pay (non-lab jobs pay far less), or who dislike uncertainty about whether the work will matter.

roles.part: Part 2: Research, frontier and governance roles
roles.title: Forward-deployed engineer / AI solutions engineer / AI consultant

what.label: What you actually do
what.md: You take a general-purpose model or data platform and make it solve a customer's real problem: production applications, agents and connectors (for example MCP servers, which let models use tools), evaluation sets, and reusable deployment patterns fed back to product teams. Examples: Anthropic's London FDE role embeds with enterprise customers with 25-50% travel, and its Applied AI Architect role is pre-sales; OpenAI lists FDE roles by industry (healthcare, legal, financial services) and for government and security customers; Palantir's FDE and Deployment Strategist roles run at customer sites including defence and government; Databricks separates FDEs (hands-on builds), Deployment Strategists and Delivery Solutions Architects (post-sales). Consultants at McKinsey/QuantumBlack or BCG X combine strategy with delivery (general knowledge, unverified for specific firms).

day.label: A typical day and week
day.md: On site or on video call with the client's engineers; scoping a use case with a business owner; building a prototype (Python, APIs, vector databases, evaluation sets); presenting to executives; writing up reusable patterns for the product team. Monday-Thursday at the client, Friday at base is a common rhythm at Palantir-style firms (practitioner commentary; unverified).

hours.label: Hours, stress and lifestyle
hours.md: Typical 45-55 hours; peaks of 60-70 during go-lives or customer escalations (estimate). Stress 4/5: client-driven deadlines, ambiguity, and responsibility for production systems. Travel: 25-50% (Anthropic FDE posting); Palantir expects about 25% on site and another employer cited up to 50% (Pragmatic Engineer, 12 August 2025). Hybrid; some customer sites are hard to reach (factories, air-gapped networks).

profile.label: Human vs. quantitative profile
profile.md: People/communication: 4/5. Quantitative/technical: 4/5. This is the role where you must both code and persuade; consulting-style roles lean to 5/5 for people and 3/5 technical.

pay.label: Compensation (approximate)
pay.md:
- US postings, ranges as printed (October 2026): OpenAI Forward Deployed Software Engineer (San Francisco, New York, Seattle) $153,000-$325,000, industry FDEs $185,000-$300,000, Manager, FDE $302,000-$385,000; Palantir new-graduate FDE (New York, Chicago) estimated $135,000-$145,000, experienced FDE roles estimated $135,000-$200,000 (stock and sign-on bonus may be added); Databricks AI FDE $152,900-$210,155, Senior FDE $182,000-$250,208, Senior Deployment Strategist $219,765-$302,220, Solutions Architect $180,000-$247,500; Scale AI Frontier Agents Engineer (Forward Deployed) $180,000-$225,000, senior $216,000-$270,000, Deployment Strategist $203,200-$254,000; Cohere FDE, Agentic Platform (US) CA$175,000-385,000 (about US$125,000-$270,000, my conversion); Anthropic Applied AI Architect, International Policy $240,000-$315,000, AI Deployment Specialist $200,000-$265,000.
- UK and Europe: Anthropic FDE, London GBP 225,000-255,000 base (4+ years' experience); Applied AI Architect, Industries, London GBP 165,000-190,000 (5+ years). OpenAI, Palantir, Databricks, Scale AI and Cohere post FDE or deployment roles in London, Paris, Munich, Zurich, Amsterdam and Stockholm without printed ranges: no reliable data found. Anthropic Milan Applied AI Architect: no range; requires native or C1 Italian, 5+ years' customer-facing technical experience, office at least 25%. Anthropic Paris FDE: no range; 8+ years, native French.
- Levels.fyi (9 October 2026): OpenAI solution architect median $418,000 total; Mistral AI solution architect (US) $326,625; Palantir software engineer (which includes FDE) median $230,000 (711 submissions).
- Consulting (general, not AI-specific; weak third-party guides that disagree): UK Big Four starting salaries about GBP 32,000-40,000 in London; Accenture UK analyst about GBP 33,500 (undated); UK consultancy graduate average GBP 32,924 (graduate-jobs.com, October 2026); McKinsey/BCG/Bain UK analysts with a master's about GBP 49,500-52,000 base. No reliable data found for AI-specific consulting pay.
- Italy: Levels.fyi software engineer median EUR 39,258; no reliable data found for FDE or solutions roles in Italy beyond the unpriced Anthropic Milan posting.
- Asia and Gulf: Palantir, Databricks, OpenAI, Cohere and Scale AI list FDE, deployment or applied-AI roles in Tokyo, Seoul, Singapore, Sydney, Abu Dhabi, Dubai, Riyadh or Doha, but none printed a range. Proxies: UAE software engineer median AED 337,547 (Levels.fyi, tax-free); Singapore research scientist median SGD 90,299.

path.label: Career path
path.md: Software engineer or consultant (0-3 years) -> FDE/solutions engineer (2-5) -> senior FDE or solutions architect (5-8) -> staff/principal, engineering manager or customer-engineering lead (8+). Postings across employers show the ladder: FDE, senior FDE, "Manager, Forward Deployed Engineering", "Staff FDE" and pre-sales programme leads.

exits.label: Exit opportunities
exits.md: After 2-3 years: product engineering, startup founding engineer, consulting, solutions-architect roles at cloud providers. After 7-10 years: head of customer engineering, chief technology officer at an AI startup, partner-track consulting, or founder (customer exposure is a classic startup apprenticeship).

tiers.label: Tier list of employers (alphabetical within each tier)
tiers.md:
- Tier 1: Palantir (the role's originator) and frontier labs (Anthropic, Google Cloud/DeepMind customer engineering, OpenAI).
- Tier 2: AI-native startups (Cohere, Ramp, Lindy and others cited by the Pragmatic Engineer), cloud providers (AWS, Google Cloud, Microsoft), Databricks, Salesforce, Scale AI, Snowflake; consultancies' AI arms (QuantumBlack, BCG X, Accenture, Deloitte; general knowledge).
- Tier 3: systems integrators, regional consultancies and in-house AI enablement teams at banks and pharma.

Tier groupings reflect industry consensus and practitioner perception, not objective fact.

enter.label: How to enter
enter.md: The role is rarely a first job at a frontier lab: Anthropic's FDE postings want 4+ years (London) and 8+ (Paris), its Architect roles 5+. But Palantir and Databricks have earlier-career doors: Palantir's feed lists New Grad and Internship tracks for Forward Deployed Software Engineer and Deployment Strategist (New York, London, Chicago, Seoul, Washington DC, Paris and others; US new-grad FDE pay about $135,000-$145,000, estimated in the posting), and Databricks lists new-graduate product roles. Paths: software engineer who has built LLM applications (Part 1 branch) plus customer exposure; consultant who can code. A bachelor's or equivalent is enough per Anthropic; computer science, engineering, data or maths are common, but economics, management and finance graduates enter via consulting and sales engineering. Portfolio: two or three real applications on LLM APIs (agent with tool use, retrieval, evaluation set) and a short case study; cloud certifications help for solutions-architect roles at cloud firms (not at labs). Interviews: Python technical interview, customer scenario role-play, system design, executive communication. Language: several European roles require local fluency (Anthropic Milan Italian C1, Paris native French; OpenAI lists Spanish-speaking roles in London and Madrid), an opening for Italians and Francophones. Common mistakes: treating it as pure coding; promising capabilities models cannot deliver; no evidence of production experience. Alternative routes: management consultants and data scientists who upskill in coding; technical account managers. Entry difficulty: 3/5 at consulting and integrators; 4/5 at frontier labs and Palantir.

downsides.label: Honest downsides and who it is NOT a good fit for
downsides.md: Travel and context-switching are real; the Pragmatic Engineer notes the role can feel like two jobs (customer delivery and platform engineering) and that expectations vary. You live with customers' messy data and politics, and your success depends on things outside your control. Consultancies add up-or-out pressure. Not a fit for people who want deep research time, dislike travel, or prefer a single focused technical problem. Not a fit if you cannot present to executives.

roles.part: Part 2: Research, frontier and governance roles
roles.title: AI governance, policy and responsible-AI specialist

what.label: What you actually do
what.md: Four sub-jobs. (a) Public policy: drafting or analysing legislation, consultations, standards input and briefings; at the EU AI Office you support the Act's rules for general-purpose models (units for regulation and compliance, AI safety, and innovation policy). (b) Lab and company policy: OpenAI's "Model Policy Manager" roles, "Senior Product Policy Lead, Regulation" and "Research Program Manager, Governance"; Anthropic's Policy Design Manager (owns the usage policy, builds threat models) and Product Policy Manager; Google DeepMind's "Frontier Public Affairs Lead"; Cohere's public policy roles. (c) Corporate responsible AI / compliance: inventorying AI systems, risk-classifying them under the EU AI Act, writing governance policies, running impact assessments with legal, privacy, security and data teams; Citi's AI Business Risk and Control Director (October 2026) holds approval authority for AI use cases and aligns the framework to the EU AI Act and NIST AI RMF. (d) Think-tank or consulting research: reports, workshops, client advice.

day.label: A typical day and week
day.md: Reading regulation and draft guidance; drafting a policy paper or compliance checklist; meetings with legal, engineering and business teams; stakeholder calls with regulators or civil society; in the lab setting, reviewing a product launch against policy. Week-ending output: memo, briefing or risk assessment.

hours.label: Hours, stress and lifestyle
hours.md: Typical 40-50 hours in regulators, think tanks and corporate roles; 50-60 at labs and law/consulting firms; peaks of 60+ around regulation deadlines, consultations and legislative sessions (estimate). Stress 3/5 (4/5 at law firms, labs during incidents, and policy shops during legislative crunch). Hybrid is common outside labs. Travel: moderate (Brussels, DC, Geneva, summits).

profile.label: Human vs. quantitative profile
profile.md: People/communication: 5/5. Quantitative/technical: 2/5 (rising to 3/5 for technical policy and evaluation-oriented roles). The job is persuasion, writing and interpretation; technical policy roles require reading model evaluations and understanding ML basics.

pay.label: Compensation (approximate)
pay.md:
- US labs and AI companies, base ranges (October 2026): OpenAI Model Policy Manager $207,000-$335,000, Senior Product Policy Lead, Regulation $302,000-$335,000, Research Program Manager, Governance $239,000-$328,000; Anthropic Policy Design Manager and Product Policy Manager $245,000-$285,000; Google DeepMind Frontier Public Affairs Lead $221,000-$307,000 (mirror); Cohere Global Public Policy Manager $150,000-$240,000 and Lead, US Government Affairs $175,000-$330,000; xAI Senior Security Engineer, GRC & AI Governance $152,000-$258,000.
- US big tech (mirrors of 2026 Google postings): AI Policy Manager II, Washington DC $182,000-$248,000 base (7 years' tech-policy experience); Responsible AI Program Manager, Google Public Sector $165,000-$239,000 (needs Top Secret/SCI clearance).
- US finance: Citi AI Business Risk and Control Director (Getzville, New York or Tampa; posted 5 October 2026) $200,000-$300,000 base; M&T Bank model-risk analyst validating AI models (mirror) $103,000-$171,600. Junior compliance pay at banks sits below lab bands, but senior risk-and-control jobs overlap with them.
- US fellowships and government: Horizon Fellowship base salaries for the 2027 cohort are $78,000 (junior), $130,000 (fellow) and $190,000+ (senior), plus a $17,000 a year benefits stipend (Horizon page); placements in executive-branch offices, Congress, national labs and think tanks. NIST AI roles in September 2026 ran $85,447-$197,200 (see 3.3). Think-tank pay: no reliable data found.
- EU: AD5 basic salary EUR 6,152.64 a month from 1 July 2025, net about EUR 4,859 without allowances (AMLA page; AD6 starts at EUR 6,961). Contract agents at function group IV (the 2026 AI Office legal and technology call) earn a basic EUR 4,449-5,034. Blue Book traineeship grant EUR 1,538.16 a month in Brussels. AD5 competition EPSO/AD/427/26 drew 174,727 applicants for 1,490 places (EPSO, 2026). The AI Office recruits through expression-of-interest calls and lists more than 125 staff.
- UK: Barclay Simpson's 2026 AI governance report (recruiter; central London base): analyst GBP 60,000-70,000; senior analyst 70,000-100,000; manager 100,000-130,000; lead/head of 130,000-150,000; AI counsel 100,000-150,000; chief AI officer/director 150,000-250,000; UK-wide about GBP 5,000-10,000 lower. Other signals (search summaries): a London Head of AI Governance for a qualified lawyer at recruiter Taylor Root GBP 150,000-180,000; a Ministry of Justice Head of AI Governance advert (2025) GBP 71,381-80,419 (London 75,674-85,257). UK AISI technical pay is in 3.3.
- Italy: no reliable data found for AI governance or compliance salaries. The Hays Italia Salary Guide 2026 exists but I did not read its tables; Il Sole 24 Ore reports rising demand. Context only: average private-sector pay in Lombardy about EUR 35,137 gross (JP Salary Outlook 2026).
- Switzerland, Singapore, Gulf, other Asia: no reliable data found.
- Corporate responsible AI / compliance salaries (global): the IAPP report I read contains no salary figures.

path.label: Career path
path.md: Policy analyst/assistant, compliance analyst, or trainee/fellow (0-2 years) -> senior analyst/manager (3-6) -> head of AI policy/governance, director (7-12) -> chief AI officer/responsible AI lead or senior official. In law: trainee/associate -> senior associate -> partner (10+). The IAPP report finds organizations usually build governance teams gradually, starting with existing staff and then hiring senior managers, and often hire managers with prior digital governance experience such as privacy.

exits.label: Exit opportunities
exits.md: After 2-3 years: privacy, compliance and risk roles; tech-policy jobs at platforms; consultancy; law firm. After 7-10 years: chief privacy/AI officer, head of policy at a lab or regulator, partner at a firm, senior official, NGO leadership.

tiers.label: Tier list of employers (alphabetical within each tier)
tiers.md:
- Tier 1: Frontier-lab and big-tech frontier policy teams (Anthropic, Google DeepMind, OpenAI), the European Commission's AI Office, the UK AI Security Institute and DSIT, US White House/Commerce/CAISI, leading research centres (GovAI, and similar), top Brussels and Washington think tanks.
- Tier 2: Big-tech public policy and responsible-AI teams (Amazon, Google, Meta, Microsoft), national regulators and data-protection authorities (Italy's Garante, AgID, ACN; general knowledge), international organisations (OECD, UN, Council of Europe), law-firm AI practices, Big Four and consultancy AI-governance practices, global banks' responsible-AI leadership roles (Citi, for example).
- Tier 3: Corporate compliance and risk teams in banks, pharma and insurance; startups building governance tooling; national associations and standards committees.

Tier groupings reflect industry consensus and practitioner perception, not objective fact.

enter.label: How to enter
enter.md: Degrees: law, public policy, international relations, political science, economics, computer science (technical policy). Lab policy postings ask for a bachelor's or equivalent plus domain experience (Anthropic's do; Google's AI policy role wants 7 years of tech-policy work). 80,000 Hours says policy master's degrees are particularly useful in Washington and law degrees and relevant PhDs help; executive-office roles (OSTP, OMB, NSC) are among the hardest to obtain; it advises against starting in civil service without experience and lists the Presidential Innovation Fellowship, Horizon, TechCongress and AAAS fellowships. Horizon applications run roughly July to early September (2027 cohort deadline 30 August 2026; selection November-December). Other fellowships: Anthropic Fellows economics and policy track (4 months, rolling, next cohort January 2027, no visa sponsorship, US/UK/Canada work authorisation), Constellation Astra's strategy and governance track, and GovAI's summer fellowship (2026 applied track paid GBP 12,000 over three months in London, per an aggregator). Europe: EU Blue Book traineeship (five months; applications ahead of March and October starts), EPSO competitions (heavy competition), AI Office expression-of-interest calls (the 2026 call closed 8 September). Italy: the Garante, AgID, ACN and ministries via public competitions (concorsi), and compliance roles in banks, insurers and consultancies preparing for the AI Act. Certifications: IAPP's AIGP exam costs US$649 for members and $799 for non-members (100 questions, 2.75 hours; IAPP, October 2026); it is common in compliance postings and shows commitment but does not replace a degree or domain experience (my assessment). Portfolio: policy writing samples (a consultation response, an AI Act analysis for a sector), a clear explanation of how a model is evaluated, familiarity with the NIST AI Risk Management Framework and ISO/IEC 42001 (general knowledge). Interviews: written briefing note, panel interview, regulation case study. Common mistakes: relying on AIGP alone; staying too abstract; ignoring technical literacy; writing like a lawyer for a technical audience. Alternative routes: privacy/IP lawyers, engineers moving into technical policy, consultants, think-tank research assistantships. Entry difficulty: 4/5 for lab, regulator and top fellowship roles; 3/5 for corporate compliance and consulting.

downsides.label: Honest downsides and who it is NOT a good fit for
downsides.md: Pay outside labs and consultancies is modest relative to technical AI roles (UK recruiter bands for managers are GBP 90,000-130,000, against six-figure dollar bases at labs). Roles depend on political cycles: the EU delayed high-risk obligations to December 2027 and August 2028, which shifts hiring plans, and the AI Office's 2027 contract-agent hiring depends on budget decisions. Policy teams at companies can be overruled by commercial priorities. Government processes are slow. Not a fit for people who want to build things, dislike ambiguity about whether their work changes outcomes, or dislike bureaucracy.

roles.part: Part 2: Research, frontier and governance roles
roles.title: AI product manager

what.label: What you actually do
what.md: You define what an AI product should do and how to measure it: owning strategy, roadmap and delivery for a product area, turning model capabilities into usable experiences with metrics, experiments and research, and working with design, engineering, data science, research and marketing. Distinctive AI-PM work: defining evals that stand for product quality, deciding when a model is "good enough", managing cost per request, handling prompt and model changes, working with safety teams on misuse (OpenAI lists PMs for multimodal safety and integrity; Scale AI for cybersecurity and finance agents; Anthropic for Safeguards and Public Sector), and shaping what research should build next.

day.label: A typical day and week
day.md: User and data review; writing a product requirements document with eval criteria; syncing with engineers and researchers; reviewing launch readiness with safety teams; customer calls; prioritisation meetings. Weekly rhythm: launch planning, metrics reviews, and unscheduled escalations when model behaviour changes.

hours.label: Hours, stress and lifestyle
hours.md: Typical 45-55 hours, peaks 60-70 around launches (estimate). Stress 3-4/5: fast-changing technology, high visibility, and launch deadlines. Hybrid at big tech; frontier-lab and AI-startup roles are mostly on-site in San Francisco, New York or Seattle (Cohere's PM roles list Toronto). Travel: low to moderate.

profile.label: Human vs. quantitative profile
profile.md: People/communication: 5/5. Quantitative/technical: 3/5. You need to read experiment results and understand model limitations, but the main skill is alignment of people and judgment.

pay.label: Compensation (approximate)
pay.md:
- Employer postings, US base ranges (October 2026): OpenAI Product Manager, API Agents $293,000-$325,000, Core Models $347,000-$490,000, Integrity $347,000-$385,000, Financial Services $401,000-$530,000; Anthropic Product Manager, Claude $385,000-$460,000 (8+ years preferred); Scale AI Senior AI Product Manager $205,600-$257,000, Staff PM, Agentic Platform $210,000-$345,000; Databricks Senior PM, Databricks AI $148,800-$215,250, Staff PM, Agentic AI Applications $172,200-$236,850; Cohere PM, Agent Harness (Toronto) $160,000-$320,000, currency as printed.
- Entry: Databricks Associate Product Manager, New Grad (2027 start; Bellevue, Mountain View, San Francisco) $133,000-$150,000; Levels.fyi entry-level total comp (9 October 2026) Meta E3 rotational PM $174,000 and Microsoft level 59-60 PM $168,000-$180,000; Google L4 PM $308,000.
- Levels.fyi (9 October 2026), US total comp: all employers median $230,000 (25th $169,000; 75th $330,000; 90th $450,000); Google median $402,000 (L4 $308,000, L5 $391,000, L6 $588,000); Meta E4 $265,000, E5 $418,000, E6 $674,000; Microsoft median $253,000; Anthropic $407,000; OpenAI $750,000; Palantir $180,000. No AI-specific PM series.
- UK, Italy, Switzerland and Asia/Gulf: no reliable data found; Mistral and London labs are likely to sit well below US levels (unverified).

path.label: Career path
path.md: Associate PM / technical program manager (0-3 years) -> product manager (2-5) -> senior PM (5-8) -> group PM or head of product (8-12) -> VP/Chief Product Officer. Also: engineers, data scientists and consultants lateral into AI PM after 3-6 years.

exits.label: Exit opportunities
exits.md: After 2-3 years: PM roles in other tech companies, startup product leads. After 7-10 years: head of product, founder, general manager, venture capital.

tiers.label: Tier list of employers (alphabetical within each tier)
tiers.md:
- Tier 1: Frontier labs (Anthropic, Google DeepMind, OpenAI), Google and Microsoft AI products, Meta.
- Tier 2: AI-native startups (Cohere, Mistral, Perplexity-type companies; general knowledge), Adobe, Databricks, NVIDIA, Salesforce, Scale AI.
- Tier 3: AI product teams at banks, pharma, consultancies and enterprise software firms.

Tier groupings reflect industry consensus and practitioner perception, not objective fact.

enter.label: How to enter
enter.md: Rarely a first job at a lab (Anthropic's PM, Claude posting prefers 8+ years and products with millions of users), but associate-PM doors exist: Databricks' 2027 new-graduate APM and Meta's rotational PM level. Typical routes: associate PM programmes at big tech, engineer-to-PM, data scientist-to-PM, consultant-to-PM, startup founder. Degrees: any; computer science, engineering and business dominate; an MBA helps at some companies. Skills: designing evaluations, writing a spec with acceptance criteria for probabilistic behaviour, using LLM APIs, understanding cost and latency. Portfolio: shipped side projects, a teardown of an AI product, a prototype with an evaluation set. Interviews: product sense, execution, analytics, behavioural and technical-fluency. Certifications: little weight. Common mistakes: confusing demos with products; neglecting evals and safety; chasing hype over user needs. Alternative routes: technical program managers and customer success/solutions staff moving into product; non-target-school candidates through startup experience. Entry difficulty: 4/5 at frontier labs and top big tech; 3/5 elsewhere.

downsides.label: Honest downsides and who it is NOT a good fit for
downsides.md: Roadmaps get overturned when models change; you are accountable for outcomes you do not control; and AI PM is a crowded aspiration, so many candidates compete for few roles. Not a fit for people who need stable, long-horizon plans, or who dislike ambiguity about technical feasibility. Not a fit for those who want to do the technical work themselves.

roles.title: Product / experimentation data scientist

what.label: What you actually do
what.md: You sit inside a product team (checkout, search, ads, growth) and own the numbers behind decisions. Concrete tasks: define the success metric and guardrail metrics for a feature; design and size an A/B test (power, sample size, test duration); write SQL against event tables to compute conversion lift and confidence intervals; investigate why a metric dropped 3% on Tuesday; build a causal estimate when you cannot randomise (difference-in-differences, matching, instrumental variables); forecast user growth; present a recommendation ("ship, don't ship, or run it longer") to a product manager and engineers. Tools: SQL (daily), Python or R, a notebook environment, an experimentation platform, dashboards. Deliverables: experiment readouts, metric definitions, analysis memos, occasionally a model.

day.label: A typical day and week
day.md: Mornings: check experiment dashboards and metric alerts; answer ad-hoc questions in chat. Midday: write SQL and Python for an analysis; a 30-minute sync with the product manager and designer. Afternoon: write up a readout. Weekly: planning meeting, experiment review, a deeper project (e.g. redefining "active user"). Roughly 30-40% of time is meetings and communication (consensus).

hours.label: Hours, stress and lifestyle
hours.md: Typical 40-50 hours a week, peaks around launches or quarter planning of 55-60 (consensus; no survey found). Stress 3/5: steady deadlines, pressure when a launch decision hangs on your readout, but rarely overnight crises. Flexible hybrid is common in tech; fully remote less so since 2023 (consensus). No travel beyond offsites. In the US the big employers pay for the flexibility with at-will culture and periodic layoffs (consensus).

profile.label: Human vs. quantitative profile
profile.md: People/communication: 4/5. Quantitative/technical: 3/5. Your statistics must be correct, but the scarce skill is persuading a non-technical team to act on a result, so Meta's interview rubric reportedly values product thinking over complicated maths (Glassdoor candidate report, anecdotal).

pay.label: Compensation (approximate)
pay.md:
- US (Levels.fyi, 9 Oct 2026, total compensation = base + stock + bonus): Google data scientist L3 US$196k, L4 US$281k, L5 (senior) US$380k; Meta IC3 US$153k, IC4 US$240k, IC5 US$375k, IC6 US$486k (median all levels US$320k); all-employer US median US$180k (n=3,376), 25th percentile US$134k, 75th US$250k, San Francisco Bay Area median US$250k, NYC US$190-200k. Self-reported and skewed to big tech; BLS median for all data scientists is US$120,230 (May 2025), 10th percentile US$67,240, 90th US$199,130.
- UK: London all-levels median GBP 91,096 (Levels.fyi, 9 Oct 2026, n=326; Meta ~GBP 144.7k and JPMorgan ~GBP 143.8k at the top); 25th percentile GBP 65.7k. No reliable entry-level figure for big-tech product data science found; Morgan McKinley's 2026 guide gives GBP 85-100k as an average London range for data scientists (all levels).
- Continental Europe: Germany median EUR 77,643 (Levels.fyi, 9 Oct 2026, n=207); Berlin EUR 112,951; Delivery Hero EUR 108k, Wolt EUR 107k, Zalando EUR 102k. Italy: median EUR 46,145 (n=23, all levels), Milan EUR 56,058 (small sample); Glassdoor (Feb 2026, 214 salaries) junior data scientist in Italy about EUR 29,000 gross (EUR 26-33k); Indeed Italy average EUR 34,617 (Aug 2026, 160 salaries). Pay for pure product data science in Italy: no reliable data found (the few such roles are at multinationals' Milan offices or Italian scale-ups).
- Asia hubs: Singapore median SGD 120,084 (Levels.fyi, n=128), Grab ~SGD 160k; Tokyo median JPY 8.76m (n=16; PayPay ~JPY 18.4m); Hong Kong median HKD 803k (n=12); Dubai median AED 437,560 (n=20). The last three are very thin samples.

path.label: Career path
path.md: Data scientist (0-3 years; Google L3/Meta IC3) → data scientist II/senior (3-6 years; L4-L5/IC4-IC5) → staff/lead, or manager of data science (7-10 years). Titles drift: "product analyst" or "analytics" at smaller firms.

exits.label: Exit opportunities
exits.md: After 2-3 years: ML/AI roles at the same firm, product management, growth/strategy at start-ups, other tech employers. After 7-10 years: head of analytics/data science, product management leadership, chief-of-staff or strategy roles, startup founder, consulting. Meta's Alex Schultz is a recent example of a growth/analytics leader being promoted to chief data officer (July 2026).

tiers.label: Tier list of employers
tiers.md:
Tier groupings reflect industry consensus and practitioner perception, not objective fact.
- Tier 1: Meta, Google, Netflix, Airbnb, Uber, Stripe, DoorDash, Pinterest, Snap. Highest total compensation (Netflix US$500k, DoorDash and Stripe US$450k median on Levels.fyi), most rigorous experimentation cultures and tooling, but the hardest interviews and the thinnest entry intake.
- Tier 2: Microsoft, Amazon, Spotify, Booking.com, Zalando, Delivery Hero, Wolt, Revolut, Monzo, Grab, Rakuten. Strong analytics, pay 30-50% below Tier 1 in the US, closer in Europe, broader scope.
- Tier 3: retailers, telecoms, media, marketplaces and fintechs outside the top group; agencies. Smaller teams, less mature experimentation, more dashboard work, lower pay, more generalist learning.

enter.label: How to enter
enter.md:
- Degrees and backgrounds: Bachelor's in statistics, mathematics, economics, computer science, engineering or a quantitative social science; a master's is common at the top firms but not required. Economists with causal-inference training are a classic feeder. Bachelor's is BLS's typical entry requirement for data scientists; some employers want a master's.
- Internships and graduate programmes: US tech internships (summer, applications opened in the preceding autumn). Monzo's Associate Data Scientist internship (London, STEM/CS degree graduating 2028, SQL and Looker; employer listing, 30 Sep 2026) is an example of European early-stage hiring. Recruiting calendars: US autumn (Aug-Oct) for the following summer; UK graduate schemes open Aug-Sep and many close Sept-Dec (consensus, consistent with the banking examples in 3.5).
- Interviews: for Meta, a recruiter screen, a technical phone screen on SQL and probability, then a 4-5 round virtual onsite covering SQL (window functions, rolling averages), product sense (define metrics and guardrails for a fictional app), experimentation (sample size, power, novelty and network effects), statistics intuition and behavioural questions (Interview Query and Glassdoor candidate reports, 2025-26; anecdotal). Take-homes are common at smaller firms.
- Certifications: do not matter here; a portfolio does. Skills and portfolio: strong SQL, Python (pandas, statsmodels), hypothesis testing, causal inference basics (Mostly Harmless Econometrics-style methods), a project with a real experiment or natural experiment (e.g. a public dataset where you estimate the effect of a policy or a price change).
- Common mistakes: overweighting machine learning (product roles test SQL and judgement), ignoring business context, reporting p-values without effect sizes, poor communication.
- Alternative routes: analyst → data scientist after 1-3 years inside the same company; business or marketing graduates can reach product analytics via strong SQL, a statistics minor and a reference project; non-target schools rely on projects and smaller firms.
- Entry difficulty: 4/5 at Tier 1 and 2 (hundreds of applicants per opening, consensus; 2025-26 junior freeze), 3/5 elsewhere.

downsides.label: Honest downsides and who it is NOT a good fit for
downsides.md: Entry intake has contracted as AI tools absorb routine analysis; the role at some firms has become a dashboard-and-ad-hoc-queries job with limited influence; experiments often produce flat results and stakeholders may ignore them; US big-tech layoffs happen. Not a good fit if you want to build models all day (that is ML data science or ML engineering) or you dislike negotiating with product managers.
