roles.title: Operations manager (manufacturing, retail, services)

what.label: What you actually do
what.md: Run the daily output of a plant, warehouse, store cluster, call centre or service operation. Concrete tasks: set shift schedules, resolve absences, monitor OEE (overall equipment effectiveness, the share of planned time a machine makes good product), investigate quality defects, manage health-and-safety incidents, control labour and overtime budgets, and lead improvement projects (Lean, 5S, Kaizen). Deliverables: daily/weekly performance reviews, budget variance reports, root-cause analyses, headcount plans. Tools: ERP/MES (manufacturing execution systems), Excel, Power BI, and standard Lean tools.

day.label: A typical day and week
day.md: "You run the 7am shift handover for 40 operators, chase a late supplier, sign off an overtime request, and present weekly OEE figures to the plant manager on Thursday." Prospects' production manager profile describes 40-45 hours a week, sometimes starting before 7am, with shift work, weekend on-call and extra hours for deadlines or new systems (Prospects, accessed Oct 2026). BLS notes industrial production managers may be on call for emergencies and some work night or weekend shifts (BLS, May 2025 edition).

hours.label: Hours, stress and lifestyle
hours.md:
- Hours: 45-50 per week typical; peak 60+ during launches, shutdowns, peak season or incidents (Prospects gives 40-45 as the baseline; peak is practitioner consensus).
- Stress: 4/5 (incidents, targets and people problems land on you, often outside office hours).
- Lifestyle: on-site, early starts, on-call. Low flexibility; no remote work on the shop floor.
- Travel: moderate between sites; international for multi-site manufacturers.

profile.label: Human vs. quantitative profile
profile.md: People/communication: 4/5. Quantitative/technical: 3/5. You lead and coach shop-floor teams and handle conflict; you also read production, cost and quality data and use basic statistics for process improvement.

pay.label: Compensation (approximate)
pay.md:
- US: BLS median pay for industrial production managers is $126,060 (May 2025), but BLS notes five years of related experience is typical; for general and operations managers, secondary sites quote $102,950 (May 2024, not verified at bls.gov). New-graduate Amazon Area Managers appear at about $65,000-$75,000 (single aggregator listing, 2026).
- UK: Prospects: trainee production managers about £24,000-£39,000; after about two years often over £40,000 (average about £44,000); experienced or senior £50,000-£63,000, up to about £78,000. Payscale (aggregator, 2026) gives plant managers an average of £68,784 (base £50k-£113k) and operations directors £68,510. Amazon UK early-career £27k-£45k (Payscale).
- Italy: no reliable role-level data found. A contractual floor for a metalworking-industry level D1 employee is €1,784.94 gross a month from 1 June 2026 (CCNL metalmeccanici renewal, DottrinaLavoro), paid over 13 or more monthly instalments, so about €23,200+ a year before supplements (my arithmetic); graduates are normally placed above the minimum and plant managers are paid under individual agreements (managerial contracts such as dirigenti). Payscale lists "Project Manager, Operations" at an average of €45,009 in Italy (2026; mixed seniority).
- Dubai: Payscale (aggregator) puts an experienced operations manager with project-management skills at roughly AED 168k a year (about AED 14,000 a month, my conversion; labels hard to read).
- Asia: no reliable data for operations managers.

path.label: Career path
path.md: Shift or team lead / operations supervisor (0-2 years) → operations manager / department manager (3-6 years) → senior operations manager or plant manager (7-12 years) → director of operations, VP operations or COO (12-20 years). Lean credentials help but experience dominates: BLS typically asks for five or more years of related experience for production and top-executive roles.

exits.label: Exit opportunities
exits.md:
- After 2-3 years: supply chain planning, continuous improvement or quality roles, procurement, project management, an MBA.
- After 7-10 years: plant manager or operations director in a smaller firm, consulting operations practice, general manager of a business unit, COO of an SME, entrepreneurship in a family business.

tiers.label: Tier list of employers
tiers.md:
- Tier 1: companies known for operations excellence and training managers: global FMCG (P&G, Unilever, Nestlé, Ferrero), automotive and industrial groups (BMW, Siemens), pharma plants. Strong Lean culture, structured career ladders, international transfers.
- Tier 2: e-commerce and large logistics (Amazon: managers can lead 300-500 staff at the Operations Manager level per Amazon Pathways page), supermarkets, large retailers, airlines, utilities. High responsibility early, high turnover pressure.
- Tier 3: SMEs, subcontract manufacturers, small chains. Less training, wider scope, pay depends on the owner.
- Tier groupings reflect industry consensus and practitioner perception, not objective fact.

enter.label: How to enter
enter.md:
- Degrees: business or management, engineering, sciences, logistics. Unrelated degrees can work with study for professional qualifications; apprenticeships (Level 4 Process Leader; Level 6 Manufacturing Management in the UK) and promotion from technician or team leader are also real routes (Prospects).
- Programmes: Amazon Area Manager (US) / Graduate Ops Area/Shift Manager (UK); Ferrero International Graduate Program in Lean and Continuous Improvement; BMW AcceleratiON; Rheinmetall trainee; supermarket area manager schemes.
- Calendar: UK schemes recruit from autumn for the next September; Amazon recruits on a rolling basis with several start dates (July-October 2026 in the UK listing).
- Assessment: online tests, behavioural interview, site visit or assessment day; Amazon uses situational and leadership-principle interviews (general knowledge; unverified here).
- Certifications: Lean Six Sigma Green Belt is the common one. Aggregators report a salary gap (Payscale 2025: about $96,000 for Green Belt holders vs $76,000 for White Belt; Lightcast: median advertised $103,000), but this is correlation, not proof, and the sources are weak. Employer-paid training is better than paying yourself. Also useful: NEBOSH/IOSH (health and safety) in the UK, depending on sector.
- Skills: shop-floor credibility, Excel, root-cause analysis, basic labour law, conflict handling.
- Common mistakes: never having worked a shift; imposing theory on experienced operators.
- Non-target routes: start as a team leader, shift supervisor, or quality officer.
- Entry difficulty: 2/5 for supervisor and team-leader routes (many openings); 3/5 for named schemes such as Amazon or FMCG, where ISE shows heavy competition.

downsides.label: Honest downsides and who it is NOT a good fit for
downsides.md: Shift work, early starts, weekend call-outs and accountability for safety incidents are real. Pay at entry is low outside retail and logistics schemes. Poor fit: people who want a pure desk job, predictable evenings, or analytical work without people conflict.

roles.title: Project / programme manager

what.label: What you actually do
what.md: Define scope, plan, budget and run change projects. Typical tasks: build a work breakdown and schedule, run the risk and issue log, track budget and resources, hold weekly status meetings and steering committees, manage vendors, report to sponsors. A PMO analyst/coordinator (the usual entry job) maintains plans, collects updates, produces dashboards and runs governance packs. Tools: MS Project/Excel/PowerPoint, Jira/Asana/Smartsheet, and ServiceNow or similar for IT change. Programme managers also manage benefits and dependencies across projects.

day.label: A typical day and week
day.md: "Monday status call with five workstream leads, Tuesday risk review with the sponsor, midweek chasing an overdue vendor deliverable and updating the plan, Thursday steering committee deck, Friday re-forecasting the budget." Prospects: normal business hours Monday to Friday, extra hours at deadlines, paid overtime unlikely, home working common, some client/team travel (Prospects, accessed Oct 2026). BLS: normally business hours, but flexibility may be needed across time zones.

hours.label: Hours, stress and lifestyle
hours.md:
- Hours: 40-45 per week; peak 50-55 around go-live, delivery deadlines or a failed milestone (practitioner consensus).
- Stress: 3/5 (deadline-driven, accountability without formal authority; 4/5 on a crisis project).
- Lifestyle: most flexible of the role families here; hybrid common (Prospects).
- Travel: moderate for client or multi-site projects.

profile.label: Human vs. quantitative profile
profile.md: People/communication: 4/5. Quantitative/technical: 2/5. The job is stakeholders and follow-up; numeracy is budgets and schedules. In IT and engineering, domain knowledge matters more than methodology (Prospects).

pay.label: Compensation (approximate)
pay.md:
- US: BLS median for project management specialists is $102,320 (May 2025). PMI's 14th Earning Power survey (Nov 2025) shows US PMP-certified respondents at a median $135,000 vs $109,157 for non-certified (a 24% gap) and a 17% premium across 21 countries; pharma/aerospace median $150,000 (PMI press release 13 Nov 2025). Self-selected sample; correlation, not proof. Entry-level US pay: no reliable data found.
- UK: junior project managers £30,000-£38,000; experienced £45,000-£80,000; senior above £100,000; contractors £350-£750 a day (Prospects, accessed Oct 2026). APM Salary Survey 2025 (3,800 respondents, YouGov, Oct-Nov 2024): average £52,500, up from £47,500 in 2023; APM Project Management Qualification holders £57,500; chartered £82,500; London highest (30% of London respondents earn £70,000+) (APM, 2025). PMO figures from the older APM survey (Nov 2020: PMO officer £32,500, PMO manager £55,000) are outdated.
- Italy: no reliable role-level data from recruiter guides. Payscale: "Project Manager, Operations" average €45,009 (early-career €33k-€50k) (aggregator, 2026); Indeed Italy average €39,015 from postings (July 2026). Treat as rough.
- Dubai: an Institute of Project Management guide (training provider, 2026) gives AED 12,000-45,000 a month, average about AED 22,000; weak source.
- Asia: no reliable data found.

path.label: Career path
path.md: Project coordinator / PMO analyst (0-2 years) → project manager (2-5) → senior project manager (5-8) → programme manager (8-12) → head of PMO / portfolio director (12+). Titles vary; "delivery manager" and "scrum master" are adjacent. Chartered status (APM) and a PMP help at senior level in the UK and US.

exits.label: Exit opportunities
exits.md:
- After 2-3 years: product or operations roles, business analyst, consulting associate (implementation), change management.
- After 7-10 years: programme director, head of transformation, COO-track roles, independent contracting (UK day rates £350-£750 per Prospects), consulting.

tiers.label: Tier list of employers
tiers.md:
- Tier 1: employers with large capital or transformation programmes and mature PMOs: big pharma, aerospace, energy and utilities, large banks' change functions, Big 4/consulting delivery teams (APM: energy/utilities and consultancy £62,500 average UK; PMI: pharma and aerospace $150,000 US median).
- Tier 2: corporates' IT/PMO teams in telecoms, retail, insurance; construction and engineering contractors.
- Tier 3: small agencies, public bodies with tight budgets, small firms where "project manager" means administration (APM reports government and public sector lower; sector breakdown beyond top two not fully read).
- Tier groupings reflect industry consensus and practitioner perception, not objective fact.

enter.label: How to enter
enter.md:
- Degrees: any degree accepted (business, engineering, computer science common) (Prospects). Many enter via support, administrative or technical jobs (Prospects).
- Programmes: employer graduate schemes in IT or engineering, PMO analyst roles, consultancy delivery analyst roles. I did not find a dedicated "project management graduate programme" list; unverified.
- Calendar: PMO analyst roles hire year-round; large employers' graduate schemes follow the usual autumn cycle.
- Assessment: interview, scenario questions on risk and stakeholders; sometimes a case study.
- Certifications: CAPM (PMI): needs a secondary diploma and 23 hours of project management education, no experience (training providers restating PMI, 2024-26; PMI's page could not be opened). PMP: four-year degree plus 36 months leading projects plus 35 hours of education or CAPM; 60 months with a high-school diploma. PRINCE2 (PeopleCert/AXELOS): common in UK public sector and some corporates; APM Project Management Qualification; Scrum (PSM/CSM) and PMI-ACP in tech. Whether they matter: PMP counts in the US, Gulf and large engineering/pharma; PRINCE2 and APM in the UK; for graduates they are a differentiator but not a gate. BLS does not require certification. A UK training-provider blog reports median PRINCE2 PM salary fell from £62,500 (2023) to £47,500 (2025), so a certificate is not a salary guarantee (secondary source).
- Skills: planning, Excel/PowerPoint, clear status reports, managing without authority.
- Common mistakes: collecting certifications with no project experience; treating the role as scheduling rather than stakeholder management.
- Non-target routes: start as PMO analyst or business analyst; volunteer to run a student project and document it as a case.
- Entry difficulty: 2/5 (many openings, any graduate; larger programmes 3/5).

downsides.label: Honest downsides and who it is NOT a good fit for
downsides.md: Accountability without authority, blame when dependencies slip, and meeting overload. Roles at the junior end are administrative. AI and automation target status reporting, so the coordinator role may shrink (inference, not sourced). Poor fit: people who need deep technical craft, or dislike chasing people.

roles.title: HR / people professional (HRBP, talent acquisition, L&D, reward)

what.label: What you actually do
what.md: HR generalists/officers handle contracts, onboarding, absence, policy questions and case work. HRBPs advise a business unit's leaders on structure, performance, hiring and restructuring. Talent acquisition (TA) specialists source, screen and interview candidates and manage hiring managers. L&D designs training and capability programmes. Reward (compensation and benefits) runs pay reviews, salary benchmarking, bonus and benefits design. Tools: HRIS systems (Workday, SAP SuccessFactors), applicant-tracking systems, Excel, survey tools, and increasingly AI screening tools.

day.label: A typical day and week
day.md: "Tuesday: hiring-manager call about three open roles, review a probation case with a line manager, answer payroll queries, prepare data for the monthly headcount report; Thursday: sit in on a disciplinary hearing." Prospects: standard 37-hour Monday-Friday, occasional shift or weekend work; TargetJobs: 9-5 at officer level; on-call when working in small teams; National Careers Service: 38-40 hours.

hours.label: Hours, stress and lifestyle
hours.md:
- Hours: 38-45 per week; peak 50+ during restructures, annual pay rounds and graduate recruitment season (practitioner consensus).
- Stress: 3/5 (emotionally heavy cases, 4/5 during redundancies; payroll or compliance errors are costly).
- Lifestyle: office-based but increasingly hybrid; predictable.
- Travel: low, except recruiters (BLS: recruiters may travel).

profile.label: Human vs. quantitative profile
profile.md: People/communication: 5/5. Quantitative/technical: 2/5 (reward and people analytics are 3-4/5). It is relationship and judgement work; the numerate subfields (reward, workforce planning, HR analytics) pay more.

pay.label: Compensation (approximate)
pay.md:
- US: BLS median pay: HR specialists $75,940 (May 2025; 939,700 jobs; +6% growth 2025-35); HR managers $149,280 (5+ years' experience); compensation and benefits managers $149,230 (growth +1%); training and development managers $133,000 (BLS, May 2025). Entry-level: no reliable data found beyond BLS median.
- UK: Prospects (using CIPD HR-inform data): HR officer £30,681-£51,800, rising to £35,923-£60,650 with experience; National Careers Service: £24,000 starter to £40,000 experienced; a TargetJobs graduate HR listing offered £34,000 plus £2,000 welcome payment (deadline 31 October 2025, so a 2025 intake). Senior HRBP adverts from Michael Page show £80,000-£95,000 (undated adverts); Robert Walters' UK HRBP page gives London ranges of £60k-£135k (2026, range across seniority). Aggregator figures (£42k-£75k for HRBP) conflict.
- Italy: no reliable recruiter-guide data accessible. A secondary site attributing figures to Michael Page 2026 gives HR Manager gross €60,000-65,000 with under 5 years, €65,000-70,000 at 5-10 years, €70,000-80,000 beyond (unverified); the same site cites Hays 2026 for a junior HR manager (2-5 years) at €49,000-60,000 (unverified). Entry-level pay: no reliable data found.
- Dubai: a Michael Page UAE 2026 summary (via whatson.ae) puts entry-level TA specialists, L&D officers and HR coordinators at about AED 25,000 a month on average (secondary; seems high for true entry-level, treat with caution); HR manager AED 20,000-35,000 a month in a 2024 Cooper Fitch figure quoted by a secondary site.
- Asia (HK/SG/Tokyo): no reliable data found.

path.label: Career path
path.md: HR assistant/coordinator or graduate scheme (0-2 years) → HR advisor/officer or TA specialist (2-4) → HRBP / senior specialist (4-8) → HR manager / head of reward, L&D or TA (8-12) → HR director / CHRO (15+). BLS asks for five years' experience to be a manager. In the UK the CIPD levels (3 foundation, 5 associate, 7 advanced) map onto this ladder.

exits.label: Exit opportunities
exits.md:
- After 2-3 years: another HR specialism, recruitment agency, people analytics, L&D in consulting, operations or project roles.
- After 7-10 years: HR director, reward or talent consultancy, in-house leadership in smaller firms, independent HR consulting, employee relations/legal-adjacent roles with further study.

tiers.label: Tier list of employers
tiers.md:
- Tier 1: large multinational HR graduate programmes with rotations (Unilever Future Leaders HR stream, LVMH SPRING Human Resources with three 8-month missions, Amazon graduate HR roles), plus the big reward/talent consultancies (named from general knowledge, not verified this round: Mercer, WTW, Aon, Korn Ferry).
- Tier 2: large banks, pharma, tech and industrial groups with HR centres of expertise; public sector and NHS-type HR (more stable, lower pay).
- Tier 3: SMEs, recruitment agencies, charities (broad exposure, less structure, lower pay).
- Tier groupings reflect industry consensus and practitioner perception, not objective fact.

enter.label: How to enter
enter.md:
- Degrees: HR, business, psychology, communications or any discipline (BLS; National Careers Service).
- Programmes: Unilever Future Leadership Programme - Human Resources UK (closing date 12 October 2026 per search listing); LVMH SPRING HR; Amazon graduate HR partner roles (a visa-sponsor site shows about £41,911 for one listing, secondary).
- Calendar: UK graduate schemes open September-December; many HR entry jobs (assistant, coordinator, recruiter) are advertised year-round. Italy: stage in the HR office of a firm or a master in HR (Bocconi, Cattolica-type) is the usual route (general knowledge; unverified).
- Assessment: online application, psychometric tests, interview, assessment centre; role-plays on handling an employee case.
- Certifications: CIPD Level 3 has no entry requirement; Level 5 suits people with some HR work or a degree; Level 7 is postgraduate-level (BPP, ICS, National Careers Service naming). SHRM-CP in the US: SHRM says no HR title, degree or prior experience is required, though working knowledge of HR is recommended (SHRM eligibility page); SHRM-SCP needs three years in strategic HR duties (or three years as SHRM-CP). BLS notes certification is usually voluntary. CIPD matters in the UK/Ireland for HR careers beyond entry; SHRM matters in the US; in Italy the equivalent credibility comes from a master's in HR and, for payroll/labour relations, knowledge of the CCNL system.
- Skills: communication, confidentiality, employment-law basics, Excel/HRIS, people analytics.
- Common mistakes: choosing HR for "liking people" without wanting to handle conflict and compliance; ignoring commercial understanding of the business.
- Non-target routes: HR administrator or recruitment coordinator, internal transfer from operations; CIPD studied alongside a first job.
- Entry difficulty: 3/5 (HR graduate schemes are competitive; entry via assistant/coordinator roles is easier at 2/5).

downsides.label: Honest downsides and who it is NOT a good fit for
downsides.md: HR can be seen as a cost centre; you carry the dismissals and the "policy police" role; early-career work is administrative; automation targets recruiting screening and admin. BLS shows modest growth (6% for specialists; 1% for compensation and benefits managers). Poor fit: people who dislike emotionally heavy conversations, ambiguity, or being the messenger of unpopular decisions.

roles.title: Corporate strategy and business development (in-house)

what.label: What you actually do
what.md: Corporate strategy: build the annual or multi-year plan, model markets and competitors, assess acquisition targets and new-market entries, prepare board and CEO papers, run strategic initiatives. Business development/partnerships: identify potential partners or customers, structure and negotiate deals, manage joint ventures and alliances. Deliverables: market sizing models, strategy decks, deal memos, business cases, partnership term sheets. Tools: Excel/financial models, PowerPoint, market databases (Statista, Bloomberg-type), CRM for BD.

day.label: A typical day and week
day.md: "Monday refresh a market-sizing model for the CFO, Tuesday interview a division head for the plan, Wednesday draft the board paper, Thursday call with a potential partner's BD team, Friday review with the head of strategy." Planning and board cycles create peaks.

hours.label: Hours, stress and lifestyle
hours.md:
- Hours: 45-55 per week; peak 60-70 near annual planning, board meetings or a live acquisition (practitioner consensus; no published statistic found).
- Stress: 3/5 (lower than consulting but 4/5 around live deals).
- Lifestyle: office/hybrid, mostly HQ-based; some travel for partner meetings.

profile.label: Human vs. quantitative profile
profile.md: People/communication: 4/5. Quantitative/technical: 4/5. You must persuade executives and run models; BD leans more to negotiation (people 5/5) than strategy.

pay.label: Compensation (approximate)
pay.md:
- US: Payscale (aggregator, 2026): Corporate Strategy Manager base $96k-$177k, median about $123k, bonus $5k-$73k; early-career corporate strategy manager base $79k-$116k, median about $100k. A 2025 H-1B filing for an Adobe Corporate Development/Strategy Partner in San Francisco shows $140,000 base (single data point). Entry-level graduate figures: no reliable data found, since few firms hire graduates directly into strategy.
- UK, Italy, Asia, Gulf: no reliable data found.

path.label: Career path
path.md: Typically 2-5 years in consulting, banking or an operating role first, then analyst/associate in strategy (year 3-5) → strategy manager (6-9) → director/head of strategy (10-15) → chief strategy officer or divisional general manager (15+). Direct graduate hires exist in some large firms (rotational "strategy and corporate development" programmes) but are rare; unverified for specific firms.

exits.label: Exit opportunities
exits.md:
- After 2-3 years: commercial roles (marketing, sales operations), product, a business-unit role, MBA; or join the consulting firm you used to buy from.
- After 7-10 years: general-manager or P&L (profit and loss) ownership of a division, CSO, start-up founder, PE/VC.

tiers.label: Tier list of employers
tiers.md:
- Tier 1: strategy teams of large technology, pharma, energy and financial groups, which hire from top consultancies and have board access (examples not verified by firm this round).
- Tier 2: mid-size listed corporates, regional champions, large family groups with a strategy function.
- Tier 3: small firms where "strategy" means the owner plus one analyst, or "business development" is mainly sales.
- Tier groupings reflect industry consensus and practitioner perception, not objective fact.

enter.label: How to enter
enter.md:
- Degrees: business, economics, engineering, sciences plus a strong quantitative record; master's or MBA common. Strategy is rarely a first job.
- Programmes: some corporates offer rotational schemes with a strategy rotation (Unilever/Nestlé-type); I did not verify a specific "corporate strategy graduate programme".
- Calendar: usually through the group's standard graduate cycle (autumn) or lateral hiring from consulting.
- Assessment: case study, modelling test, executive interviews.
- Certifications: not important. CFA/other finance credentials matter only for corporate development.
- Skills: modelling, structured thinking, writing for executives, industry knowledge.
- Common mistakes: expecting to start in strategy at 22; weak commercial grounding.
- Non-target routes: join the company in a commercial, finance or operations job and transfer in after 2-4 years; take a rotation in a strategy team; BD roles in start-ups.
- Entry difficulty: 4/5 as a graduate hire; 3/5 for BD roles in smaller firms.

downsides.label: Honest downsides and who it is NOT a good fit for
downsides.md: Small teams mean few seats and slow promotion (forum advice: leaving consulting often means a pay cut or a lateral move; anecdotal). Impact is limited if the executive team ignores the plan. Poor fit: people who need hands-on delivery, or want a clear promotion ladder.

roles.title: Public-sector and non-profit manager (shorter)

what.label: What you actually do
what.md: Policy, programme or operational management in government or NGOs: draft briefings and policy options, manage budgets and grants, run service-delivery teams, handle ministerial or board questions, and monitor funded programmes. Tools: Word/Excel/PowerPoint, case-management systems, grant-management and monitoring frameworks.

day.label: A typical day and week
day.md: Meetings with stakeholders, writing and clearing briefings through several approval layers, managing a team's casework, and responding to parliamentary or press queries. Hours are mostly regular.

hours.label: Hours, stress and lifestyle
hours.md:
- Hours: 37-45 per week; peaks 50+ around budgets, crises or elections (practitioner consensus).
- Stress: 2/5 typically (3/5 for politically exposed posts or field NGOs).
- Lifestyle: stable; hybrid common in the UK and EU institutions; field NGOs involve deployment.

profile.label: Human vs. quantitative profile
profile.md: People/communication: 3/5 to 4/5. Quantitative/technical: 2/5. Writing, process knowledge and stakeholder management matter more than modelling.

pay.label: Compensation (approximate)
pay.md:
- UK Fast Stream: first-year £31,554 and fourth-year £40,098 in 2025-26 (Institute for Government); a 2026-27 award was not found. The 2026 campaign was expected to open mid-October 2026 and run for four weeks (Commons written answer, May 2026); start dates in September of the following year. Eligibility is restricted by nationality (see below).
- EU institutions: a new AD5 official earns a basic €6,152.64 gross per month at step 1, about €7,137 with the 16% expatriation allowance in Brussels or Luxembourg (pay table in force from 1 July 2025, via redopositor.com; press quotes €5,000-€5,400, so the figure is secondary). Blue Book traineeship grant €1,538.16 a month (25% of AD5 step 1, per `research/careers/public-policy-and-academia.md`).
- Italy: no reliable data found on funzionario pay for the 2026 concorsi (the Ministry of Economy and Finance sought 485 funzionari in a concorso that closed 27 Jan 2026, per the public-policy file; secondary).
- US federal and NGOs: no reliable data found (not researched this pass).

path.label: Career path
path.md: UK Fast Stream: scheme years 1-4 → Grade 7 / deputy director in about 10-12 years (general knowledge; not sourced here). EU: AD5 → AD7/AD8 in 8-12 years → head of unit. NGOs: officer → programme manager → country director.

exits.label: Exit opportunities
exits.md:
- After 2-3 years: another ministry, consultancy, regulators, think tanks, large corporates' public affairs.
- After 7-10 years: head of unit/director, international organisations, consulting in the public sector, social enterprises.

tiers.label: Tier list of employers
tiers.md:
- Tier 1: Fast Stream, EU institutions (Commission, Parliament, ECB), UN family via YPP or JPO, central banks (Banca d'Italia: 45 Esperti places, 8,307 applications in Dec 2025 competition, per the public-policy file).
- Tier 2: national ministries and agencies, major INGOs, development banks.
- Tier 3: local government, small NGOs, charities.
- Tier groupings reflect industry consensus and practitioner perception, not objective fact.

enter.label: How to enter
enter.md:
- Degrees: any, with a 2:2 or above for most Fast Stream schemes; EPSO AD5 requires a three-year degree, reasoning tests, an EU-knowledge test and an essay; Italian concorsi require a laurea and written tests.
- Programmes: UK Fast Stream (generalist and specialist schemes); EPSO AD5 competition (EPSO/AD/427/26: 174,727 applicants, 1,490 reserve-list places, Italy 45% of applicants; reasoning tests planned from November 2026); Blue Book traineeship (five months, about 1,000 places per session); contract-agent database.
- Nationality: the Fast Stream is effectively closed to EU graduates who arrived after 2020 unless they have settled or pre-settled status (Civil Service Careers, as noted in the public-policy file).
- Calendar: Fast Stream applications open each autumn (2025: 10 October); EPSO competitions are announced irregularly.
- Assessment: online tests, e-tray exercises, assessment centre (Fast Stream); multiple-choice reasoning for EPSO.
- Certifications: not required; PRINCE2 or APM can help for programme-delivery roles.
- Common mistakes: treating AD5 as a safe plan (about 0.85% selection); leaving no fall-back.
- Non-target routes: Blue Book traineeship, contract agents, NGOs' entry roles, temporary civil-service roles, local government graduate schemes.
- Entry difficulty: 5/5 for Fast Stream and AD5; 2-3/5 for local government and many NGOs.

downsides.label: Honest downsides and who it is NOT a good fit for
downsides.md: Lower pay than the private sector, slow decisions, political exposure, and long selection cycles. NGOs often pay little and rely on short grants. Poor fit: people who need fast promotion, high pay or clear individual attribution of results.

roles.title: Buyer / procurement specialist / category manager

what.label: What you actually do
what.md: You source suppliers, run RFQs and tenders, negotiate price and terms, manage contracts, track supplier performance, and fix problems (late delivery, quality failure, price rise request). At category-manager level you own a spend category and its multi-year strategy and savings target. Tools: ERP purchasing modules (SAP Ariba or similar), spend-cube spreadsheets, e-sourcing platforms, supplier risk databases. Deliverables: savings reports, sourcing strategies, signed contracts. Example: you replace a Chinese packaging supplier hit by a new tariff with a Polish one, re-validate quality samples, and negotiate a 6% saving against a 4% price rise elsewhere.

day.label: A typical day and week
day.md: Morning: review open purchase orders and supplier messages in ERP; midday: price negotiation call with a supplier and an internal meeting with engineering on specifications; afternoon: update a savings tracker and draft a tender document. Weekly: category review with the business owner, supplier performance meeting, month-end savings reporting. Senior roles add board-level supplier risk reviews.

hours.label: Hours, stress and lifestyle
hours.md: Typical 37-45 hours a week; peaks 50-55 when a supplier fails or at month/quarter end. UK Prospects gives 37-40 hours mostly office-based, with occasional overseas travel (Prospects, CIPS salary guide 2025 data). Stress: 3/5 (rises to 4 in direct procurement when a plant is about to stop). Hybrid working is common in indirect procurement and office-based sourcing; direct buyers are often at or near plants. Supplier visits and trade shows mean occasional travel, more for category managers who audit suppliers in Asia.

profile.label: Human vs. quantitative profile
profile.md: People/communication: 4/5. Quantitative/technical: 3/5. Negotiation, influencing internal stakeholders and reading contracts matter as much as cost modelling; the maths is mostly total-cost-of-ownership, price indices and spreadsheet analysis.

pay.label: Compensation (approximate)
pay.md:
- US: BLS median for buyers and purchasing agents US$77,710 (May 2025), lowest 10% under US$48,380, highest 10% above US$128,870 (BLS). Entry in practice roughly US$50-65k (inferred from the BLS low end and ASCM; no reliable direct entry figure found). ASCM's 2025 report puts the median buyer at US$69,300 and procurement managers at US$95,000-142,700 (ASCM 2025 salary report via Supply Chain 24/7). BLS purchasing managers' median was US$139,510 (May 2024).
- UK: entry about GBP 27,000; purchasing officers about GBP 28,000 up to 40,000; procurement/purchasing managers about GBP 54,576, rising to about GBP 76,000; very senior over GBP 122,000 (Prospects quoting the 2025 CIPS Procurement Salary Guide).
- Italy: no reliable data found for general buyers. Indicative: junior procurement specialist EUR 30-38k and technical buyer EUR 32-40k in renewable energy (Talenty.green 2026 guide; sector-specific and likely above average); a training-site table gives EUR 30-38k for "Responsabile acquisti e logistica" at 0-2 years (Masterin.it, weak source). Mercer data show average first-job pay of EUR 30,500 in Italy (ItaliaOggi, 2024).
- Singapore: buyer/planner about S$50k, S$75k, S$90k at 5-10, 10-15 and 15+ years (Morgan McKinley 2025 permanent data); procurement managers about S$110-115k at 5-10 years (Morgan McKinley, 2025-26). Entry not given.

path.label: Career path
path.md: Junior buyer/purchasing assistant (0-2 years) → buyer/procurement specialist (2-4) → senior buyer or category manager (4-8) → procurement manager / head of category (8-12) → director / chief procurement officer (12+). Large companies run rotational programmes; smaller ones may require changing employer to progress (Prospects).

exits.label: Exit opportunities
exits.md: After 2-3 years: planning, supplier quality, project procurement, or procurement at a larger or better-known firm. After 7-10 years: head of procurement, supply chain director, consulting (procurement/cost-reduction practices), private-equity operating partner roles at the senior end, or moving into commercial/contract management.

tiers.label: Tier list of employers
tiers.md:
Tier groupings reflect industry consensus and practitioner perception, not objective fact.
- *Tier 1 (large, structured, best brand and training):* Gartner Supply Chain Top 25 style companies, the 2025 list led by Schneider Electric (No. 1) and NVIDIA (No. 2), with "Masters" Amazon, Apple, P&G and Unilever (Gartner 2025, via Supply Chain 24/7); also large pharma, automotive OEMs (VW, BMW, Stellantis) and defence primes. Sizeable category scope, formal programmes, but narrow slices at entry.
- *Tier 2 (large industrial and consumer groups, strong regional brands):* Italian groups such as Barilla, Ferrero, Luxottica/EssilorLuxottica, Pirelli, Leonardo, Fincantieri (employer names in Italy are general knowledge, programmes and procurement hiring not verified), mid-cap manufacturers, big retailers' buying teams.
- *Tier 3 (smaller firms, distributors, public bodies):* wider variety, faster responsibility but weaker structured training; public sector (NHS Procurement Graduate Scheme is a two-year paid programme, Prospects).

enter.label: How to enter
enter.md: Business, supply chain, economics, engineering (for technical buying), or any degree plus procurement exposure. Programmes: Unilever Future Leaders Programme supply chain track (36 months in the UK, STEM, other science-based or supply chain degrees; UK window ended 12 October 2026 per a careers mirror; Dutch track closed 21 March 2026 and asks for a Dutch WO master's); P&G supply chain graduate roles; NHS Procurement Graduate Scheme; Maersk, DHL and Kuehne+Nagel programmes mostly lean logistics-side rather than procurement (Maersk has run procurement graduate programmes in other markets, e.g. South Africa 2021, not currently verified). Recruiting calendar: UK large-company schemes open from autumn and close roughly November-March; Prospects advises looking from late October; Dutch tracks close around March. Certifications: CIPS (Chartered Institute of Procurement & Supply; MCIPS needs accredited qualification, three years' experience and ethics certificate, CPD of 30 hours a year per Prospects) matters in the UK and for Commonwealth/Gulf employers; CPSM (ISM) is the US equivalent (unverified, BLS does not name it); in Italy and Germany certifications matter much less than a relevant master's. Skills: Excel, a spend-analysis tool, SAP or Ariba familiarity, contract basics, negotiation practice, Power BI. Common mistakes: applying only to big-name schemes; underestimating how important commodity or technical knowledge is in direct buying. Alternative routes: start as purchasing assistant and do a CIPS apprenticeship (levels 3, 4 and 6) or take a first job in customer service or planning at a manufacturer. Entry difficulty: 2/5.

downsides.label: Honest downsides and who it is NOT a good fit for
downsides.md: Cost-saving targets can push you into unpleasant negotiations and conflicts with engineers and sales; you are often the person blamed for late materials; strategic sourcing roles at well-known employers are fewer than operational buying roles; AI and automation are removing routine "tail-spend" purchasing work. Not a good fit for people who dislike confrontation or who want a mostly analytical, solo job.

compare.name: Buyer / procurement / category manager
compare.pay: US about US$50-65k base (inferred; BLS buyer median US$77,710 all levels, 2025) / GBP 27k base (CIPS 2025) / about EUR 30-38k energy-sector junior (2026, weak); general Italy: no reliable data

summary: US about US$50-65k base (inferred; BLS buyer median US$77,710 all levels, 2025) / GBP 27k base (CIPS 2025) / about EUR 30-38k energy-sector junior (2026, weak); general Italy: no reliable data

roles.title: Demand / supply planner and S&OP analyst

what.label: What you actually do
what.md: A demand planner produces and improves the statistical forecast, adjusts it for promotions and launches, and works with sales on consensus. A supply planner converts that into a production and purchasing plan against capacity, materials and lead times. An S&OP/IBP analyst prepares the monthly cycle: gap analysis, scenarios, financial view. Tools: SAP IBP, Kinaxis RapidResponse/Maestro, o9, Blue Yonder, Excel and SQL/Power BI. Example: you re-run the 12-week forecast in SAP IBP, find a 20% shortfall on a top SKU after a competitor's promotion, and negotiate an expedited air shipment while telling finance the margin impact.

day.label: A typical day and week
day.md: Morning: check overnight system exceptions (stock-outs, overstocks, late POs); midday: sales/customer forecast review; afternoon: supply review with plants and procurement; weekly: demand review, supply review, then the S&OP executive meeting once a month. Month-end is heavy; during disruptions (tariffs, port closures) you replan constantly.

hours.label: Hours, stress and lifestyle
hours.md: 40-45 hours typical; 50-55 in S&OP weeks or crises. Stress: 3/5, spiking to 4 during shortages. Largely office-based and hybrid-friendly; limited travel (some plant visits). Time-zone calls for global teams are common (e.g. P&G's Warsaw hub works across Europe).

profile.label: Human vs. quantitative profile
profile.md: People/communication: 3/5. Quantitative/technical: 4/5. The maths is forecasting error metrics, safety stock formulas and heavy spreadsheet or SQL work; the people part is negotiating a forecast with sales who over-promise and operations who under-deliver.

pay.label: Compensation (approximate)
pay.md:
- US: ASCM 2025 report shows analysts at a median of US$85,000 across all levels (ASCM via Supply Chain 24/7); supply chain managers US$100,000-145,000; supply chain directors US$160,000-184,200 (ASCM 2025). Entry planner pay: no reliable data found (inferred US$55-70k from BLS logistician/buyer ranges; weak).
- UK: coordinators, planners and analysts GBP 27,000-29,000 rising to about GBP 37,000 (Prospects, current page); P&G graduate GBP 37,000 plus bonus (2024 cycle); DHL Supply Chain graduate programme GBP 30,500 plus GBP 500 joining payment (2027 start).
- Italy: Milan junior demand planner at a staffing agency RAL EUR 25-28k under the CCNL Commercio (a single job listing); a training-site table gives EUR 26-32k for logistics analysts at 0-2 years (Masterin.it, weak). Aggregated averages (Jooble) are not reliable for junior pay.
- Singapore: planning manager about S$115k / S$160k / S$200k at 5-10, 10-15 and 15+ years (Morgan McKinley 2026 contract bands, not permanent).

path.label: Career path
path.md: Planning analyst/junior planner (0-2) → demand or supply planner (2-4) → senior planner / S&OP lead (4-7) → planning manager (7-10) → supply chain director / VP planning (12+). Graduate schemes at FMCG often rotate through planning, logistics and procurement for 2-3 years.

exits.label: Exit opportunities
exits.md: After 2-3 years: procurement, logistics, project roles, planning-systems roles, or specialist planning at another industry. After 7-10 years: head of supply chain, S&OP/IBP transformation lead, supply chain consulting, planning-software vendor roles (solution consultant), or general operations management.

tiers.label: Tier list of employers
tiers.md:
Tier groupings reflect industry consensus and practitioner perception, not objective fact.
- *Tier 1:* P&G, Unilever, Nestle, Coca-Cola, big pharma, Apple/Amazon, major electronics firms; structured rotations, sophisticated tools and strong CV value (Gartner Top 25 "Masters" include P&G, Unilever, Amazon, Apple).
- *Tier 2:* Italian and European consumer and industrial companies, retailers' central planning teams, specialised planning consultancies and system integrators (Accenture, Capgemini, Deloitte, boutiques around Kinaxis/o9/SAP).
- *Tier 3:* SMEs and distributors (often planning in Excel with less tool exposure; broader responsibility, narrower training).

enter.label: How to enter
enter.md: Supply chain management, industrial engineering/ingegneria gestionale, economics, mathematics, statistics or business; engineering or science helps for Unilever's UK track. Programmes: Unilever Future Leaders Programme (supply chain, 36 months; includes roles such as response planner, logistics projects and procurement executive), P&G supply network operations programme (Warsaw hub roles in production planning, demand planning, materials supply, artwork, distribution), DHL Supply Chain Supply Chain & Logistics Specialist Graduate Programme (2-2.5 years, any degree subject, no minimum grade, September 2027 start, no visa sponsorship), DE&S Operations Supply Chain Graduate Scheme (UK, two years, GBP 27,840-28,880, SC security clearance required). Calendar: typically autumn to early spring for large schemes (see 3.1). Certifications: ASCM CPIM (planning and inventory) and CSCP: they matter in the US and Asia and for mid-career moves, much less for graduate entry. ASCM's 2025 report links certification to higher pay (roughly 18-20% in different sources; confounded by seniority). Skills: Excel at an advanced level (pivots, lookups), SQL, Power BI, basic forecasting statistics, an introduction to SAP IBP or Kinaxis (vendor training is free), and a Python basics module. Common mistake: treating the forecast as a pure number and not talking to sales. Alternative routes: customer service at a manufacturer, inventory control roles, supply chain analyst jobs in 3PLs, a master's in supply chain management (the MIT and Rotterdam-type programmes are well regarded; unverified). Entry difficulty: 3/5.

downsides.label: Honest downsides and who it is NOT a good fit for
downsides.md: You will be blamed for forecast error even when sales caused it; routine forecasting tasks are being automated and some sources claim agentic AI will reduce entry-level hiring (unverified); the work can feel like spreadsheets and meetings. Not a good fit if you want a clearly visible product or hands-on work, or if you dislike ambiguity and repeated re-planning.

roles.title: Logistics and transport coordinator/manager (incl. freight forwarding and customs)
roles.shortName: Logistics and transport coordinator/manager (incl. forwarding, customs)

what.label: What you actually do
what.md: Arrange and track shipments by road, rail, air and sea; book carriers; prepare or check documents (bills of lading, invoices, certificates of origin); manage customs declarations and duty; handle exceptions; negotiate rates. In a forwarder you work in teams per mode (ocean, air, road) or per customer; in a shipper you buy transport from forwarders and carriers. Tools: TMS (transport management system), carrier portals (K+N myKN), customs systems, Excel, email. Example: a vessel is rolled (bumped) at Rotterdam; you rebook on another carrier, update the customer's ETA, and check the new Incoterm cost impact.

day.label: A typical day and week
day.md: Morning: review overnight alerts, vessel and flight schedules, customs holds; midday: quotes and bookings; afternoon: documentation, invoices, calls with agents in other time zones; weekly: customer reviews. Peak weeks (before Chinese New Year, Q4 peak, tariff deadlines) bring double-hours. Month-end closes can pull people into overtime (employee reviews at DSV in Dubai and Singapore report this; self-reported, weak signal).

hours.label: Hours, stress and lifestyle
hours.md: Typical 40-45; peaks 50-60. Prospects says logistics managers can work up to 60 hours and may work shifts, evenings and weekends in 24-hour operations. Stress: 4/5 in forwarding and transport operations; 3/5 in a planned shipper-side role. Mostly office-based with desk phones and screens; some roles require port, airport or site visits; remote work possible but limited; on-call duty is common in air freight and customs.

profile.label: Human vs. quantitative profile
profile.md: People/communication: 4/5. Quantitative/technical: 3/5. You spend the day talking to carriers, customers and agents; the technical load is rules (customs, Incoterms, dangerous-goods regulations) and cost arithmetic.

pay.label: Compensation (approximate)
pay.md:
- US: BLS logisticians median US$82,320 (May 2025), 10th percentile under US$50,890, 90th over US$133,160; transportation and warehousing industry median US$63,530; federal government US$103,790; manufacturing US$83,990 (BLS OOH). 255,100 jobs, growth projected at 18% in 2025-35.
- UK: entry about GBP 25,000 average (Prospects); real postings: freight forwarding operations coordinator GBP 34,000 (Redditch), import/export coordinator GBP 30,000-32,000 (Coventry), customs specialist GBP 30,000-35,000 (Essex, April 2025), European operations coordinator GBP 30,000-35,000 (Selby) (job postings, weak signal); managers GBP 41,000-65,000 and heads of logistics over GBP 90,000 (Prospects). Kuehne+Nagel UK graduate GBP 28,500 plus GBP 1,000 joining bonus (2026 listing); DHL graduate GBP 30,500.
- Italy: logistics clerk roles EUR 22,000-28,000 (Randstad listing, Tortona, not graduate); logistics analyst EUR 26,000-32,000 at 0-2 years (Masterin.it, weak). No reliable recruiter salary guide found.
- Netherlands: average freight forwarder base about EUR 34,206 (Payscale, 2026). Germany: one export specialist posting EUR 50,000-60,000 (posting, upper-range example).
- Singapore: logistics specialist about S$48,000 and S$62,000 at 5-10 and 10-15 years (Singsaver 2026 blog, source unclear).

path.label: Career path
path.md: Operations/coordinator trainee (0-2) → senior coordinator or customs specialist (2-4) → team lead / key-account manager (4-7) → branch or operations manager (7-12) → regional/country director. Customs routes lead to compliance manager or director of trade compliance.

exits.label: Exit opportunities
exits.md: After 2-3 years: procurement, planning, carrier sales, or customs brokerage. After 7-10 years: head of logistics or supply chain at a shipper, branch/country manager at a forwarder, trade-compliance director, consulting, or founding your own forwarding agency (common among long-experienced forwarders).

tiers.label: Tier list of employers
tiers.md:
Tier groupings reflect industry consensus and practitioner perception, not objective fact. Reference: Armstrong & Associates top forwarders by revenue/volume (2025) and the Alphaliner list for carriers.
- *Tier 1 (global forwarders/integrators):* Kuehne+Nagel, DSV (with DB Schenker), DHL Global Forwarding, UPS Supply Chain Solutions, Expeditors, CEVA, Sinotrans, Nippon Express. Systematic graduate programmes and training; K+N and DSV are cutting white-collar roles with technology, and employee review sites show more overtime complaints at DSV than at K+N (anecdotal).
- *Tier 2 (large regional/national forwarders and 3PLs):* In Italy Savino Del Bene, Fercam, Arcese, Gruber, Geodis, BRT; in the Netherlands and Belgium large regional forwarders; asset-based trucking groups. More personal culture, hands-on responsibility.
- *Tier 3 (small forwarders, customs brokers):* low pay, high autonomy, little formal training.

enter.label: How to enter
enter.md: Any business, geography, economics, languages or international trade degree; logistics-specific degrees help; a driving licence is often required for UK programmes (Prospects, K+N, DHL listings). Programmes: Kuehne+Nagel graduate programme (UK: two-year rotation with a professional qualification, mentor and buddy; the official page is dated and asks for a 2:2, HR scheme a 2:1 and right to work; no sponsorship), Maersk UK Graduate Programme (pathways including sales, customs, customer experience and finance; video interview, assessment centre at East Midlands Gateway, leadership interview; no visa sponsorship; an Maersk Contract Logistics Management scheme closed May 2026), DHL Supply Chain & Logistics Specialist Graduate Programme (see 3.2). DSV and CEVA run graduate schemes (unverified). Calendar: UK schemes mostly open September-November with rolling closings; forwarders also hire all year round for coordinator roles. Certifications: CILT (Chartered Institute of Logistics & Transport, UK; accredits some degrees, offers diplomas and chartered membership per Prospects); FIATA diploma (unverified); customs qualifications such as the US licensed customs broker exam (unverified, twice yearly) or Italian "spedizioniere doganale" licensing (unverified). They matter for customs roles but not for generalist operations roles. Skills: Incoterms, shipping documents, customs classification, Excel, a TMS, a second language (German, Italian, Spanish, Mandarin are valued in different hubs). Common mistakes: ignoring documentation detail (a single wrong HS code can freeze a container); expecting 9-to-5. Alternative routes: entry-level forwarding clerk/coordinator roles with no degree, then CILT part-time study; customs clerk to customs broker. Entry difficulty: 2/5 for coordinator posts; 3/5 for Tier 1 graduate programmes.

downsides.label: Honest downsides and who it is NOT a good fit for
downsides.md: Reactive, deadline-driven, often poorly paid at entry with variable bonus; forwarders are in cost-cutting mode and automating booking and quoting; you are measured on exceptions. Not a good fit for people who need predictable hours or who dislike phone-heavy, interrupt-driven work.

roles.title: Warehouse / distribution operations manager

what.label: What you actually do
what.md: Run a shift or a department of a warehouse or fulfilment centre: staffing, safety, picking and packing productivity, inbound and outbound flow, inventory accuracy, and customer service levels. You use a WMS, labour management dashboards and daily KPIs, and you lead operatives, often through supervisors. Example: a pick-path jam delays outbound trailers; you re-allocate 12 people, change the batching and clear the backlog before the trucks leave.

day.label: A typical day and week
day.md: Shift start briefing and safety talk; walk the floor, review KPIs; solve problems (equipment faults, absenteeism, damage); meet with the next shift. On a 4-on, 3-off or 12-hour pattern; peak season (November-December, the pre-Christmas "Q4 peak") means extra shifts and compulsory overtime.

hours.label: Hours, stress and lifestyle
hours.md: 45-55 hours on shift patterns; 60+ in peak; nights and weekends common. Amazon postings describe on-site work, 10-12 hours of standing and walking per day, some roles 12-hour shifts, 3x2 pattern in Brazil, 4-on/3-off in Australia (Amazon postings, 2025-26). Stress: 4/5. No remote work. Travel is limited to the site (relocation is common); UK programmes expect mobility and a driving licence (DHL, K+N).

profile.label: Human vs. quantitative profile
profile.md: People/communication: 5/5. Quantitative/technical: 2/5. It is leadership of a large front-line workforce; the numeracy is KPIs, rate calculations and basic process analysis.

pay.label: Compensation (approximate)
pay.md:
- US: Amazon Area Manager listing in Portland US$70,000-90,900 (2025 listing, one data point); Amazon Canada Area Manager graduate program C$69,000 base plus sign-on and equity (2025). Senior operations manager US$142,688-182,700 (Patterson, California listing). Third-party aggregators vary widely (US$60,000-85,000), and are unreliable. BLS warehouse/logistics-sector median for logisticians US$63,530 (transportation & warehousing, May 2025) is a different job family.
- UK: DHL Supply Chain graduate GBP 30,500 (2027 start); K+N contract logistics graduates around GBP 28,500 (project support listing, 2026); experienced logistics/distribution managers GBP 41,000-65,000 (Prospects). Amazon UK area manager pay: no reliable data found.
- Italy: no reliable data found for graduate-level warehouse managers. Operational logistics clerks EUR 22,000-28,000 (Randstad listing).
- Singapore: no reliable data found.

path.label: Career path
path.md: Shift supervisor / area manager (0-2) → operations manager / site department head (2-5) → general manager of a site (5-9) → regional operations director (9-14) → VP operations. Transfers into continuous improvement, planning, or network design are common.

exits.label: Exit opportunities
exits.md: After 2-3 years: continuous improvement, planning, transport management, or retail operations. After 7-10 years: site general manager, regional operations director, supply chain director in a retailer, consulting (operations), or operations lead in start-ups or quick-commerce.

tiers.label: Tier list of employers
tiers.md:
Tier groupings reflect industry consensus and practitioner perception, not objective fact.
- *Tier 1 (best structured training, brand value, scale):* Amazon operations (high scale and volume, exposure to robotics, but tough hours), DHL Supply Chain, Kuehne+Nagel contract logistics, GXO, big grocery chains' DCs, P&G/Unilever manufacturing distribution.
- *Tier 2:* Regional 3PLs, fashion and retail distribution (Zalando, Inditex), pharma logistics.
- *Tier 3:* Small 3PLs, local distributors; pay and training weaker, autonomy higher.

enter.label: How to enter
enter.md: Any degree (logistics, business, engineering) or none; the key hiring signal is leadership, resilience and shift flexibility. Programmes: Amazon Area Manager programme (entry-level, on-site role), DHL Supply Chain graduate programme (any degree, no minimum grade, mobile across UK sites), Maersk contract logistics management graduate programme (logistics, business or related degree, driving licence; 2026 intake closed in May), Kuehne+Nagel graduate programmes. Calendar: Amazon, DHL and 3PLs hire year-round with some autumn graduate cycles. Certifications: not required; lean or Six Sigma yellow/green belt helps; IOSH/NEBOSH-type safety certificates are valued in the UK (unverified); CILT for later career. Skills: Excel, KPI reading, basic WMS, leadership. Common mistakes: underestimating physical and shift demands; thinking this is an office job. Alternative routes: team leader from the floor with part-time study; military logistics veterans are well regarded (unverified). Entry difficulty: 2/5.

downsides.label: Honest downsides and who it is NOT a good fit for
downsides.md: Long shifts, nights and weekends; heavy exposure to injuries, strikes and burnout; automation reduces the number of operative roles, and Amazon-style productivity metrics are controversial (unions are critical, reported). Not a good fit for people who want desk-based, predictable hours or who dislike being on their feet.

roles.title: Shipping and maritime roles (chartering, ship broking, liner operations)
roles.shortName: Shipping and maritime (broking, chartering, liner ops)

what.label: What you actually do
what.md: *Ship brokers* help shipowners find cargoes and charterers find ships, in dry bulk, tankers, containers or sale-and-purchase (S&P); they quote, negotiate rates, draft fixtures on BIMCO-based contracts, and follow up post-fixture. *Chartering/operations* in a shipowner or trader: they manage voyages, laytime and demurrage claims, port agents and bunkers (fuel). *Liner operations* at a container line: customer service, pricing, network planning, equipment repositioning, port and terminal coordination. A trainee broker at Hagland, as posted in 2026, shadows client meetings, drafts charter contracts, tracks vessel positions and prepares market reports (TargetJobs listing).

day.label: A typical day and week
day.md: Brokers: early start on market reports and vessel positions, phones and chats most of the day, deals in the afternoon, client entertainment in the evening. Liner operations: monitoring vessel schedules, rerouting around Hormuz or the Cape, handling customer exceptions. Both are highly sensitive to geopolitical shocks.

hours.label: Hours, stress and lifestyle
hours.md: Brokers: 50-60 hours typical (longer during active markets) with an early start and client entertainment; stress 4/5. Liner operations: 40-50 hours with weekend and on-call coverage; stress 3-4/5. Mostly office-based, some travel (Posidonia in Athens, Marintec, ports); remote work rare for junior brokers. Hours data for brokers rests on practitioner descriptions rather than a published survey (unverified).

profile.label: Human vs. quantitative profile
profile.md: People/communication: 5/5 for brokers and 3-4/5 for liner customer-facing; Quantitative/technical: 3/5. Brokers need fast arithmetic (freight rate and voyage estimates), market knowledge and relationships; liner network planning is more analytical (Excel, SQL).

pay.label: Compensation (approximate)
pay.md:
- US: no reliable data found (chartering is concentrated in London, Singapore, Athens, Oslo and the Gulf; liner and port roles in the US are typically paid like other logistics jobs).
- UK: trainee shipbroker GBP 25,000-28,000 plus performance bonus (Edinburgh posting); around GBP 27,000 plus potential bonus, with funded ICS exams (Hagland Aberdeen, 2026); London trainee pay at Clarksons, Braemar and SSY: no reliable data found (anecdotally higher; unverified). Experienced broker pay depends on bonus and is highly variable; Clarksons' CEO total package of GBP 11.9m is not representative.
- Italy: no reliable data found (Genoa/Trieste ship-agency and liner jobs are paid within logistics bands, EUR 25-35k; unverified).
- Singapore/Gulf: no reliable data found.

path.label: Career path
path.md: Trainee broker or operations trainee (0-1, often with a 12-18 month training) → junior broker (1-3) → broker (3-7) → senior broker / desk head / director (7-15) with equity or bonus participation. Liner: customer service or pricing analyst → sales/pricing manager → regional head.

exits.label: Exit opportunities
exits.md: After 2-3 years: another broker desk, shipowner operations, trading house chartering desks (Cargill, Trafigura, Vitol and similar; see the finance report on commodity trading), or port agency. After 7-10 years: head of chartering at a shipowner or trader, establishing a brokerage, shipping finance, or liner commercial management.

tiers.label: Tier list of employers
tiers.md:
Tier groupings reflect industry consensus and practitioner perception, not objective fact.
- *Tier 1 brokers/shipping groups:* Clarksons, Braemar, SSY, Howe Robinson (these appear in trainee-scheme searches; Clarksons runs a one-year Global Trainee Broker Programme, SSY a 12-month London trainee scheme), Maersk, MSC, CMA CGM, Hapag-Lloyd, COSCO, Evergreen, and major trading houses' shipping desks.
- *Tier 2:* Regional and specialist brokers (Nordic, Greek, Singapore), mid-size carriers (ONE, HMM, Yang Ming, ZIM), large terminal operators (PSA, DP World, APM Terminals, Hutchison; PSA handled 105m TEU globally in 2025).
- *Tier 3:* Small agencies and local port-agent firms, family-owned Italian shipping companies and agencies.

enter.label: How to enter
enter.md: Any degree (economics, business, languages, geography, law) with motivation for shipping; maritime degrees (Southampton Solent, Plymouth, Genoa, Trieste, Rotterdam/Antwerp programmes, unverified) help. Programmes: Clarksons Global Trainee Broker Programme (one year, rotations, possible overseas secondment), SSY trainee scheme (London, 12 months; applications opened 1 February for a September intake in 2024), Braemar trainee scheme, Howe Robinson trainee shipbroker, Maersk UK Graduate Programme (customs, sales, customer experience, finance pathways; no sponsorship). The ICS Graduate role with Maritime UK is also listed. Calendar: broker schemes often recruit in winter/spring for a September start (SSY); smaller brokers recruit ad hoc. Certifications: ICS (Institute of Chartered Shipbrokers) Professional Qualifying Examinations lead to MICS membership; Foundation and Advanced Diplomas exist (ICS website); many brokers fund them. They matter for broker careers (employers fund and expect them), not for general logistics. Skills: market curiosity, clear writing, Excel, numeracy, network building, familiarity with shipping news (TradeWinds, Lloyd's List). Common mistakes: applying with no evidence of interest in shipping; ignoring right-to-work (many UK brokers cannot sponsor visas, e.g. Hagland). Alternative routes: junior operator at a ship agent, port or terminal roles, then lateral moves. Entry difficulty: 4/5 for Clarksons-type schemes (few places, high competition); 2-3/5 for liner and port roles.

downsides.label: Honest downsides and who it is NOT a good fit for
downsides.md: Earnings swing with the freight market, early hours, a heavy culture of entertainment and long working weeks, a small industry where reputation follows you, and a trend toward consolidation. Liner roles are exposed to cyclical profit swings. Not a good fit for people who dislike sales-oriented, relationship-based work, who want fixed pay, or who need structured work-life balance.

roles.title: Supply chain analyst / supply chain systems specialist

what.label: What you actually do
what.md: Analysts clean and combine data from ERP, WMS and TMS; build dashboards (inventory, service level, transport cost); run scenarios (for example a tariff impact on landed cost); and recommend actions. Systems specialists configure, test and support planning and execution systems (SAP, Kinaxis, o9, Blue Yonder), manage master data, and work with IT and vendors. Tools: SQL, Excel, Power BI/Tableau, Python or R, and the planning systems. Example: you model a new tariff on a Vietnamese supplier and show a Mexican source is cheaper for 40% of volume.

day.label: A typical day and week
day.md: Pull data, validate it, build or refresh reports, answer ad hoc requests from planners and managers; workshops with users; test releases for systems. Project work follows a sprint or milestone pattern.

hours.label: Hours, stress and lifestyle
hours.md: 38-45 hours typical; peaks 50 during go-lives and quarter-end. Stress: 2-3/5 (project go-lives are 4). Hybrid or remote is most common in this family; travel to plants or integrators for rollouts. Consultancy-side systems roles have more travel.

profile.label: Human vs. quantitative profile
profile.md: People/communication: 3/5. Quantitative/technical: 4/5. You need data skills (SQL, modelling) and the ability to explain results to non-technical operations managers.

pay.label: Compensation (approximate)
pay.md:
- US: analysts median US$85,000 across experience levels (ASCM 2025 via Supply Chain 24/7); entry level: no reliable data found (BLS logisticians 10th percentile under US$50,890).
- UK: coordinators, planners and analysts GBP 27,000-29,000 rising to about GBP 37,000 (Prospects); P&G supply chain graduate GBP 37,000 plus bonus (2024 listing); systems roles at integrators are higher (no reliable data found).
- Italy: logistics analyst EUR 26,000-32,000 at 0-2 years (Masterin.it, weak); no reliable data for SAP/planning systems specialists.
- Singapore: supply chain analyst average about S$65,000 (Morgan McKinley 2026).

path.label: Career path
path.md: Analyst (0-2) → senior analyst / systems specialist (2-5) → team lead / solution architect / supply chain data manager (5-9) → head of supply chain analytics or digital supply chain (9-14). Consulting or vendor roles accelerate pay.

exits.label: Exit opportunities
exits.md: After 2-3 years: data analyst/data scientist in other functions, planning or procurement, ERP consultant, product management. After 7-10 years: head of supply chain analytics or digital, supply chain consulting partner track, planning-software vendor solution architect, or operations research (see the data science report).

tiers.label: Tier list of employers
tiers.md:
Tier groupings reflect industry consensus and practitioner perception, not objective fact.
- *Tier 1:* Large FMCG/manufacturers' analytics centres, Amazon, Kinaxis/o9/SAP/Blue Yonder (vendors), Accenture/Deloitte supply chain technology practices.
- *Tier 2:* Mid-size manufacturers and retailers' internal teams, regional integrators, 3PL analytics teams.
- *Tier 3:* Small firms using Excel with little formal tooling; broad exposure, little training.

enter.label: How to enter
enter.md: Industrial engineering, computer science, data science, mathematics, statistics, economics, supply chain; strong SQL and Excel are the core. Programmes: P&G Talent Development Programme (analysis projects in Warsaw), DHL technology specialist graduate programme (prefers IT degrees but welcomes supply chain interest), Unilever, Kuehne+Nagel digital/analytics tracks (unverified), DE&S Operations Supply Chain scheme. Calendar: autumn to early spring for graduate schemes; analyst jobs hire all year. Certifications: ASCM CPIM/CSCP are optional signals; SAP certifications and vendor-specific training (Kinaxis, o9) matter for systems roles; Lean Six Sigma green belt helps for process analytics. Skills: SQL, Excel, Power BI, Python, supply chain fundamentals, one planning system, clear presentation. Common mistake: dashboards with no recommended action. Alternative routes: planner or logistics coordinator who becomes the team's "Excel person" and moves into analytics; bootcamps plus a supply chain portfolio project. Entry difficulty: 3/5.

downsides.label: Honest downsides and who it is NOT a good fit for
downsides.md: Data is messy and ERP data is often wrong; systems projects overrun; AI tools are automating routine reporting, so pure dashboard builders are less safe than analysts who also own decisions. Not a good fit for people who want frontline operations or negotiation, or who dislike repetitive data cleaning.

roles.title: Supply chain consultant (shorter)

what.label: What you actually do
what.md: Work in a team for a client on a project of weeks to months: analyse inventory, design a distribution network, reduce procurement spend, redesign an S&OP process, assess tariff exposure, or implement a planning system. Deliverables are models, slide decks and implementation plans. For detail on firms, hours and recruiting see the management consulting report.

day.label: A typical day and week
day.md: Client site or video workshops, analysis in Excel/Alteryx/Python, slides for steering committees, weekly status review. Travel to client sites 3-4 days a week is common in the UK, Germany and the US; Italy and Gulf projects are often local or regional (management consulting report).

hours.label: Hours, stress and lifestyle
hours.md: 50-60 hours typical, 60-70 at deadlines (practitioner norms; see management consulting report); stress 4/5; travel heavy; remote only partly.

profile.label: Human vs. quantitative profile
profile.md: People/communication: 4/5. Quantitative/technical: 4/5.

pay.label: Compensation (approximate)
pay.md:
- US: Big 4 consulting analyst base US$78-112k and Accenture Strategy about US$105k (Road to Offer / PrepLounge 2026, via the management consulting report); operations-specific figures not separated.
- UK: Big 4 and Accenture graduate base roughly GBP 32-37k, Capgemini Invent GBP 51k (PrepLounge UK 2026, via the management consulting report).
- Italy: no reliable data found; indicative EUR 26-30k at Deloitte/Accenture Italy (Indeed Italy, self-reported, management consulting report).
- Senior: Big 4 manager US$105-150k base; UK senior consultant/manager GBP 92-125k (management consulting report). Supply-chain-specific bands: no reliable data found.

path.label: Career path
path.md: Analyst/consultant (0-2) → senior consultant (2-4) → manager (4-7) → senior manager/director (7-10) → partner. Many leave before manager level.

exits.label: Exit opportunities
exits.md: After 2-3 years: supply chain roles in industry (planning, procurement, strategy), MBA. After 7-10 years: head of supply chain or transformation at a corporate, private-equity operations partner, or partner track.

tiers.label: Tier list of employers
tiers.md:
Tier groupings reflect industry consensus and practitioner perception, not objective fact.
- *Tier 1:* McKinsey, BCG, Bain operations practices, Kearney (supply chain strength; unverified ranking).
- *Tier 2:* Big 4 operations practices, Accenture Operations, Capgemini Invent, Alvarez & Marsal, AlixPartners.
- *Tier 3:* Boutique planning/ERP consultancies and local firms (BIP, Reply in Italy; see the management consulting report).

enter.label: How to enter
enter.md: Engineering, business, economics, supply chain; a master's helps; relevant internship in planning or procurement. Programmes and calendar: see the management consulting report (UK Big 4 recruitment is rolling, opening around September with deadlines in spring). Certifications: ASCM CSCP is a modest plus; no certification is needed at strategy firms. Skills: Excel/PowerPoint, structured problem solving, supply chain fundamentals, SQL/Alteryx. Common mistakes: applying only to MBB; treating supply chain as a purely technical subject. Alternative routes: 2-3 years in industry planning or procurement, then lateral hire into an operations practice; technology-implementation roles at integrators. Entry difficulty: 4/5 for MBB, 3/5 for Big 4/Accenture operations practices.

downsides.label: Honest downsides and who it is NOT a good fit for
downsides.md: Long hours and travel, an up-or-out culture, work on slides rather than operations, and a slowdown since 2023 with AI changing junior work (management consulting report). Not a good fit for people who want to own a real operation, need stable hours, or dislike presenting.
