roles.title: External auditor (associate → partner)

what.label: What you actually do
what.md: You test whether a client's numbers are right. As an associate you might pick 25 sampled sales invoices, match each to a contract, delivery note and bank receipt, record the result in the firm's audit software, and chase the client's finance team for missing evidence. You also send confirmation letters to banks and customers, count inventory at a warehouse, recompute depreciation in a spreadsheet, and write short memos on what you tested and concluded. Tools: Excel, the firm's audit platform (e.g. EY Canvas, KPMG Clara, Deloitte Omnia, PwC Aura), data analytics on full ledgers, ERP exports (SAP, Oracle). Seniors plan sections, review juniors and talk to client controllers; managers handle the client relationship and judgement areas (revenue, estimates, going concern); partners sign the opinion and manage risk.

day.label: A typical day and week
day.md: A client-site or hybrid day: stand-up with the team, a morning of testing against a checklist, a call to ask the client for outstanding items, afternoon documentation, and a status email at the end. Weeks vary by the "audit calendar". For December year-ends, busy season (the high-pressure stretch roughly January to April when most year-end audits finish) is crushing; June-September is lighter (interim testing, training, exams). Many firms assign you to 3-6 clients a year. Remote work is common for desk-based testing; site visits happen for inventory and fieldwork. Offshore teams increasingly do evidence collection and routine testing for the home team.

hours.label: Hours, stress and lifestyle
hours.md:
- Hours: UK Big 4 audit staff disclosed to the FRC (Firm Metrics, July 2026, timesheet-based) an average week of about 41 hours at PwC, rising to about 44 in the January-March peak; busy-period utilisation for unqualified staff was 108-121% of contracted hours across the four firms (about 38-42 hours, my conversion). These are averages across all staff and exclude unrecorded time. US evidence is worse: in a 2025 recruiter-run survey of 110 tax and audit professionals (Distinct, via Accounting Today), nearly 80% worked over 51 hours a week in busy season, 31% over 61, and 38% of managers over 70 (small sample, weak source). Typical range 40-50; peak range 55-75 (higher at US/Italian Big 4 in busy season; Reddit/practitioner reports of 60-80 are common but anecdotal).
- Stress: 3 off-season, 4 at the peak. Seniors take the brunt: 75% of seniors in the same survey rated busy season somewhat or extremely stressful versus 22% of associates (weak source).
- Lifestyle: some travel to clients (a lot in Italy and the US for small-city clients), limited flexibility in busy season, good flexibility otherwise. A caba (ICAEW-related charity) 2024 survey of over 300 UK chartered accountants found 74% had felt burnout symptoms in the past year and 41% had considered leaving the profession (self-reported, not Big 4 specific).

profile.label: Human vs. quantitative profile
profile.md: People/communication: 3/5. Quantitative/technical: 3/5. You rarely do hard maths, but you need accounting-standards knowledge, comfort with large spreadsheets, and the diplomacy to ask clients for uncomfortable evidence. Judgement and professional scepticism matter more than formulae.

pay.label: Compensation (approximate)
pay.md:
- Entry:
  - UK (London): about GBP 30,000-40,000 base for Big 4 graduates (Financial Times via eFinancialCareers, 30 Sep 2026: Big 4 about GBP 36k, mid-tier about GBP 30k, Grant Thornton intending GBP 40k; secondary). Regional offices GBP 26,000-33,000 per one aggregator (Learnsignal, 2026, weak).
  - US: roughly USD 60,000-70,000 base at Big 4 in a major city (blog aggregators, 2026; low reliability; no firm-published figure found).
  - Italy: EUR 24,000-28,000 gross per year at Big 4 (Trend-online, 12 Jun 2024, outside the two-year window), and a Deloitte job posting cited by an Indeed summary at EUR 27,900 for an audit talent programme in Rome (2026; one posting). Milan is usually slightly higher; no reliable Milan-specific data.
  - Hong Kong: no reliable 2026 data found (anecdotal 2024 forum report of about HKD 29,900 per month incl. allowances, unverified). Singapore: S$3,500 per month for a Deloitte associate in 2022 (Bloomberg via Going Concern; old). Dubai: no published Big 4 bands found; blogs quote tens of thousands of AED per year for seniors, not reliable.
- ~5 years (senior/assistant manager, newly or recently qualified):
  - UK London: audit senior about GBP 50,000-61,000 (one recruiter guide, 2026, publisher unclear); newly qualified ACA about GBP 50,000-65,000 across sources (Learnsignal, Hays job ad of GBP 55-65k for an industry role in July 2025).
  - US: no reliable firm-level figure found; Robert Half lists senior accountant at USD 81,500-111,250 (US 2027 guide, industry roles, not audit).
  - Italy: no reliable data found (anecdotal EUR 36,000 for 4-5 years' experience, undated).
- Senior (manager/partner):
  - UK London audit manager GBP 62,000-75,000 (Morgan McKinley, 2026). Partner pay at Big 4 is typically several hundred thousand pounds (not verified from a primary source this cycle).
  - US: no reliable data found. Italy/Asia/Gulf: no reliable data found.

path.label: Career path
path.md: Typical Big 4 ladder: associate/staff (years 0-2), senior (years 3-4, usually after qualifying), assistant manager/manager (years 5-8), senior manager/director (years 8-12), partner (12-16+, only a small share make it). Promotion timings are practitioner lore, not from employer pages. Italy: junior revisore, senior, manager, with the revisore legale title needed to sign. Mid-tier ladders are similar but partner promotion can come sooner.

exits.label: Exit opportunities
exits.md:
- After 2-3 years (often right after qualification): financial controller or group reporting roles in industry, internal audit, FP&A, finance roles in PE-backed companies, transaction services (see finance report), tax, risk/compliance, fintech.
- After 7-10 years: finance director, corporate controller, CFO of mid-size companies, internal audit head, regulator or standard-setter roles, or stay for partner.

tiers.label: Tier list of employers
tiers.md:
Tier groupings reflect industry consensus and practitioner perception, not objective fact.
- Big 4 (Deloitte, PwC, EY, KPMG): biggest brands, global mobility, structured training, funded qualification, largest listed-company clients; heaviest busy-season load and most offshoring/AI investment.
- Mid-tier networks (BDO, Grant Thornton, RSM, Forvis Mazars, Baker Tilly, Crowe; in Italy BDO, Mazars, RSM, Baker Tilly, Crowe and similar; verify local membership): broader exposure sooner, smaller teams, a few listed clients, often slightly lower pay (UK mid-tier about GBP 30k vs Big 4 GBP 36k per FT-reported figures); increasingly PE-backed in the US.
- Local/small practices: owner-managed businesses, tax-heavy, shorter busy seasons, more autonomy, more client-facing early, less structured training; in Italy the "studio commercialista" is the common route.

enter.label: How to enter
enter.md:
- Degrees: accounting or finance help but are not required; Big 4 UK firms accept any subject (KPMG UK says graduates have "degrees in a variety of subjects"); in the US you need enough accounting credits to sit the CPA (typically 24-30 accounting credit hours, state-specific), so a non-accounting degree usually needs added coursework. In Italy, economics degrees (laurea in Economia, classes L-18/L-33, then LM-77 magistrale) are the standard route.
- Internships/programmes: summer internships and spring insight weeks, converted to offers; UK applications run roughly September to January for September starts; US recruiting for fall of junior year (internships) and fall of senior year; Italy recruits year-round with big pushes in autumn and spring. Many Big 4s run school-leaver and apprentice routes in the UK (e.g. Deloitte BrightStart).
- Qualifications: US CPA (four exam sections, passed within a window; typically 150 credit hours or, in states that enacted it, 120 hours plus two years' experience; time 1-3 years, cost several thousand USD in exam fees and prep, required to sign audits); UK ACA (ICAEW; 15 modules and about three years of supervised experience, usually employer-funded, unverified this cycle) or ACCA (13 exams without exemptions, global; ACCA exemptions end at Applied Skills, per ACCA, 2026); in Scotland, ICAS; Italy: dottore commercialista exam after a laurea magistrale and 18 months of tirocinio (traineeship), plus a separate registered-auditor (revisore legale) qualification needing a 3-year audit traineeship and an integrative exam (Parma University call for 2026, University of Parma; the Italian rules overlap and change, so confirm with CNDCEC or the Ordine); Hong Kong: HKICPA Qualification Programme (reported 14 modules plus capstone) and 3 years' experience with an authorised employer; Singapore: CA Singapore via ISCA (Foundation 6 papers or Professional 4 papers plus capstone, depending on degree; 3 years' experience; public-company auditors must be ACRA-registered); Gulf: ACCA widely used; Big 4 firms recruit ACCA affiliates (secondary).
- Skills: Excel, data analytics (SQL/Python for audit analytics), writing clear working papers, client communication, professional scepticism.
- Common mistakes: leaving before qualifying (the qualification is the portable asset); failing too many exam attempts (KPMG UK says exceeding the permitted attempts may end your contract); choosing only the Big 4 and skipping mid-tier; ignoring regional offices (44% of Deloitte UK's 2026 intake started outside London).
- Alternatives: conversion from non-accounting degrees via ACCA/ACA or US credit top-ups; UK school-leaver and degree-apprenticeship routes; mid-tier to Big 4 lateral moves at senior level are common.
Entry difficulty: 3/5 (Big 4 UK/US intakes shrank, but audit remains the most open high-brand entry in finance; Italy and mid-tier are more accessible).

downsides.label: Honest downsides and who it is NOT a good fit for
downsides.md: Long, uneven hours in busy season; repetitive work in the first two years (increasingly offshored or automated, so the learning-by-doing stage is being thinned); exam failure can end a contract; low pay relative to hours at the bottom of the pyramid; a very steep partner pyramid. Not a good fit if you hate documentation, dislike chasing people, need predictable hours year-round, or want to avoid exams. Also weak fit if you expect rapid client-facing strategy work.

roles.title: Tax advisor / tax accountant

what.label: What you actually do
what.md: You prepare corporate tax computations (turning accounting profit into taxable profit), review the tax return, calculate deferred tax for financial statements, research tax rules for a transaction, and write advice memos or client emails. Transfer pricing specialists build benchmark studies and intercompany agreements; indirect tax/VAT staff reconcile VAT returns and advise on cross-border supplies; private client advisers handle personal tax returns, trusts and wealthy-family structuring. Tools: Excel, tax software (OneSource, CCH, Corptax), tax-authority portals, research databases.

day.label: A typical day and week
day.md: Mix of desk work and calls: computing a provision or return, answering a client's question about a restructuring, updating a workbook. Peaks follow filing deadlines (US individual/business deadlines March-April and the extension season September-October; UK 31 January self-assessment; Italy's dichiarazione dei redditi season, typically summer to autumn). Hybrid is common; tax is easier to do remotely than audit.

hours.label: Hours, stress and lifestyle
hours.md: - Typical 40-48 hours; peak 55-70 during filing seasons. Stress: 3 (4 at deadlines). Little travel; more flexibility than audit. Compliance work is more deadline-driven; advisory work is more project-driven. A 2025 survey summarised above found busy-season stress is highest among seniors (weak source).

profile.label: Human vs. quantitative profile
profile.md: People/communication: 3/5. Quantitative/technical: 3/5 (rule-heavy and detail-heavy rather than math-heavy; transfer pricing leans quantitative). Advisory roles reward explaining complex rules simply.

pay.label: Compensation (approximate)
pay.md:
- Entry: UK Big 4 tax graduates similar to audit, about GBP 30,000-40,000 (see 3.1); US Big 4 tax about USD 60,000-70,000 (weak). The Robert Half US 2027 guide lists "tax preparer" at USD 41,500-60,250 and gives no tax accountant/manager data. Italy: about EUR 24,000-28,000 at Big 4 (Trend-online 2024, assumed same as audit; unverified for tax). Hong Kong/Singapore/Dubai: no reliable data found.
- ~5 years: UK corporate tax senior typically GBP 60,000-90,000 in London (Morgan McKinley 2026; median about GBP 75,000 in one guide; wide). US/Italy: no reliable data found.
- Senior: UK tax manager GBP 60,000-90,000 (Morgan McKinley 2026; the same range appears for senior and manager in different sources, so treat as approximate); higher for directors/partners (no reliable data found).

path.label: Career path
path.md: Associate (years 0-2), senior (3-4), manager (5-8), senior manager/director (8-12), partner. Specialisation (transfer pricing, M&A tax, VAT) usually by year 3-4. In Italy, the dottore commercialista title opens a path to run a studio.

exits.label: Exit opportunities
exits.md:
- After 2-3 years: in-house tax at multinationals, boutique tax firms, law-firm tax teams, tax authority roles.
- After 7-10 years: head of tax at a corporate, partner at a Big 4/mid-tier/boutique, tax director at a PE-backed group, or independent adviser.

tiers.label: Tier list of employers
tiers.md:
Tier groupings reflect industry consensus and practitioner perception, not objective fact.
- Big 4 tax: broad international and M&A coverage, structured training, funded qualifications.
- Mid-tier (BDO, Grant Thornton, RSM, Baker Tilly, Forvis Mazars, Crowe) and specialist tax/transfer pricing boutiques: more hands-on sooner, less brand but strong in specific niches.
- Local firms and in-house tax: owner-managed clients and compliance; in Italy the dottore commercialista studio; in-house tax at multinationals is the usual destination for experienced people.

enter.label: How to enter
enter.md:
- Degrees: accounting, finance, economics, law and some business degrees; STEM graduates are accepted at larger firms for tax technology and transfer pricing.
- Internships: same Big 4 summer programmes as audit; direct tax graduate routes (UK applications autumn-winter; US recruiting fall of senior year; Italy year-round).
- Qualifications: CTA (UK Chartered Tax Adviser, CIOT; about 2-3 years; 2026 written paper fees GBP 238 and GBP 289, annual subscription GBP 452, per ATT/CIOT; the structure changes for students enrolling from September 2027); ADIT for international tax (most finish within 3 years; fees not verified); ACA or CPA are also accepted; Italy: dottore commercialista and potentially revisore legale; US: CPA (and EA for IRS representation, unverified); Hong Kong/Singapore: HKICPA/ISCA-accredited accountancy plus tax diplomas (not verified this cycle).
- Skills: tax research, Excel, communication, curiosity about law; tax technology is becoming a differentiator.
- Common mistakes: treating tax as "easier audit" (it is rule-dense and requires reading legislation); not choosing a specialism; skipping the qualification.
- Alternatives: law degree plus tax postgraduate; lateral move from audit; tax authority entry then private-sector move.
Entry difficulty: 3/5 (comparable to audit; advisory and transfer pricing teams are more selective).

downsides.label: Honest downsides and who it is NOT a good fit for
downsides.md: Deadline crunches; heavy reading of legislation and changing rules; some work (compliance) is being automated; advisory work depends on deal cycles; US peak seasons are intense. Not a good fit if you dislike detail and reading rules, or want rapid client contact in strategic decisions without legal depth.

roles.title: Financial accountant / financial controller (in industry)

what.label: What you actually do
what.md: You keep a company's books and produce its financial statements. A staff accountant posts and reconciles journal entries, supports the month-end close (finalising the month's numbers: accruals, revenue cut-off, bank and intercompany reconciliations), and prepares schedules for auditors. A senior accountant reviews, runs consolidations and prepares IFRS or US GAAP statements. A financial controller owns the close, controls, audit relationship and reporting to the CFO. Tools: ERP (SAP, Oracle, NetSuite), Excel, consolidation tools (Hyperion, OneStream), reconciliation software.

day.label: A typical day and week
day.md: Cyclical: week one of the month is the close (long days, deadlines to group headquarters), weeks two to three are lighter analysis, controls and process improvements, week four is accrual planning and audit liaison. Year-end and audit time bring extra load. Hybrid or remote is common; shared-service centres in Poland, India, Philippines and Malaysia run standardised processes.

hours.label: Hours, stress and lifestyle
hours.md: - Typical 38-45 hours; peak 50-60 at close and year-end. Stress: 2-3. Predictable, limited travel (more for group controllers). The Robert Half US guide for 2027 reports mid-point staff accountant pay of USD 76,500 and notes the market is driven by AI/data skills (US 2027 guide).

profile.label: Human vs. quantitative profile
profile.md: People/communication: 3/5. Quantitative/technical: 3/5. You collaborate with procurement, sales and auditors; the technical core is standards (IFRS/US GAAP) and systems.

pay.label: Compensation (approximate)
pay.md:
- Entry:
  - US: staff accountant USD 67,000-89,500 (Robert Half US 2027 guide; national average low/mid/high); BLS median accountant/auditor USD 83,680, 10th percentile under USD 56,020 (BLS May 2025).
  - UK: no reliable entry-level industry figure found in sources this cycle.
  - Italy: accountant/specialista contabilita EUR 28,000-50,000 for under five years' experience, bonus 10-15% (Michael Page Italy 2026 salary study; national, medium-size company sample; the low end is entry-level).
  - Hong Kong: management/systems/revenue accountants about HKD 45,000-52,000 per month (Morgan McKinley, 2026 average ranges; mid-career roles). Dubai: general ledger accountants about AED 13,000-18,000 per month at SMEs and 15,000-20,000 at multinationals (secondhand report of Michael Page UAE 2026; tax-free).
- ~5 years: US senior accountant USD 81,500-111,250; accounting manager USD 98,250-128,500 (Robert Half 2027). Italy 5-10 years: EUR 50,000-60,000 (Michael Page Italy 2026, accountant row). UK: no reliable data found.
- Senior: US corporate controller USD 154,500-216,250 (Robert Half 2027). UK financial controller GBP 63,000-92,500 (25th-75th percentile, median GBP 76,750; Robert Half UK 2026), financial-services FC median GBP 89,250. Italy controller >10 years: above EUR 90,000 (see 3.4). Hong Kong financial controller in financial services HKD 73,000-120,000 per month (Morgan McKinley 2026). Dubai financial controller AED 35,000-55,000 per month (secondhand Michael Page UAE 2026).

path.label: Career path
path.md: Staff accountant (0-2 years), senior accountant (2-4), accounting manager (4-7), assistant controller (6-9), financial controller (8-12), VP finance/CFO (12-20). A professional qualification (CPA, ACA, ACCA, CIMA) usually speeds promotion; many controllers are ex-audit.

exits.label: Exit opportunities
exits.md:
- After 2-3 years: senior accountant, analyst roles (FP&A), shared-service team lead, audit or tax if you want advisory work.
- After 7-10 years: financial controller, group reporting manager, CFO track at mid-size companies, finance transformation lead, ERP implementation roles.

tiers.label: Tier list of employers
tiers.md:
Tier groupings reflect industry consensus and practitioner perception, not objective fact.
- Multinationals and listed groups (FTSE 100, Fortune 500, FTSE MIB such as Eni, Enel, Generali, Intesa Sanpaolo, Prysmian, Leonardo): complex reporting, graduate programmes, strong brand, more bureaucracy.
- Mid-size and PE-backed companies: broader scope, faster promotion, more hours around reporting to investors.
- Small companies and shared-service centres: more routine tasks, narrower scope, less brand; SSCs offer volume and process skills but fewer promotion slots.

enter.label: How to enter
enter.md:
- Degrees: accounting, finance, economics, business; STEM graduates with accounting modules are accepted.
- Programmes: corporate finance graduate schemes; for example Siemens Graduate Program and ABB's Global Early Talent Program ask for a master's, and Siemens and Bosch require at least four months abroad (project prior research, 2026). Airbus caps prior experience at three years. Most hiring is direct application, often after 1-3 years in audit.
- Qualifications: CPA (US; helpful, not always required), ACCA or ACA (UK/Europe/Asia/Gulf), CIMA for management accounting; Italy: none strictly required for in-house roles, though dottore commercialista or revisore title helps for CFO tracks (practitioner view).
- Skills: ERP fluency, Excel, close discipline, IFRS or US GAAP, communication with auditors.
- Common mistakes: staying in a narrow AP/AR role without learning the full close; skipping the qualification; ignoring the shared-service trap (volume work without progression).
- Alternatives: apprenticeship and bookkeeping routes in the UK; AAT (UK) then ACCA; promotion from accounts assistant.
Entry difficulty: 2/5 (many openings; competitiveness rises at big-brand graduate programmes).

downsides.label: Honest downsides and who it is NOT a good fit for
downsides.md: Repetitive month-end cycle; pay plateau without qualification or promotion; offshoring and automation target transactional accounting (AP/AR, bookkeeping) hardest; low visibility compared with strategy or finance roles. Not a good fit if you want constant variety, front-office intensity or high early pay. Also weak fit for people who dislike process discipline.

roles.title: Management accountant / controller (controlling, cost and performance)

what.label: What you actually do
what.md: You build budgets and forecasts, analyse why actual results differ from plan (variance analysis), calculate product or customer margins, support pricing and investment decisions, and report KPIs to business unit heads. In a German or Italian manufacturer you may sit in a plant or business unit as the "controller", challenging managers on spending and presenting monthly performance packs. Tools: Excel, SAP CO/BW, Power BI, planning software (Anaplan, Hyperion). In the US this overlaps with cost accounting and FP&A (see finance report).

day.label: A typical day and week
day.md: Monthly rhythm: close support, then analysis week, then management review meetings. Daily work mixes data pulls, reconciling numbers, answering ad-hoc questions from operations, and building decks. More business partnering than financial accounting.

hours.label: Hours, stress and lifestyle
hours.md: - Typical 40-46 hours; peak 50-60 during budget season (Q3-Q4) and reporting weeks. Stress: 3. Lifestyle is stable; modest travel to plants or subsidiaries; hybrid or remote common.

profile.label: Human vs. quantitative profile
profile.md: People/communication: 4/5. Quantitative/technical: 3/5. You influence managers with numbers, so you must explain findings plainly and push back politely.

pay.label: Compensation (approximate)
pay.md:
- Entry: US cost accountant USD 77,000-97,000 (Robert Half 2027; mid-level). UK newly qualified management accountant GBP 42,000-56,000 (Learnsignal 2026, weak source). Italy: controller with under five years' experience EUR 35,000-60,000, bonus 15-20% (Michael Page Italy 2026; sample is medium-size companies; entry-level sits at the low end; the document sets ranges by years of experience in role). Milan figures not separated.
- ~5 years: UK qualified management accountant 3-5 years post-qualification GBP 50,000-68,000, median about GBP 57,000 (Learnsignal 2026, weak); London median about GBP 66,000 vs North East about GBP 43,000 (same source). Italy: controller 5-10 years EUR 60,000-90,000 (Michael Page Italy 2026). Hong Kong management accountant about HKD 48,000-50,000 per month (Morgan McKinley 2026).
- Senior: Italy controller >10 years above EUR 90,000 (Michael Page Italy 2026); UK financial/finance director roles: GBP 76,000-107,000 for group financial controller (Robert Half UK 2026). Dubai/US: US controller see 3.3.

path.label: Career path
path.md: Junior controller/cost accountant (0-3), controller (3-6), senior controller/head of controlling (6-10), finance director or CFO (10-18). CIMA/CGMA or ACCA speeds it; in Italy and Germany an economics master's is the norm.

exits.label: Exit opportunities
exits.md:
- After 2-3 years: FP&A, business finance partner, corporate strategy, commercial finance, consulting (finance transformation).
- After 7-10 years: head of controlling, finance director, divisional CFO, general management in operations.

tiers.label: Tier list of employers
tiers.md:
Tier groupings reflect industry consensus and practitioner perception, not objective fact.
- Large multinationals and industrial groups (e.g. Siemens, Bosch, ABB, Airbus, Nestle; in Italy Eni, Enel, Pirelli, Prysmian, Ferrero-style private groups): structured programmes, strongest training; some require a master's and international experience.
- Mid-size manufacturers and consumer firms: broader scope, faster promotion, less structure.
- Banks and insurers: more regulatory reporting, higher pay, more bureaucracy (see section 4).

enter.label: How to enter
enter.md:
- Degrees: management, finance, accounting, economics, engineering with business modules.
- Programmes: rotational graduate schemes (Siemens SGP and ABB GETP require a master's; Bosch JMP targets master's and PhD, with Finance and Controlling tracks, per employer pages, 2026); Airbus Finance NextGen rotates graduates through project control, budgetary control, treasury and M&A. Recruiting calendars vary: Siemens recruits on a rolling basis, Airbus AGGP opens each September.
- Qualifications: CIMA/CGMA (about 3-5 years part-time, roughly GBP 5,000-9,000 if self-funded, three years of verified practical experience for the full designation; tuition-provider estimates, weak), ACCA, or no qualification in continental Europe (experience and the degree matter more).
- Skills: Excel/Power BI, SAP, financial modelling, business partnering, German or local language where needed (Bosch Germany asks for good German).
- Common mistakes: ignoring operational understanding; being the "numbers person" who never speaks to the business; waiting for a perfect programme instead of starting in a controlling-adjacent role.
- Alternatives: move from audit into controlling after 2-3 years; internal transfers from financial accounting.
Entry difficulty: 3/5 (graduate programmes at big industrials are competitive; direct entry at mid-size firms is easier).

downsides.label: Honest downsides and who it is NOT a good fit for
downsides.md: Can be "the department that says no" to managers; can degenerate into manual reporting in poorly automated firms; work follows corporate cycles (budget season); title and pay vary a lot between countries. Not a good fit if you want independence from the business, dislike meetings, or want purely technical accounting work.

what.label: What you actually do
what.md: You assess whether a company's processes and controls work, then report to management and the audit committee. A typical audit: scope procurement-to-payment, interview process owners, test a sample of 40 purchase orders for approval and three-way match (order, receipt, invoice), find a control gap, draft a finding and agree remediation. In the US, SOX teams test key financial-reporting controls each quarter. IT audit, third-party risk and regulatory audits are growing. Tools: audit management software (TeamMate), Excel, data analytics, interviews, process maps.

day.label: A typical day and week
day.md: Project-based. During fieldwork you might travel to a subsidiary for a week of interviews and testing; then a reporting phase writing findings and presenting to managers. Weeks are less deadline-bound than external audit, with peaks before audit committee meetings and SOX quarter-ends. Travel can be substantial in global groups.

hours.label: Hours, stress and lifestyle
hours.md: - Typical 38-45 hours; peak 50-55 around reporting. Stress: 2-3. Some travel (10-40% depending on company). Hybrid is common.

profile.label: Human vs. quantitative profile
profile.md: People/communication: 4/5. Quantitative/technical: 3/5. You are paid to ask awkward questions; tact and influence matter as much as technical skill. Data-analytics and IT-audit skills raise your value.

pay.label: Compensation (approximate)
pay.md:
- Entry: US internal auditor advertised midpoint about USD 89,000 (2026 job-posting analysis by a third-party site; not employee pay; weak); IIA historical data show CIA holders earning more (a 2012-13 survey: USD 26,500 premium; outdated). Robert Half's 2027 US guide lists no internal auditor row. UK, Italy, Hong Kong, Singapore, Dubai: no reliable data found; Michael Page Italy 2026 excerpt had no internal auditor row visible.
- ~5 years: US internal audit manager about USD 140,000 advertised midpoint (same 2026 analysis; weak). Others: no reliable data found.
- Senior: Director of internal audit about USD 190,000 and CAE about USD 235,000 advertised midpoints (same 2026 analysis; weak). Others: no reliable data found.

path.label: Career path
path.md: Internal audit associate/analyst (0-2), senior auditor (2-4), manager (4-8), senior manager/director (8-12), chief audit executive (12+). Many people use internal audit as a stepping stone to controllership, risk, compliance or business roles.

exits.label: Exit opportunities
exits.md:
- After 2-3 years: financial control, SOX compliance, risk and compliance, operations finance, external audit if you moved from outsourced IA.
- After 7-10 years: chief audit executive, head of risk or compliance, finance director, operations roles; for example Novartis advertises an internal audit role in Basel as a launchpad into future leadership (Novartis early-careers page, 2026, via prior research).

tiers.label: Tier list of employers
tiers.md:
Tier groupings reflect industry consensus and practitioner perception, not objective fact.
- Big 4 risk/IA outsourcing and specialist firms (Protiviti, Crowe, RSM): variety of clients, training, longer hours.
- Large multinationals and banks: in-house IA with global scope and structured training; banks pay more and are heavily regulated.
- Mid-size and public sector: narrower scope, often better hours, lower pay.

enter.label: How to enter
enter.md:
- Degrees: accounting, finance, business, IT/information systems (for IT audit), data and engineering for analytics.
- Programmes: corporate IA graduate schemes and Big 4 internal audit/risk graduate tracks; most IA hires come after 1-3 years in audit or controls.
- Qualifications: CIA (Certified Internal Auditor, IIA; three exam parts; the exam was updated in January 2025 to the Global Internal Audit Standards; US exam fees USD 990 for IIA members and USD 1,515 for non-members, excluding study materials; a bachelor's degree or equivalent experience; certification needs documented work experience; official IIA pricing page, 2026); CISA for IT audit (not verified this cycle); CPA/ACA/ACCA also valued.
- Skills: risk assessment, interviewing, writing, data analysis, SOX framework knowledge.
- Common mistakes: regarding IA as "audit light"; underestimating writing and influencing skills.
- Alternatives: transfer from finance or operations; from external audit after 2-3 years.
Entry difficulty: 3/5 (competitive for graduate schemes at big banks and multinationals; mid-size more open).

downsides.label: Honest downsides and who it is NOT a good fit for
downsides.md: You can be seen as "the police" by colleagues; recommendations are not always acted on; the career can stall without a rotation into the business; some IA teams are checklist-driven. Not a good fit if you dislike confrontation, want to build something rather than assess it, or need quick promotion.

what.label: What you actually do
what.md: You investigate suspected fraud, corruption and financial misstatement, and quantify damages in disputes. Tasks: tracing payments through bank statements, reviewing expense claims and vendor files for red flags, analysing millions of ledger lines with data tools, interviewing witnesses, writing reports for lawyers or regulators, and sometimes testifying as an expert. Tools: Excel, SQL/Python, e-discovery platforms, link-analysis tools.

day.label: A typical day and week
day.md: Project-based: some weeks are intense document review ahead of a regulator deadline or hearing; others are quieter. Cases can involve travel and confidentiality.

hours.label: Hours, stress and lifestyle
hours.md: - Typical 42-50 hours; peak 55-70 near deadlines or trial. Stress: 3-4. Travel moderate; remote work possible but evidence handling is controlled.

profile.label: Human vs. quantitative profile
profile.md: People/communication: 3/5. Quantitative/technical: 4/5. Strong data skills and scepticism are central; communication matters in interviews and reports.

pay.label: Compensation (approximate)
pay.md:
- Entry: no reliable firm-published data found. US forensic accountant (mid-level) USD 89,250-125,250, mid-point USD 111,500 (Robert Half US 2027 guide). UK/Italy/Asia/Gulf: no reliable data found.
- ~5 years / senior: no reliable data found beyond the Robert Half US range above.

path.label: Career path
path.md: Analyst/associate (0-2), senior (2-4), manager (4-7), director (7-12), partner/managing director. Many enter after 2-4 years in audit or risk.

exits.label: Exit opportunities
exits.md:
- After 2-3 years: compliance, financial crime teams in banks, internal audit, litigation support.
- After 7-10 years: head of investigations, chief compliance officer, expert witness practice, or law-enforcement/regulator roles.

tiers.label: Tier list of employers
tiers.md:
Tier groupings reflect industry consensus and practitioner perception, not objective fact.
- Big 4 forensic and specialist consultancies (FTI Consulting, Kroll, Alvarez & Marsal, Stout): large cases, structured careers, high intensity.
- Mid-tier forensic teams and boutique investigators: smaller cases, more varied work.
- In-house corporate investigations, regulators (SEC, FCA, SFO, Guardia di Finanza) and law firms: different pace and pay.

enter.label: How to enter
enter.md:
- Degrees: accounting, finance, law, data/computer science; criminology or investigation postgraduates.
- Internships/programmes: Big 4 forensic and investigations graduate tracks; direct entry from audit is the main route.
- Qualifications: CFE (Certified Fraud Examiner, ACFE; ACFE membership, a points system with 40 points to sit the exam, then at least two years of professional experience and 50 points to certify, per ACFE candidate handbook, 2025 edition; not required), CPA/ACA, CAMS for anti-money laundering (not verified).
- Skills: data analytics, interviewing, writing for lawyers, and ethics.
- Common mistakes: treating it as glamorous CSI work (most work is document and ledger review); lacking audit grounding.
- Alternatives: law enforcement or regulatory backgrounds.
Entry difficulty: 4/5 (small number of graduate seats; most hires come from audit or investigations).

downsides.label: Honest downsides and who it is NOT a good fit for
downsides.md: Case flow is lumpy; work can involve difficult interviews and legal pressure; the best seats are few; some cases are repetitive document review. Not a good fit if you dislike confrontation or ambiguity, or want regular predictable hours.

what.label: What you actually do
what.md: You help companies prepare sustainability reports (collecting emissions, energy, workforce and governance data and mapping it to ESRS or ISSB) or you provide assurance on them (testing data sources, controls and estimates, and giving limited assurance conclusions). Tasks include reconciling site data to sustainability reports, reviewing greenhouse-gas calculations, double-materiality assessments (which topics matter financially and for society), and discussing evidence with data owners. Tools: Excel, data platforms, ESRS/ISSB checklists, assurance software.

day.label: A typical day and week
day.md: Fieldwork-style: requests to data owners across HR, facilities and supply chain; testing calculations; drafting assurance documentation. Peak is the reporting season (spring) as with audit.

hours.label: Hours, stress and lifestyle
hours.md: - Typical 40-48 hours; peak 50-60 in reporting season. Stress: 3. Moderate travel. The market is shifting: after the Omnibus I scope cut, fewer EU companies need CSRD reports from FY2027, but ISSB-based regimes in other jurisdictions and voluntary reporting continue.

profile.label: Human vs. quantitative profile
profile.md: People/communication: 3/5. Quantitative/technical: 3/5 (data and standards; engineering or environmental knowledge helps).

pay.label: Compensation (approximate)
pay.md:
- Entry: no reliable data found. Roles often sit on audit or advisory pay scales at Big 4 (see 3.1) or specialist verifiers; do not assume a premium.
- ~5 years / senior: no reliable data found.

path.label: Career path
path.md: Associate (0-2), senior (2-4), manager (4-8), director/partner. Mobility between audit, advisory and in-house sustainability reporting roles is common.

exits.label: Exit opportunities
exits.md:
- After 2-3 years: in-house sustainability reporting, ESG data roles, investor relations, standard-setting support.
- After 7-10 years: head of sustainability reporting, CFO-office sustainability lead, partner in assurance or advisory.

tiers.label: Tier list of employers
tiers.md:
Tier groupings reflect industry consensus and practitioner perception, not objective fact.
- Big 4 sustainability assurance and mid-tier networks: biggest client lists, standardised methodology, but hiring tied to regulation.
- Specialist verifiers and certifiers (DNV, Bureau Veritas, SGS, TUV, ERM CVS): technical environmental assurance; less finance focus.
- In-house at large corporates and financial institutions: strongest job security where reporting is mandatory.

enter.label: How to enter
enter.md:
- Degrees: accounting, finance, environmental science, engineering, economics; useful if you pair finance with sustainability data skills.
- Programmes: sustainability teams inside Big 4 assurance/advisory graduate schemes; most hires come after 1-3 years in audit or consulting.
- Qualifications: ACA/ACCA/CPA plus sustainability credentials (ACCA/ICAEW sustainability certificates, ISSB's FSA credential; not verified this cycle); no mandatory qualification for most roles; ISSA 5000 knowledge for assurance.
- Skills: data handling, greenhouse-gas accounting basics, writing, regulatory reading.
- Common mistakes: assuming CSRD demand will remain at 2023 levels; entering without any accounting/data skill base.
- Alternatives: engineers/environmental scientists moving into assurance with finance training.
Entry difficulty: 3/5 (few dedicated graduate seats; competition from a wider pool of ESG graduates).

downsides.label: Honest downsides and who it is NOT a good fit for
downsides.md: Regulatory uncertainty (the Omnibus scale-back removed most CSRD companies and delayed standards); the field is smaller than promised; much of the work is data chasing; some firms have reduced sustainability teams. Not a good fit if you want a stable regulatory tailwind or are seeking a purely policy role.

roles.title: Brand manager

what.label: What you actually do
what.md: An assistant brand manager (ABM) supports a brand manager, who supports a senior brand manager, who reports to a marketing director. You write briefs for ad agencies, build the annual brand plan and budget, track weekly sales and market share data (from NielsenIQ or Circana), plan promotions with sales, and manage launches with R&D, supply chain and finance. In practice: you review a 10-week sales trend, see a promotion lost money, and rewrite next quarter's plan. Deliverables: brand plan, creative brief, launch timeline, P&L (profit and loss) forecast, post-campaign review. Tools: Excel/PowerPoint, retailer data portals, agency briefs. The "mini-CEO" label is half true: you own the brand's numbers but depend on sales, supply chain and the retailer for execution.

day.label: A typical day and week
day.md: Mornings: sales and share data, email from the sales team about a retailer's request, a call with the agency about a script. Midday: cross-functional meeting (supply chain flags a shortage, finance questions the discount). Afternoon: write or review a brief or deck. Rhythm: monthly business reviews and budget cycles; quarterly plan presentations to the marketing director. Frequent shoots and launches add travel bursts.

hours.label: Hours, stress and lifestyle
hours.md: Typical 40-50 hours; peaks 55-60 around launches, annual planning and agency shoots (practitioner estimate, unverified; no statistics found). BLS says marketing managers often work over 40 hours with stress near deadlines. Stress 3/5. Hybrid is normal at multinationals. International mobility is a condition of the fast track: P&G describes reassignments every 2-3 years (P&G Germany graduate ad, June 2026).

profile.label: Human vs. quantitative profile
profile.md: People/communication: 4/5. Quantitative/technical: 3/5. You persuade sales, agencies and finance constantly, and you are expected to read market-share, price-elasticity and ROI data without a data team.

pay.label: Compensation (approximate)
pay.md:
- Entry: UK £35,000 on Unilever UFLP plus bonus and a benefits envelope worth 25% of pensionable pay (Unilever, 2026 intake) and £35,000 at L'Oreal UK (advert text, 2026); Germany €67,500 plus bonus at P&G (P&G ad, 16 June 2026). Italy: Michael Page Italy 2026 shows Brand Manager at €40-50k for under 5 years' experience (bonus 0-5%), so entry sits below that range; pharma brand manager €35-55k (bonus 15-20%). Hong Kong: Brand Manager HK$35-45k per month (Morgan McKinley, 2026). US: no reliable entry data found.
- ~5 years: Italy €50-65k (Michael Page Italy 2026); UK brand manager London lower to upper quartile £51k-£75k, median £58k; UK national median £50.8k (Ashdown Group 2026 guide, which skews to recruiter-placed roles); Singapore consumer-goods brand manager about S$120k for 5-10 years' experience (Morgan McKinley 2026). Paris luxury: weak data, €32-42k for a junior luxury product manager (simulator and career article, anecdotal).
- Senior: Italy marketing director €75-85k (<5 years in the role) to over €100k (Michael Page Italy 2026); US marketing managers median $166,790 and advertising/promotions managers $133,660 (BLS, May 2025); UK head of marketing median £100k London (Ashdown 2026).

path.label: Career path
path.md: ABM (0-2 years) to brand manager (2-4) to senior brand manager (4-7) to marketing director/ category lead (7-12) to general manager or CMO (12+). Typical promotion every 2-3 years at the academies (P&G's reassignment cycle is the verified proxy; other timelines unverified). A sales or customer-development rotation and one international move are usual for general-management tracks.

exits.label: Exit opportunities
exits.md: After 2-3 years: another FMCG or luxury firm, retail e-commerce, start-up growth roles, consulting (a minority). After 7-10 years: marketing director elsewhere, general manager, CMO at a mid-sized firm, founder of a consumer brand, or move into strategy. FMCG brand names are strong CV currency.

tiers.label: Tier list of employers
tiers.md:
- Tier 1 ("marketing academies" by reputation): P&G, Unilever, L'Oreal, Nestle, Mars, Coca-Cola, PepsiCo, Mondelez, Diageo, Reckitt. Tier 1 luxury: LVMH, Kering, Hermes, Chanel, Richemont, Prada. Hardest to enter; best brand training.
- Tier 2: Ferrero, Henkel, Colgate-Palmolive, Beiersdorf, Danone, Kraft Heinz, Estee Lauder, Barilla, Lavazza, Campari; mid-sized luxury and premium brands.
- Tier 3: regional or mid-sized consumer firms, private label teams at retailers, smaller brands; faster ownership, less formal training.
Tier groupings reflect industry consensus and practitioner perception, not objective fact.

enter.label: How to enter
enter.md:
- Degrees: employers state no required subject. Unilever UK accepts degrees "across all disciplines", P&G Germany asks for a Bachelor's or Master's with strong results, LVMH SPRING asks for a Master's and no prior luxury experience (employer pages, 2025-26).
- Programmes (verified): Unilever Future Leaders Programme (UK, starts September, four-stage online/digital interview/discovery centre process), L'Oreal Marketing Management Trainee (London, 18 months, three rotations, up to 40 graduates), P&G graduate brand roles (hired straight into a brand role in Germany), LVMH SPRING Future Leaders (3 years, three 10-month missions). Experience windows are tight: Unilever 24 months post-graduation, LVMH three years.
- Calendar: Unilever applications typically open Q4 (autumn) with rolling close; L'Oreal rolling. Assessments: cognitive and personality tests, digital interview, case and assessment centre. L'Oreal Brandstorm (240,000 participants in 2025; about 500 first roles a year, roughly 0.2%) is practice and a recruiter touchpoint, not a route.
- Skills: Excel, a worked P&L model, data reading, a structured launch case; internships in marketing or sales. Certifications (CIM, Google, Meta) are not required by the employers reviewed.
- Competition: UK retail/FMCG/tourism received 290 applications per graduate vacancy in 2025, versus 140 across all sectors (ISE 2025; applications, not applicants).
- Mistakes: gap years that burn the experience window; assuming English is enough on the continent (P&G Germany needs solid German); applying to two programmes.
- Alternative routes: agency or sales first (P&G and Unilever value sales rotations), internships at second-tier FMCG, start-up consumer brands, retailer category/trade marketing into brand roles.
Entry difficulty: 5/5.

downsides.label: Honest downsides and who it is NOT a good fit for
downsides.md: Slow, process-heavy and political; much time goes to decks and alignment; ownership is real but limited by sales and supply chain; layoffs happen (P&G announced 7,000 cuts in June 2025; Unilever 7,500 in March 2024 - via secondary summaries). Mobility demands can cost you a relationship or city. Not for people who dislike spreadsheets, bureaucracy or being relocated, or who want fast autonomy (a start-up fits better).

roles.title: Digital / performance marketing specialist

what.label: What you actually do
what.md: You run paid campaigns and optimise them with data. Example: you rebalance a €40k weekly Meta and Google budget towards the campaigns with the best ROAS (return on ad spend), pause weak ads, test new creatives and landing pages, and write the Monday performance report. Sub-specialisms: SEM/PPC (pay-per-click) specialist, paid social specialist, SEO specialist, programmatic specialist, marketplace advertising (Amazon), CRO (conversion rate optimisation). Tools: Google Ads, Meta Ads Manager, Google Analytics 4, Looker Studio, tag managers, Excel/SQL for reporting. Deliverables: campaign setups, test results, weekly and monthly dashboards, budget recommendations.

day.label: A typical day and week
day.md: Check spend and cost-per-acquisition overnight, adjust bids and budgets, brief designers on new ad variants, review an A/B test, answer client or internal questions on why results moved. Weekly: report and planning; monthly: budget re-forecast. Big sales events (Black Friday, Prime Day, January sales) bring long days.

hours.label: Hours, stress and lifestyle
hours.md: Typical 37-40 hours (Prospects, November 2024), peaks 50 hours in peak trading seasons or at agencies (practitioner estimate). Stress 3/5: money is spent live, so mistakes (a budget typo) cost real euros, and agencies carry client pressure. Hybrid is common: 64% of Italian digital professionals work hybrid (Michael Page Italy 2026). Travel is minimal.

profile.label: Human vs. quantitative profile
profile.md: People/communication: 2/5. Quantitative/technical: 4/5. Mostly screen-based analysis, with communication limited to clients, designers and stakeholders.

pay.label: Compensation (approximate)
pay.md:
- Entry: UK digital marketing assistant £23,500-£25,000 (Prospects, November 2024); Italy SEO specialist €25-35k, SEM/biddable media specialist €30-40k, ad trafficker €23-33k (Michael Page Italy 2026, bands for under 5 years' experience). US: no reliable entry data found.
- ~5 years: UK digital marketing manager median £65k London, £57k national (Ashdown 2026; UK Prospects says "experienced" £27-30k at officer level, so the two sources describe different levels); Italy digital performance manager €50-60k (5-10 years), digital marketing manager €45-65k (Michael Page Italy 2026); Singapore digital manager S$100k at 5-10 years; Hong Kong digital marketing manager HK$40-68k per month (Morgan McKinley 2026).
- Senior: UK digital marketing manager £40-60k (Prospects) to head of digital; Italy head of digital €65-80k (>10 years, bonus 10-20%); Singapore digital marketing director S$180-280k (Morgan McKinley 2026).

path.label: Career path
path.md: Executive/specialist (0-2 years) to senior specialist/manager (3-5) to head of performance/growth or digital director (6-10) to CMO or founder. Specialisation (retail media, marketplace advertising) is rewarded; Michael Page Italy says digital roles are heading towards "hyper-specialisation".

exits.label: Exit opportunities
exits.md: After 2-3 years: in-house growth or e-commerce teams, product or CRM roles, marketing analytics (see data analytics branch). After 7-10 years: head of growth, e-commerce director, agency leadership, consulting in digital, or founder.

tiers.label: Tier list of employers
tiers.md:
- Tier 1: in-house growth teams at scale-ups and tech (Google, Meta, Booking, Spotify-type firms), top performance/data agencies in Publicis (Epsilon, Publicis Media) and WPP Media; Amazon Ads.
- Tier 2: large e-commerce and retail (Zalando, Amazon sellers, fast fashion), mid-size agencies, fintechs.
- Tier 3: small agencies and SMEs; broad scope, thin training, high turnover.
Tier groupings reflect industry consensus and practitioner perception, not objective fact.

enter.label: How to enter
enter.md:
- Degrees: any; marketing, business, economics, statistics or computing help. Prospects calls the field "open to all graduates", most graduate schemes want a 2:1.
- Entry: agency graduate schemes (autumn in the UK), apprenticeships (UK Digital Marketer apprenticeship), direct applications; internships carry weight.
- Certifications: Google Ads and Google Analytics certificates, Meta Blueprint, HubSpot: free or cheap and useful to prove hands-on familiarity; they rarely decide a hire (practitioner view; Prospects lists CIM and IDM diplomas).
- Skills and portfolio: run a real small ad budget (a friend's shop or a local charity), document the test, build a dashboard in Looker Studio; learn SQL.
- Mistakes: collecting certificates without a live campaign; only reporting clicks, not results.
- Alternative routes: sales or customer service to growth marketing; media agency to in-house.
Entry difficulty: 2/5.

downsides.label: Honest downsides and who it is NOT a good fit for
downsides.md: Platform automation (Performance Max, Advantage+) and AI take over trafficking and basic optimisation, shrinking junior task lists; tools and rules change constantly; results are judged weekly. Not for people who dislike numbers or want long strategy cycles.

roles.title: Content, social and community marketer

what.label: What you actually do
what.md: You plan and produce content: social posts and short video, newsletters, blog articles, case studies, creator partnerships; you reply to comments and DMs, track engagement and report monthly. Examples: a content calendar for TikTok and Instagram, briefing influencers, repurposing a webinar into five posts, community moderation. Tools: Canva/Adobe, CapCut, scheduling tools (Hootsuite, Later), analytics dashboards, AI writing/image tools, a CMS. Deliverables: calendar, posts, short videos, monthly performance report.

day.label: A typical day and week
day.md: Morning: check overnight comments and trends, post scheduled content; midday: shoot or edit; afternoon: brief creators, update the calendar, review analytics. Weekly: content meeting and report. Events, launches and crises (a negative viral post) break the rhythm, and social is a 7-day medium.

hours.label: Hours, stress and lifestyle
hours.md: Typical 38-45 hours; peaks 50+ around launches and crises (practitioner estimate; Prospects gives 37-40 hours for digital roles). Weekend or evening monitoring is common. Stress 3/5: public visibility, negative comments, short deadlines. Remote/hybrid is common.

profile.label: Human vs. quantitative profile
profile.md: People/communication: 3/5. Quantitative/technical: 2/5. Writing, taste and speed matter more than statistics, but you must read engagement data.

pay.label: Compensation (approximate)
pay.md:
- Entry: Italy social media manager €23-30k, digital PR and influencer marketing €23-30k, marketing & communication specialist €23-30k (Michael Page Italy 2026, <5 years' experience). UK marketing assistants £25-27k, marketing executives £29-34k (Prospects, November 2025). No reliable US entry data found.
- ~5 years: Italy €30-38k (social media manager, 5-10 years); UK content manager £42k median national, £48k London (Ashdown 2026); Hong Kong content manager HK$35-52k per month (Morgan McKinley 2026).
- Senior: Italy €38-45k (social media manager, >10 years), digital PR €45-50k; UK content manager upper quartile £52.6-60k (Ashdown 2026); Singapore head of content S$130-220k (Morgan McKinley 2026, senior bands). Pay ceilings are lower than for performance or product marketing.

path.label: Career path
path.md: Content/social executive (0-2 years) to content or social manager (3-5) to head of content/brand communications (6-10) to director. Moves into brand management, product marketing (B2B content), or creator-economy roles are common.

exits.label: Exit opportunities
exits.md: After 2-3 years: performance marketing, PR/communications, brand teams, agency account roles. After 7-10 years: head of content, brand director, editor, founder or freelance creator.

tiers.label: Tier list of employers
tiers.md:
- Tier 1: major consumer brands with large social teams (Nike, Red Bull, LVMH Maisons), top social/creative agencies, strong B2B content shops at software firms.
- Tier 2: mid-size brands, publishers, influencer agencies.
- Tier 3: small companies where one person does everything; flexible but low-paid.
Tier groupings reflect industry consensus and practitioner perception, not objective fact.

enter.label: How to enter
enter.md:
- Degrees: communications, marketing, journalism, languages, design; portfolio matters more than the degree.
- Entry: internships, agency junior roles, apprenticeship routes, freelance and student-society accounts.
- Certifications: Meta Blueprint, HubSpot content certificates, Google Analytics - optional proof; CIM for UK career builders.
- Portfolio: a channel you grew (with numbers), 3-5 short videos, a content calendar with results, writing samples; show AI tools used with judgement.
- Mistakes: showing follower counts without explaining what you did; copying AI output without editing; ignoring analytics.
- Alternative routes: customer support, community moderation, journalism, freelance.
Entry difficulty: 3/5 (many openings but the portfolio is the filter, and AI is cutting first-draft work).

downsides.label: Honest downsides and who it is NOT a good fit for
downsides.md: Low entry pay (Italy €23-30k), always-on pressure, public criticism, thin career ladders at small firms, and high exposure to AI-generated content. Not for people who dislike public exposure, irregular hours or ambiguous metrics.

roles.title: Product marketing manager (tech/B2B)

what.label: What you actually do
what.md: You decide how a product is described and sold. Example: before a new feature ships you interview customers, write the positioning, a launch plan, the pricing page copy, a sales deck and a battlecard comparing it with competitors, and train sales reps before launch day. Tools: customer interviews, win/loss analysis, product analytics, CRM (Salesforce/HubSpot), presentation and writing tools. Deliverables: positioning, messaging, launch plan, sales enablement, customer case studies.

day.label: A typical day and week
day.md: Sync with product managers, review a demo, write a messaging document, join sales calls to learn objections, brief designers on launch assets. Launch weeks are intense; between launches work is research and enablement. For product management itself see the product management branch; for marketing analytics see the data analytics branch.

hours.label: Hours, stress and lifestyle
hours.md: Typical 40-50 hours; peaks 55-60 at launches and quarter-end (practitioner estimate; no statistics found). Stress 3/5. Hybrid/remote common in tech; travel for sales kick-offs and customer events.

profile.label: Human vs. quantitative profile
profile.md: People/communication: 4/5. Quantitative/technical: 3/5. You need technical fluency to talk to engineers and customers, plus enough data skill to measure launch impact.

pay.label: Compensation (approximate)
pay.md:
- Entry: PMM is rarely a first job; "associate" PMM roles exist at big tech. No reliable entry data found for the US, UK or Italy; Hong Kong PMM HK$35-45k per month (Morgan McKinley 2026, all levels in one band). Michael Page Italy: Product Manager (FMCG/industrial context) €50-55k for under 5 years and product specialist €28-32k (not the tech PMM role).
- ~5 years / senior: no reliable data found for the US or UK from sources I could open. The Ashdown 2026 guide does not list product marketing. Treat any figure from salary sites as weak.

path.label: Career path
path.md: Associate PMM or marketing generalist (0-2 years) to PMM (2-5) to senior PMM (5-8) to PMM lead / director of product marketing (8-12) to head of marketing or product leader. Typical timelines are practitioner estimates, unverified.

exits.label: Exit opportunities
exits.md: After 2-3 years: product management, growth marketing, sales enablement, customer success. After 7-10 years: VP marketing, head of product, chief of staff, start-up founder.

tiers.label: Tier list of employers
tiers.md:
- Tier 1: Google, Microsoft, Amazon (AWS), Salesforce, Adobe, Stripe-type scale-ups (by perception and brand).
- Tier 2: established SaaS (HubSpot, Atlassian, Datadog-type) and well-funded Series C+ companies.
- Tier 3: early-stage start-ups (broad scope, equity upside, instability).
Tier groupings reflect industry consensus and practitioner perception, not objective fact.

enter.label: How to enter
enter.md:
- Degrees: business, marketing, computer science, engineering; technical literacy is the differentiator. Imperial's MSc Strategic Marketing class of 2024 sent 18% of graduates into tech (Imperial employment report).
- Typical routes: marketing internships at tech, SDR/sales to PMM, product analyst or customer-success to PMM, content marketing at a SaaS firm, or MBA/master's hire into rotational programmes.
- Calendar: US big-tech internships recruit the preceding autumn; many PMM roles are posted year-round.
- Assessments: written messaging exercises, a launch plan case, a presentation.
- Certifications: Pragmatic Institute, Product Marketing Alliance certificates are optional signals.
- Portfolio: a positioning teardown of a real product, a mock launch plan, a customer-interview summary.
- Mistakes: writing feature lists instead of customer problems; skipping sales exposure.
- Alternative routes: from sales (SDR to PMM is a recognised pivot), customer success, or consulting.
Entry difficulty: 4/5.

downsides.label: Honest downsides and who it is NOT a good fit for
downsides.md: Hard to enter directly after graduation; influence without authority (product and sales own the decisions); tech layoffs hit marketing teams; impact is hard to attribute. Not for people who want direct control, or who dislike technical products.

roles.title: CRM / lifecycle marketing specialist

what.label: What you actually do
what.md: You manage the customer's journey after the first purchase: welcome series, abandoned-basket emails, win-back flows, loyalty tiers, app notifications, segmentation. Example: you build a segment of customers inactive for 90 days, send a tested offer, and report revenue and unsubscribe rate. Tools: Braze, Salesforce Marketing Cloud, Klaviyo, HubSpot, SQL, customer data platforms, A/B testing. Deliverables: automated journeys, campaign calendars, segment definitions, retention dashboards. In luxury, "clienteling" extends this to store staff using client data.

day.label: A typical day and week
day.md: Build or QA an email flow, pull a segment with SQL or a BI tool, check deliverability and results, write the monthly retention report, meet with e-commerce and brand teams about the promotional calendar. Calendar-driven peaks: Black Friday, January sales, Christmas.

hours.label: Hours, stress and lifestyle
hours.md: Typical 37-42 hours; peaks 50 hours in peak trading weeks (practitioner estimate). Stress 2/5: errors (wrong audience, broken link) are embarrassing but usually fixable, and work is calendar-driven. Hybrid common. No travel.

profile.label: Human vs. quantitative profile
profile.md: People/communication: 2/5. Quantitative/technical: 4/5. Segmentation, testing and SQL matter; you work with data and tools more than with people.

pay.label: Compensation (approximate)
pay.md:
- Entry: Italy marketing automation specialist €25-35k; CRM manager €35-40k (<5 years; Michael Page Italy 2026). UK CRM analyst: London lower quartile £35k, median £48k (Ashdown 2026; not strictly entry). US: no reliable entry data found.
- ~5 years: Italy CRM manager €40-55k (5-10 years), in retail/GDO €45-60k; UK CRM manager £60k London median, £52.6k national (Ashdown 2026); Hong Kong CRM manager HK$48-68k per month (Morgan McKinley 2026).
- Senior: Italy CRM manager €55-70k (>10 years); Hong Kong CRM director HK$68-90k per month; UK upper quartile CRM manager £75k London (Ashdown 2026).

path.label: Career path
path.md: CRM executive/assistant (0-2 years) to CRM specialist/manager (3-5) to head of CRM / retention (6-10) to director of customer or marketing. Often merges with growth, e-commerce and data roles.

exits.label: Exit opportunities
exits.md: After 2-3 years: performance marketing, e-commerce, analytics, product growth. After 7-10 years: head of customer/retention, e-commerce director, CMO in direct-to-consumer firms, martech consulting.

tiers.label: Tier list of employers
tiers.md:
- Tier 1: scaled consumer tech and subscription firms (Spotify, Booking, Uber-type apps), leading fintechs, large retailers with strong data (Zalando, Amazon).
- Tier 2: retailers, airlines, luxury groups, banks' marketing teams, CRM agencies.
- Tier 3: small e-commerce and SMEs (a CRM generalist doing everything).
Tier groupings reflect industry consensus and practitioner perception, not objective fact.

enter.label: How to enter
enter.md:
- Degrees: marketing, business, economics, statistics, computing; data comfort matters.
- Entry: junior CRM/email roles at retailers or fintechs, agency CRM teams, internships; graduate schemes at retailers (Tesco-type loyalty teams in the UK).
- Certifications: HubSpot, Salesforce Marketing Cloud, Braze and Klaviyo certifications are cheap, concrete and recognised by practitioners (impact on hiring: moderate, weak evidence).
- Skills/portfolio: build a mock lifecycle plan with segments, triggers, KPIs; SQL; run a newsletter with measured open/click rates.
- Mistakes: focusing on design not retention economics; ignoring GDPR consent rules.
- Alternative routes: customer service, e-commerce operations, analytics.
Entry difficulty: 3/5 (open to numerate graduates; relevant tool experience is the filter).

downsides.label: Honest downsides and who it is NOT a good fit for
downsides.md: Repetitive build/QA work, pressure to push promotions, depends on data quality and consent rules (GDPR, ePrivacy); automation and AI-generated content compress junior tasks. Not for people who want creative variety or lots of face-to-face interaction.

roles.title: Market research / consumer insights analyst

what.label: What you actually do
what.md: You find out what consumers think and do and turn it into a recommendation. At an agency: design a survey, check fieldwork, clean data, run crosstabs, write the slides. In-house at an FMCG firm: commission and interpret studies, track brand health, and present insights to brand teams. Qualitative researchers run interviews and focus groups; quantitative researchers work with survey and panel data. Tools: survey platforms, Excel, SPSS/R/Python, PowerPoint, dashboards. Deliverables: questionnaire, data tables, insight deck.

day.label: A typical day and week
day.md: Draft a questionnaire, review fieldwork progress with a field agency, analyse results, write findings, talk to the client about what they mean. Peaks before client presentations and tracker deliveries.

hours.label: Hours, stress and lifestyle
hours.md: Typical 37-42 hours (Prospects, March 2026: 9-5 for in-house and quantitative researchers, with evenings and weekends common for qualitative researchers). Peaks 45-50 at deadlines. Stress 2/5. Hybrid common; travel for fieldwork and client meetings varies.

profile.label: Human vs. quantitative profile
profile.md: People/communication: 3/5. Quantitative/technical: 4/5. Strong stats and clear storytelling both matter; senior roles are more about client advice.

pay.label: Compensation (approximate)
pay.md:
- Entry: UK around £22,000 (Prospects, March 2026); Ipsos graduate research executive London £28,000 (job-board listing, deadline 7 August 2026, weak source); Payscale UK entry average £22,965 (2026, weak). Italy: marketing analyst €30-38k (<5 years) and product specialist €28-32k (Michael Page Italy 2026). US: BLS market research analysts and marketing specialists median $78,760 (May 2025); entry data not found.
- ~5 years: UK experienced about £27k to over £38k (Prospects, March 2026); Italy marketing analyst €38-50k (5-10 years).
- Senior: UK £42k to over £61k (Prospects); Italy marketing analyst over €50k (>10 years); US median is $78,760 with 7% projected growth to 2035 (BLS), above average.

path.label: Career path
path.md: Research assistant/executive (0-2 years) to research manager (3-5) to associate director/director (6-10) to head of insights or client lead. Usually a 12-24 month graduate programme (Ipsos "Generation Ipsos" is 12 months; Kantar runs 12-24-month schemes and about 100 UK graduates, apprentices and placements a year).

exits.label: Exit opportunities
exits.md: After 2-3 years: in-house insights, brand/marketing, data analytics, consulting. After 7-10 years: head of insights, strategy/planning, CRM/analytics director, consultancy partner.

tiers.label: Tier list of employers
tiers.md:
- Tier 1: Ipsos, Kantar, NielsenIQ, Circana; insights teams at P&G, Unilever, L'Oreal.
- Tier 2: YouGov, Savanta, specialist and boutique agencies, retailer insights teams (Tesco-type Dunnhumby-style analytics).
- Tier 3: smaller research shops and field agencies; narrower scope.
Tier groupings reflect industry consensus and practitioner perception, not objective fact.

enter.label: How to enter
enter.md:
- Degrees: numerical subjects (statistics, economics, maths, business) for quantitative; psychology, sociology, anthropology for qualitative (Prospects, March 2026).
- Graduate programmes (verified): Ipsos Generation Ipsos; Kantar graduate schemes (autumn adverts, spring assessments, September starts); NielsenIQ graduate client roles.
- Certifications: MRS Advanced Certificate (some large firms build it into schemes), MRS Foundation course.
- Skills: Excel, SPSS/R/Python, survey design, clean slide writing.
- Mistakes: being able to run tests but not explain "so what"; ignoring sampling.
- Alternative routes: field agency operations or data processing, apprenticeship (Level 4 Market Research Executive), or move from marketing/analytics.
Entry difficulty: 2/5.

downsides.label: Honest downsides and who it is NOT a good fit for
downsides.md: Low entry pay in the UK; reporting can be repetitive; AI is automating desk research and tabulation (the Stanford signal on young workers in AI-exposed jobs applies by inference); the career ladder is long. Not for people who want to make the final business decisions early, or who dislike statistics and detail.

roles.title: Agency roles (account management, strategy/planning, media planning and buying)

what.label: What you actually do
what.md:
- *Account management:* you are the client's day-to-day contact and the agency's internal project driver: brief the creatives, manage budgets and timelines, protect the relationship.
- *Strategy/planning:* you turn consumer and market insights into the idea behind the brief. Rare at entry; most planners start in research, account roles or analytics.
- *Media planning and buying:* planners decide where a campaign runs (TV, social, search, outdoor); buyers negotiate and book space. Example: planning how to split a €1m launch across YouTube, Instagram, TV and out-of-home, then reporting reach and cost per outcome.
Tools: PowerPoint/Excel, planning and ad-serving tools (e.g. Nielsen/Comscore data, DV360), CRMs, project management software.

day.label: A typical day and week
day.md: Account manager: client call, internal status meeting, chase approvals, update the timeline, deal with last-minute changes. Media planner: update plans, pull performance data, answer client questions on delivery, negotiate with media owners. Pitch weeks and campaign launches mean evenings.

hours.label: Hours, stress and lifestyle
hours.md: Typical 40-50 hours (Prospects, January 2026: advertising account roles are normally 9-6 with longer hours around deadlines, launches and pitches; weekend work is rare). Peaks 55-65 in pitches (practitioner estimate). Stress 4/5: client demands and pitch deadlines. Hybrid common; client and shoot travel. Marketing Week 2025: 54.9% of marketers are asked to do more with less.

profile.label: Human vs. quantitative profile
profile.md: People/communication: 5/5 for account roles; 3/5 for media planners. Quantitative/technical: 3/5 overall (account roles about 2, media planning about 4). Account roles are relationship work; media planning is numbers-heavy.

pay.label: Compensation (approximate)
pay.md:
- Entry: UK graduate trainee £24,000-£25,000, some £20,000 (Prospects, January 2026); junior media planner £26,000 (Prospects, March 2026). Italy: digital media planner €25-35k, ad trafficker €23-33k (Michael Page Italy 2026, <5 years). Hong Kong agency account manager HK$36-50k per month (Morgan McKinley 2026; mid-level). US: no reliable entry data found; BLS reports a $133,660 median for advertising and promotions managers (May 2025), a senior figure.
- ~5 years: UK account manager £35,000-£53,000 (Prospects, January 2026) and media planner with 3-5 years £37,000-£46,000 (Prospects, March 2026); Singapore regional account manager S$120k at 5-10 years (Morgan McKinley 2026).
- Senior: UK account director £56,000-£100,000 (Prospects, January 2026); Singapore account director S$200-350k (regional/global, Morgan McKinley 2026).
Pay is lower than FMCG at entry (about 30-45% below Unilever/L'Oreal in the UK) but rises quickly with promotion.

path.label: Career path
path.md: Account executive/media assistant (0-2 years) to account manager/media planner (2-4) to senior account manager/group planner (4-7) to account director/associate director (7-10) to client services director/managing partner. Strategy: planner to senior planner to strategy director.

exits.label: Exit opportunities
exits.md: After 2-3 years: client-side marketing (often into digital, brand or CRM), another agency, media owner (Google, Meta, publishers), consulting. After 7-10 years: marketing director client-side, head of agency, consultancy partner, founder.

tiers.label: Tier list of employers
tiers.md:
- Tier 1: holding-company flagships and creative networks (WPP: Ogilvy, VML, WPP Media; Publicis: Leo Burnett, Publicis Media, Epsilon; Omnicom: BBDO, TBWA, McCann, OMD; Dentsu; Havas) and prestige independents (Wieden+Kennedy, Mother, Armando Testa in Italy).
- Tier 2: mid-size networks, strong digital and performance shops, large PR/communications agencies.
- Tier 3: small local agencies; flexible, lower pay and thin training.
Industry notes: the holding-company tier is under restructuring (Omnicom-IPG, WPP Elevate28); Publicis is growing. Tier groupings reflect industry consensus and practitioner perception, not objective fact.

enter.label: How to enter
enter.md:
- Degrees: any; business, communications, advertising, English, psychology, statistics (Prospects). UK apprenticeships (Level 3 Advertising and Media Executive).
- Graduate schemes: larger agencies, applications usually open in the autumn (Prospects, January 2026); smaller agencies recruit year-round.
- Certifications: IPA Foundation Certificate (UK; the recognised agency signal), CIM; Google/Meta certificates for digital media roles.
- Skills/portfolio: a campaign critique, a media plan with a justified budget split, the ability to write a clear brief.
- Mistakes: ignoring paid media numbers; underestimating hours.
- Alternative routes: junior roles at independents, media owner sales, client-side marketing then agency.
Entry difficulty: 3/5.

downsides.label: Honest downsides and who it is NOT a good fit for
downsides.md: Low entry pay, long hours around pitches, client-driven stress, and job insecurity: holding-company layoffs (Omnicom 4,000 cuts; WPP H1 2026 revenue down 4.7%) and AI in production and reporting. Not for people who dislike client pressure, last-minute changes or low early pay.
