summary: US: $95-132k base (OW analysts); UK: £47-52k base at top boutiques (£34-41k at others); Italy: no reliable data found

roles.title: Technology and digital consultant (business-side)

what.label: What you actually do
what.md: You help business leaders decide on and deliver technology change, without necessarily writing the code. Typical work: define the business requirements for a CRM or ERP implementation, run a digital-strategy project (e-commerce, customer journey, data and AI use cases), design a data governance or cybersecurity-risk programme in business terms, manage an agile delivery team as a product owner or project manager, or advise on AI adoption and business cases. Deliverables include requirements documents, process flows and user stories, vendor selection analyses, roadmaps, change plans and training. Tools: Jira, Confluence, Visio/Miro, Excel/Power BI, sometimes SQL for data checks. The engineering side (building and coding systems) is covered in the Computer Science branch; data-science consulting is covered in the Data Science branch.

day.label: A typical day and week
day.md: Morning stand-up with developers and business owners; midday: requirements workshop or demo; afternoon: update backlog, risks and plans; evening: steering-committee pack. Projects are long (6-24 months) and have a clear delivery schedule. Go-live and release weekends bring peaks.

hours.label: Hours, stress and lifestyle
hours.md:
- *Hours:* typical 45-55 per week; peaks 60-70 at go-live or testing (no reliable survey data; consistent with practitioner descriptions).
- *Stress:* **3/5.** Steady deadlines; incident-driven peaks at go-live.
- *Lifestyle/flexibility:* more predictable than strategy; often hybrid; offshore teams create early or late calls.
- *Travel:* moderate, depends on client; many programmes are on a long-term client site.
- *Remote/hybrid:* higher remote share than strategy work.

profile.label: Human vs. quantitative profile
profile.md: People/communication: 4/5. Quantitative/technical: 3/5. You need to speak both business and IT; you do not need to code, but you need to understand data, systems and delivery methods.

pay.label: Compensation (approximate)
pay.md:
Entry:
- *US:* Accenture Strategy about $100-125k total; Big 4 technology consulting analysts $78-112k base (Road to Offer / PrepLounge USA, 2026); non-strategy technology consulting often sits at the lower end.
- *UK:* Accenture £33.5k base; Deloitte £37k, PwC £34k; Capgemini Invent £51k (PrepLounge UK, 2026). Graduate guides give £30-40k in London for Big 4.
- *Italy:* no firm-specific data found. Indeed Italy shows around €28k for Accenture data analysts and €26-28k for junior Deloitte analysts in Milan (2026; self-reported, indicative). Junior SAP consultant averages are often quoted around €25-30k in Italy (Payscale snippet, not verified in detail).
- *Gulf/Asia:* Dubai junior business-analyst figures AED 6-8k per month for fresh graduates and AED 8-12k for 1-3 years (Resumevera, sourced from job boards; weak source); Singapore Big 4 consulting analysts S$55-70k (Skillup, 2026).

~5 years: senior consultant/manager US $110-150k base for Big 4 managers (Road to Offer, 2026); UK £65-125k across firms (PrepLounge, 2026). Italy: no reliable data. Technical specialisations (SAP, cloud, data/AI, cybersecurity) command premiums that vary widely.

Senior: partner/managing director pay is not published; no reliable data.

path.label: Career path
path.md: Analyst/Consultant → Senior Consultant → Manager → Senior Manager → Director/Managing Director → Partner. Specialisation by technology (ERP, cloud, cybersecurity, data/AI) is common from year 2-3. Because delivery work is measured on utilisation, people with niche platform skills (SAP, Salesforce) can have more bargaining power than generalists.

exits.label: Exit opportunities
exits.md:
- *After 2-3 years:* in-house IT/digital programme or product management, software vendors (pre-sales, solution consulting), another consulting practice, or a data/AI role.
- *After 7-10 years:* head of digital transformation, CIO/CTO office roles, product leadership, or partner at a technology consultancy. Technology skills tend to be portable.

tiers.label: Tier list of employers
tiers.md:
*Tier groupings reflect industry consensus and practitioner perception, not objective fact.*
- **Business-led digital strategy and transformation:** McKinsey Digital, BCG X, Bain digital, Accenture (Song and Strategy), Capgemini Invent, Deloitte Consulting.
- **Big 4 technology consulting:** Deloitte, PwC, EY, KPMG technology practices.
- **Large implementation/system integrators:** Accenture, Capgemini, IBM Consulting, Cognizant, Infosys, TCS, Sopra Steria (their engineering side is in Computer Science).
- **Specialists:** SAP, Salesforce, ServiceNow and cloud partners; Italian firms such as BIP (business-IT hybrid) and Reply (more IT-heavy).
- **Differences:** strategy-led digital teams pay more and recruit from the same funnel as strategy; implementation consultancies recruit broadly.

enter.label: How to enter
enter.md:
- *Degrees/backgrounds:* IT, information systems, engineering, business, data analytics, AI and any degree plus evidence of technical interest. Business-side consulting accepts non-technical graduates.
- *Programmes:* graduate schemes and internships at Accenture, Capgemini, Big 4, Reply, BIP and IT consultancies; Accenture and Big 4 recruit in autumn (August-October) in many countries.
- *Interview formats:* online tests, video interview, assessment centre; light case studies; technical questions for specialist tracks.
- *Certifications:* more useful here than elsewhere: cloud (AWS/Azure), SAP, Salesforce, ITIL, Scrum/PSM, PMP/Prince2, Lean Six Sigma for operations-leaning roles. They help get interviews and promotions but rarely substitute for experience.
- *Skills to build:* requirements analysis, SQL/data basics, agile delivery, Excel/Power BI, AI literacy.
- *Common mistakes:* choosing a legacy platform with no growth, ignoring communication skills, overstating technical depth.
- *Alternative routes:* career switch from IT or analytics roles; internal moves from client side; bootcamps plus certifications.
- **Entry difficulty: 3/5**

downsides.label: Honest downsides and who it is NOT a good fit for
downsides.md:
- Work can be tied to long, politically complicated programmes; some roles become "body-shopping" to a client; growth in generative AI could automate documentation and test work, and Accenture's 2025 cuts show the exposure. Entry pay is among the lowest in consulting.
- Not a fit if you want strategy-level glamour, dislike technology delivery, or want to code (move to engineering instead).

roles.title: Internal strategy / corporate transformation / in-house consulting

what.label: What you actually do
what.md: You do strategy and change work for your own employer. Examples: build the three-year strategic plan and the annual budget narrative, evaluate an acquisition target for corporate development, run the transformation office that tracks cost savings across divisions, staff an internal consulting team on a business-unit problem, prepare materials for the CEO and board, and track market and competitor trends. Tools: Excel, PowerPoint, business-intelligence tools, financial models. Because you live with the results, more of your time goes on follow-through than on the initial analysis.

day.label: A typical day and week
day.md: Morning: sync with finance and business-unit leaders; midday: modelling; afternoon: prepare a board paper; evening: usually off. Peaks occur around planning cycles, board meetings and M&A deals. You attend more meetings and negotiate with internal stakeholders who have their own agendas.

hours.label: Hours, stress and lifestyle
hours.md:
- *Hours:* typical 42-50 per week; peaks 55-60 (StrategyCase, May 2026 and July 2026 cite 40-55 hours for corporate strategy; coach sources, no survey).
- *Stress:* **2/5** to **3/5.** Occasional crunch around budget, board and M&A cycles.
- *Lifestyle/flexibility:* generally the best in the branch; hybrid and remote policies follow the company.
- *Travel:* low to moderate.
- *Remote/hybrid:* high; follows company policy.

profile.label: Human vs. quantitative profile
profile.md: People/communication: 4/5. Quantitative/technical: 3/5. Success depends on internal credibility and influence more than on analytical brilliance.

pay.label: Compensation (approximate)
pay.md:
Entry: graduates usually join through rotational/leadership development programmes or finance/strategy analyst roles; pure strategy jobs usually need 2-5 years of experience. No reliable entry-level data found for the US, UK or Italy by programme; graduate-programme pay at large corporates is generally in line with the national graduate market rather than consulting (inference; Mercer cites about €30.5k for Italian first-job pay in 2024, as quoted by Sky TG24, Jan 2025).

~5 years: a coaching site gives corporate strategy total compensation for a senior manager of $250-350k in tech, $200-280k in pharma, $200-260k in consumer and $180-240k in industrials (StrategyCase, May 2026; a coach's table with internal inconsistencies, treat as indicative). UK and Italy: no reliable data found.

Senior: Directors $260-600k, VPs $450k-1.2m and SVP/CSO $700k-2.5m+ depending on sector in the same table (US, 2026; indicative); equity makes a big difference at tech companies.

path.label: Career path
path.md: Strategy analyst/associate → manager → senior manager → director → VP strategy/CSO or business-unit general manager. Median tenure at a first corporate strategy employer was reported at 2-3 years (StrategyCase, May 2026, coach source). Typical entry is after 2-5 years of consulting or an MBA; exits to P&L roles are the aim.

exits.label: Exit opportunities
exits.md:
- *After 2-3 years:* business-unit roles, product or marketing management, corporate development, or move to a consulting firm.
- *After 7-10 years:* CSO, COO, business-unit general manager, chief of staff to the CEO, startup executive, private-equity operating roles.

tiers.label: Tier list of employers
tiers.md:
*Tier groupings reflect industry consensus and practitioner perception, not objective fact.*
- **Internal consulting arms with consulting-style staffing:** large technology firms (strategy and operations teams), some large banks, industrials and pharma groups. These are the most sought after and often recruit ex-MBB.
- **Corporate strategy/corp dev at blue-chips:** big tech, pharma, consumer goods, energy, financial services.
- **Rotational leadership programmes:** the main route for graduates (for example at consumer-goods, industrial and financial groups).
- **Differences:** whether "strategy" means CEO-adjacent decisions or running a PMO varies a lot; some teams are title-only (StrategyCase, 2026).

enter.label: How to enter
enter.md:
- *Degrees/backgrounds:* business, economics, engineering, finance and any degree with a strong analytical record. Direct graduate entry is mostly through rotational programmes, finance or planning analyst roles, or business-analytics roles.
- *Programmes:* graduate/leadership development schemes (many open in autumn; vary by employer); internships; MBA internships and post-MBA recruiting for strategy roles.
- *Interview formats:* structured behavioural interviews, case/strategy exercises, presentations to a panel; 3-5 rounds over 4-8 weeks is described for corporate strategy (StrategyCase, 2026).
- *Certifications:* usually irrelevant; Lean Six Sigma or PMP help in operations transformation roles.
- *Skills to build:* financial modelling, understanding of the industry, executive communication, ability to build coalitions.
- *Common mistakes:* assuming a degree alone gets a strategy job; skipping industry knowledge; underrating politics.
- *Alternative routes:* start in finance, FP&A, operations or product and move into strategy; join as a consultant first (the common route); internal transfer within the company.
- **Entry difficulty: 3/5** for graduate rotational programmes at well-known companies; **4/5** for strategy-team roles at top companies (few seats, experience required).

downsides.label: Honest downsides and who it is NOT a good fit for
downsides.md:
- Smaller teams and fewer promotions; strategy teams are cut in downturns; politics and slow decision-making; lower pay than consulting at the junior and mid levels; limited exposure to many industries.
- Not a fit if you want fast learning across many industries, want to be compensated for long hours, or dislike working inside one organisation for years.

roles.title: Product manager (including growth and platform/technical PM)

what.label: What you actually do
what.md: You decide what the team should build next and why. Concretely: interview customers and read support tickets; define a problem and success metric; write a one- to two-page PRD (requirements document) for, say, a new onboarding flow; agree scope with two or three engineers and a designer; prioritise the backlog; run an experiment (A/B test); launch, then review the results dashboard (SQL, Amplitude/Mixpanel/Looker-type tools) and decide to iterate or stop. You maintain a roadmap, run quarterly planning with OKRs, and present to leadership. *Growth PMs* own conversion and retention funnels and run many experiments; *platform/technical PMs* own APIs, data platforms or developer tools and spend more time with engineers on architecture; *B2B PMs* spend more time with sales and customers; *consumer PMs* spend more time on data and design.

day.label: A typical day and week
day.md: A day is mostly meetings and writing: a morning stand-up with the engineering team, a design review, a customer call or data pull, afternoon stakeholder alignment (sales, legal, marketing), and an hour of writing specs or reviewing metrics. A week includes sprint planning (the team's one- or two-week work cycle), a roadmap or prioritisation discussion, a customer interview or two, an experiment readout, and a leadership update. About half your time is communication; deep work is squeezed into early mornings or evenings.

hours.label: Hours, stress and lifestyle
hours.md: Typical 45-55 hours a week; peak 60-70 around launches, planning deadlines or incidents at startups. Stress **3/5** (steady deadlines, metrics pressure, constant trade-offs; 4/5 at an early-stage startup where the product is the company). Lifestyle is flexible in some firms but big tech has tightened return-to-office (Amazon five days a week; Google, Meta and Apple three or four, per prior Admetia research on tech RTO, 2025-26: unverified at source here). Travel is low. Remote PM postings rose 31% in 2025 (Mind the Product, December 2025).

profile.label: Human vs. quantitative profile
profile.md: People/communication: 4/5. Quantitative/technical: 3/5 (4/5 for growth and platform PMs). In practice you must persuade engineers and executives without authority over them, and still be comfortable reading funnel data, writing basic SQL and discussing API or system trade-offs.

pay.label: Compensation (approximate)
pay.md:
- *US:* Levels.fyi new-offer total compensation (base plus bonus plus stock), 2025: PM median US$234k (10th-90th percentile US$136k-350k); Senior PM US$381k; Group PM US$480k; Director US$606k (Mind the Product with Levels.fyi, December 2025; skewed to large tech and the Bay Area). All-level medians on Levels.fyi on 9 October 2026: Bay Area US$312.5k (n=1,297), New York US$211k (n=983). Entry PM (0-3 years) at smaller companies is lower; no reliable data found for non-tech corporate PM salaries in the US.
- *UK:* London median £109,949 (n=350, 25th-75th percentile £84k-147k) on Levels.fyi, 9 October 2026; recruiter 3Search data for 2025 puts "Associate PM / PM" at £50k-80k, Senior PM at £70k-110k, Head of Product £90k-125k, and says Director offers have fallen (Mind the Product, December 2025). Revolut UK PM median £135k (n=59, Levels.fyi, 30 September 2026, in prior Admetia research).
- *Italy:* Levels.fyi lists an Italian PM median of €51,181 (n=23, so thin), with Milan at €62,727 and a 25th-75th percentile range of €40.5k-70.2k (9 October 2026). Aggregator NettoCalc (Glassdoor-based estimates, 2026) gives Milan median €66,000 gross, junior (0-3 years) €48,000, and Italy-wide median €50,000, junior €36,000; an older Product Heroes/Sec Newgate survey (2023) gave €43,000 average, €35,000 junior. Italian pay is mostly base; equity is rare outside Bending Spoons-style companies.
- *Elsewhere:* Germany median €95,144 (n=239), Berlin €99,214; France €70,510 (n=54), Paris €72,220; Singapore SGD 150,330 (n=148) (all Levels.fyi, 9 October 2026). Amsterdam, Stockholm, Dubai, Tokyo, Hong Kong, Riyadh: no reliable data found.
- *Senior:* see the US and UK lines above (Group PM US$480k, Director US$606k; London Head of Product £90-125k at typical employers).

path.label: Career path
path.md: Typical ladder: Associate PM or PM (0-3 years), PM II / Senior PM (4-7 years), Group PM or Principal PM (7-10 years), Director / VP Product (10+), Chief Product Officer. Many people stall at Senior PM; promotion typically takes 2-3 years per level (practitioner estimate).

exits.label: Exit opportunities
exits.md: After 2-3 years: a bigger PM role, founder's-associate/chief of staff roles, growth or strategy roles, or a startup. After 7-10 years: Head of Product or CPO at a smaller company, general manager (GM) roles, founder, venture capital partner or operating partner (see Finance branch), or product consulting/fractional PM (fractional roles are growing, per Mind the Product).

tiers.label: Tier list of employers
tiers.md:
*(Tier groupings reflect industry consensus and practitioner perception, not objective fact.)*
- *Tier 1 (highest pay and brand):* Google, Meta, Apple, Amazon, Microsoft, plus frontier AI labs and Stripe-level scale-ups. Meta London PM median £301k and Amazon £147k on Levels.fyi (all levels, 9 October 2026). Hardest to enter; best brand for later moves.
- *Tier 2 (strong product cultures):* Uber, Airbnb, Spotify, Booking.com, Adyen, Revolut, Atlassian, Salesforce, Bending Spoons, well-funded venture-backed scale-ups. Pay lower than Tier 1 outside the US but more scope.
- *Tier 3 (corporate / non-tech):* banks, insurers, retailers, telcos, consultancies' product teams. Lower pay, slower cycles, more titles called "product owner".

enter.label: How to enter
enter.md: *Degrees:* any degree works in principle; computer science, engineering, data, economics and design have the highest hit rate at tech firms, but business and management graduates do get PM roles, mostly after a first role in operations, analytics or a startup. *Pathways:* APM/RPM programmes (3.2); a lateral move after 1-3 years in an adjacent role; MBA entry (Amazon, Microsoft and others run MBA PM tracks; the experience-requiring MBA route is common in the US); startup first. *Calendar:* APM/RPM applications run from late summer to winter (Meta in late summer/early fall, Google historically in winter, Uber late summer/September); ordinary PM roles are filled year round. *Interview formats* (practitioner consensus): product sense (design or improve a product), execution/metrics (diagnose a metric drop, define success metrics), estimation, behavioural, a technical round for platform/technical PMs (system design lite), and a take-home product case or presentation at startups and scale-ups. *Certifications:* Scrum Product Owner (Scrum.org PSPO or Scrum Alliance CSPO), Pragmatic Institute and Product School certificates are visible in Italian and European corporate job ads, but there is no evidence they matter for big-tech or scale-up hiring; treat them as a low-cost signal for non-tech and consulting roles, not a substitute for shipped work (practitioner consensus; no hard data). *Skills and portfolio:* basic SQL, ability to read experiment results, customer interviewing, clear writing, and demonstrable shipped work: a side project with users, an internal tool, a case study with real metrics. AI-assisted prototyping is increasingly expected (Builder PM postings). *Common mistakes:* applying only to the biggest brands; writing generic "I love products" statements; no evidence of shipping; ignoring SQL/analytics; underestimating how competitive junior roles are (400+ applicants within days; Mind the Product). *Alternative routes:* engineer → PM (strongest at tech firms); consultant → PM (common for B2B and strategy-heavy roles); analyst → PM (data-led companies); internal transfer after joining in operations, support or sales; startup first, where product responsibility arrives early. Entry difficulty: **4/5**.

downsides.label: Honest downsides and who it is NOT a good fit for
downsides.md: You are accountable for outcomes without authority over the people who build them. Junior openings have shrunk; the job is increasingly squeezed between engineering-led AI tooling and flatter organisations. Pay in Europe is far below US levels; Italy is lower again. Not a good fit if you dislike ambiguity and constant negotiation, cannot tolerate being blamed for decisions made by committees, or want deep technical craft or a predictable 9-to-5.

roles.title: Associate / rotational product manager (entry programmes)

what.label: What you actually do
what.md: You work as a junior PM inside a structured programme: owning a feature or small product area, running analyses and experiments, writing specs and shadowing a senior PM. At Meta's RPM you complete a four-week product bootcamp and then rotate through three product teams over 18 months (Meta Careers page, October 2026). Uber's APM runs three rotations over two years (Berkeley-hosted posting, secondary); Atlassian's runs two one-year rotations.

day.label: A typical day and week
day.md: Similar to 3.1 but more supervised: your manager reviews your PRDs, you pull data, write user stories, run weekly metrics checks, and attend programme sessions (talks, mentor meetings) in addition to team work.

hours.label: Hours, stress and lifestyle
hours.md: 45-55 hours typical, 60 at peak (launches, rotation reviews). Stress **3/5** (evaluation pressure: you are assessed for conversion to a full PM role). Hybrid; Meta's RPM is based in Menlo Park and New York, Uber's APM in the US (travel to rotations or relocation required); Google's London and Bengaluru APM cohorts have no announced dates.

profile.label: Human vs. quantitative profile
profile.md: People/communication: 4/5. Quantitative/technical: 3-4/5. Programmes skew toward technical graduates (Google targets "technically oriented" graduates), so expect questions on data, systems and sometimes coding.

pay.label: Compensation (approximate)
pay.md: *US:* Levels.fyi new-offer APM total compensation median US$171k (10th-90th percentile US$100k-245k) in 2025 (Mind the Product, December 2025); a third-party guide cites US$160-190k for Uber (unverified). *UK:* the 3Search range for "Associate PM / PM" is £50k-80k in 2025; there is no verified London APM total-comp figure for Google or Meta. *Italy:* no reliable data found; no comparable Italian APM programme exists, and the nearest junior product jobs pay about €35,000-48,000 gross (NettoCalc, 2026, Milan junior €48k, Italy junior €36k; aggregator). At about 5 years APM alumni are typically PM II or Senior PM, so use the 3.1 figures for that stage and above.

path.label: Career path
path.md: APM/RPM (1-2 years) → PM (after the programme, 1-3 years) → Senior PM (about 4-7 years) → Group PM. Conversion to a full-time role is "considered", not guaranteed (Meta page).

exits.label: Exit opportunities
exits.md: After 2-3 years: PM roles at scale-ups, startup head-of-product or founder's-associate roles, MBA. After 7-10 years: same as 3.1, with APM alumni often over-represented among startup founders and CPOs (practitioner view; unverified).

tiers.label: Tier list of employers
tiers.md:
*(Tier groupings reflect industry consensus and practitioner perception, not objective fact.)*
- *Tier 1:* Google APM, Meta RPM, Uber APM (very small cohorts, estimated acceptance below 1% by a third-party blog, unverified).
- *Tier 2:* Atlassian APM, Salesforce APM, Intuit RPM (the latter's 2026 window opened in September 2025), Microsoft, LinkedIn and Adobe early-career PM roles (details not verified), Stripe and Bloomberg rotational programmes named by one guide (unverified).
- *Tier 3:* corporate/consultancy "digital product" graduate schemes and startup associate PM roles (for example the Certa AI-builder associate PM post).

enter.label: How to enter
enter.md: *Backgrounds:* computer science, engineering, math, data and design degrees dominate; business-only graduates are rarely selected unless they show software or analytics projects (prior Admetia research on EMEA APMs, 2026; consistent with Google's "technically oriented" wording). *Calendar:* Meta applications open once a year in late summer/early fall (page says open now, with March and September 2027 starts); Google's windows vary by cohort and include London internships from 5 October to 12 November; Uber's closed on 26 September 2026 (secondary); Atlassian's ANZ round ran in January 2026. *Interviews:* resume plus short questionnaire (Meta), then product sense, execution, behavioural and sometimes technical rounds. *Preparation:* mock product questions, a shipped side project, SQL; an internship in a software team helps. *Alternative routes:* a product internship (many programmes recruit from interns), a startup associate PM role, or analyst → PM. *Certifications:* not relevant for these programmes. *Common mistakes:* applying late, generic product-sense answers, no technical evidence. Entry difficulty: **5/5**.

downsides.label: Honest downsides and who it is NOT a good fit for
downsides.md: Extremely low odds and heavy US concentration; programmes are paused or reshaped when companies cut costs; conversion is uncertain. Not for you if you cannot relocate, have no technical or analytical evidence, or need a guaranteed outcome. For most business graduates this is a lottery ticket; plan on the lateral route.

roles.title: Technical programme manager and product operations

what.label: What you actually do
what.md: *TPM:* run large, multi-team engineering programmes: map dependencies, build and track project plans, chase risks, write status reports for executives, run launch readiness reviews and post-incident reviews, and sometimes make architecture trade-off decisions with engineers. *Product ops:* build the machinery around product teams: planning cycles and OKR tracking, feedback and research repositories, launch checklists, analytics dashboards and tooling, vendor management and cross-functional communication. Tools: Jira, Confluence, Looker or Tableau, SQL, spreadsheets, Notion.

day.label: A typical day and week
day.md: TPM: stand-ups across teams, a risk review, status updates to leadership, chasing owners, and a weekly programme review; product ops: pulling data for a quarterly planning pack, running a feedback review with support and sales, fixing a broken launch process, and training new PMs on tools.

hours.label: Hours, stress and lifestyle
hours.md: 45-55 hours typical; peak 60+ during major launches or incidents (TPM). Stress **3/5**, 4/5 during outages or deadline crunches. Hybrid is the norm; TPMs in global firms handle frequent cross-time-zone calls and some travel.

profile.label: Human vs. quantitative profile
profile.md: People/communication: 4/5. Quantitative/technical: 3/5 for product ops, 3-4/5 for TPM. In practice TPMs need enough technical literacy to understand system dependencies; product ops needs spreadsheet and SQL fluency and process design skills.

pay.label: Compensation (approximate)
pay.md: *US (TPM):* Google TPM median total compensation about US$302k in the US (Levels.fyi, updated 30 June 2026; L3 US$182k, up to US$852k at L8) and Amazon about US$290k (Levels.fyi, 7 August 2025); Google L5 ("TPM III") average about US$338k and Amazon L5 about US$214k (averages, not medians; self-reported). *UK (TPM):* London all-level median £121,504 (n=62, 25th-75th percentile £92k-166k; Meta £232k, Google £168k, Amazon £122k median; Levels.fyi, 9 October 2026). *Italy:* no reliable data found (the Levels.fyi TPM sample for Italy is too small). *Product ops:* no robust survey. Levels.fyi's "Operations Product Manager" median is US$191k (updated 9 October 2025), a PM-track proxy; the vendor LaunchNotes quotes base bands of US$85-105k entry, US$105-140k mid, US$140-180k+ senior (unsourced vendor estimates, May 2025). Treat product ops pay as 10-30% below equivalent PM roles (practitioner estimate; unverified).

path.label: Career path
path.md: TPM → Senior TPM → Principal TPM / Programme Director (about 8-12 years); product ops associate → manager → head of product operations. Many TPMs move to engineering management, PM or operations leadership.

exits.label: Exit opportunities
exits.md: After 2-3 years: PM (more common from product ops), engineering programme management, operations roles. After 7-10 years: Director of Programme/Operations, Chief of Staff to a CTO or CPO, VP Operations, general management.

tiers.label: Tier list of employers
tiers.md:
*(Tier groupings reflect industry consensus and practitioner perception, not objective fact.)*
- *Tier 1 TPM:* Google, Amazon, Meta, Microsoft, Apple (the highest pay on Levels.fyi). *Tier 2:* Uber, Booking.com, Atlassian, Salesforce, Revolut, large scale-ups. *Tier 3:* consultancies, banks' technology programme offices and IT services firms (programme management titles with delivery focus).

enter.label: How to enter
enter.md: *TPM:* usually engineers, QA/SRE or IT project managers; some come from consulting delivery or from agile coaching. Most TPM hires have 3+ years' experience (practitioner consensus). *Product ops:* from analysts, bizops, project coordination or support-ops roles; typically hired at companies with 100+ staff. *Interviews:* programme-management case (plan a complex launch), technical discussion, behavioural. *Certifications:* PMP/PRINCE2 appear in corporate job ads; at tech firms they carry little weight; agile (Scrum Master, SAFe) badges are common in banking and consulting programme offices (practitioner consensus). *Skills:* project planning, SQL/analytics, comfort with technical systems, strong written communication. *Common mistakes:* presenting as a "project coordinator" without technical depth. *Alternative routes:* engineer → TPM; consultant → TPM/product ops; analyst → product ops. Entry difficulty: **3/5** for product ops and non-tech programme roles; **4/5** for big-tech TPM.

downsides.label: Honest downsides and who it is NOT a good fit for
downsides.md: Credit often goes to the teams you coordinate; roles are among the first to be cut in layoffs because they are "overhead"; career ceilings are lower than PM at some firms; product ops has no standard definition and can turn into administration. Not for you if you want ownership of what is built, need clear measurable output, or dislike chasing others for updates.

roles.title: Startup operator: founder's associate, chief of staff, bizops / strategy & operations

what.label: What you actually do
what.md: You take work off the founder's or a leader's desk: build the financial model and the monthly dashboard, run the company's quarterly goals, prepare investor updates and board packs, analyse pricing or a new market, run special projects (a first enterprise sales process, an international launch, an acquisition integration), and fill gaps (hiring, contracts, partnerships). Tools: Excel/Google Sheets, SQL, a BI tool, Notion/Slack, presentation software. Deliverables are models, memos, operating rhythms (weekly metrics reviews), and tracked projects.

day.label: A typical day and week
day.md: A day might start with a metrics check-in with the CEO, then a data pull, then a customer or partner call, then a draft of the board pack; there is no fixed job description, and priorities change weekly. A week includes the leadership meeting, an investor-update draft, one cross-functional project push, and ad hoc "fire drills".

hours.label: Hours, stress and lifestyle
hours.md: 50-60 hours typical; peak 70+ before board meetings, fundraises and launches. Stress **4/5** (close to the founder's cash and survival worries; the startup may run out of money). Mostly in-office at early-stage startups.

profile.label: Human vs. quantitative profile
profile.md: People/communication: 4/5. Quantitative/technical: 3/5. In practice you must earn trust quickly with founders and employees and also build models and read metrics well enough to be useful.

pay.label: Compensation (approximate)
pay.md: *US:* no reliable survey found for founder's associate. Product-flavoured chief of staff roles at companies under ~200 staff: US$110-135k (LaunchNotes vendor guide, 2025; unsourced). FounderPath's SaaS salary benchmark (109 salaries, February 2026) shows a median chief-of-staff base around US$116k; its early-stage bottom-quartile (~US$30k) looks like a data error. A seed-stage entry-level figure around US$81k appears on a recruiter site citing an unverified "COS Network 2025 Salary Report". *UK/Europe:* no reliable data found for role titles; for context, a junior business hire at seed in Europe earned €50-70k cash plus options of about 5-15% of salary per year (Index Ventures, 2018 data, stale). LBS MiM graduates entering tech had a mean starting base of about £35-36k in 2024-25, below consulting (LBS MiM employment reports 2024 and 2025, via prior Admetia research). *Italy:* no reliable data found; expect Milan startup junior business roles broadly in line with junior PM pay (€30-45k gross; an inference from the PM figures above, not a sourced figure). *Equity:* Carta reports Series A companies average 16 employees (down from about 25) and equity packages about 50% smaller than in 2022 outside AI (Carta compensation trends 2025, via search summary). A claimed 0.05-0.25% equity for chiefs of staff (attributed to Carta 2025) could not be verified. Value the equity near zero when comparing offers.

path.label: Career path
path.md: Founder's associate / analyst (0-2 years) → Chief of Staff or Head of Strategy & Ops (2-5) → VP/Head of Operations, General Manager or Head of a function (5-10) → COO or founder. Titles are fluid and speed of progression depends on company survival.

exits.label: Exit opportunities
exits.md: After 2-3 years: PM, product ops, strategy roles at bigger tech firms, VC associate roles, consulting (MBB lateral moves at some firms), or a second startup. After 7-10 years: COO/GM, operating partner at a VC fund (see Finance branch), or founder.

tiers.label: Tier list of employers
tiers.md:
*(Tier groupings reflect industry consensus and practitioner perception, not objective fact.)*
- *Tier 1:* top-quartile venture-backed companies post-Series B (Stripe, Revolut, Ramp-type companies in the US; Revolut, Mistral, ElevenLabs, Bending Spoons in Europe), and high-profile AI labs (no entry-level business roles found at OpenAI or Anthropic on 30 September 2026; roles ask 4-6+ years).
- *Tier 2:* seed-to-Series B startups backed by top-tier funds (Index, Atomico, Balderton, Accel, Creandum, Seedcamp), and venture studios such as Antler (investor-brand signals).
- *Tier 3:* unbacked or small bootstrapped companies, agencies, corporate innovation units.

enter.label: How to enter
enter.md: *Backgrounds:* management, economics, finance, data analytics, engineering — any, if you can model and write. *Routes:* warm introductions via investors' talent teams (Index Ventures runs a public portfolio job board); part-time or intern roles at startups while studying; summer internships; Antler- and EF-type programmes. Founders' associate roles are mostly unadvertised (practitioner consensus; unverified); Revolut's Strategy & Operations graduate scheme requires STEM and coding; Bending Spoons hires students year round (company FAQ, 2026). *Calendar:* year round, tied to funding events, not graduation cycles. *Interviews:* case or take-home analysis (build a model, size a market), a founder conversation, and a work trial. *Certifications:* none matter. *Skills and portfolio:* a financial model of a real business, a dashboard built on public data, a market analysis, shipped side projects, SQL; strong writing. *Common mistakes:* joining a weak team for the title, overvaluing equity, taking a chief-of-staff title with no real scope, ignoring the runway. *Alternative routes:* analyst or consultant first; internal transfer; BizOps at a scale-up. Entry difficulty: **3/5**.

downsides.label: Honest downsides and who it is NOT a good fit for
downsides.md: Pay is below consulting or banking at entry in Europe; equity is usually worth little; the company may fail and your job with it; the role is vague and depends on one person; you may do a lot of low-prestige work. Not for you if you need job security, structured training or clear boundaries, or if you want a recognised credential rather than a learning-by-doing path.

roles.title: Founder / entrepreneur

what.label: What you actually do
what.md: You find a problem, build and sell a first version, hire and fund the company. Early on, that means talking to 50+ potential customers, building a prototype (often with AI tools), selling to the first users, setting up a legal entity and cap table (list of who owns what), and fundraising. Later: hiring, managing cash and runway, product decisions, board and investor communication. Tools: spreadsheets for cash and metrics, a CRM, analytics, whichever product-building tools your team uses.

day.label: A typical day and week
day.md: There is no typical day: customer calls, building or reviewing product, recruiting, investor meetings, and fire-fighting. A week at seed stage might include two customer calls a day, a hiring interview, a fundraising pitch, and time to build; investor updates and cash checks come monthly.

hours.label: Hours, stress and lifestyle
hours.md: 60-80 hours a week is common and peak weeks higher; stress **5/5** when runway is short or a fundraise fails (the scale's own example of a founder close to running out of cash), 3-4/5 in stable periods. Work and life blend; investors and talent cluster in hubs.

profile.label: Human vs. quantitative profile
profile.md: People/communication: 5/5. Quantitative/technical: 3/5 (4/5 for technical founders building the product). In practice you sell, recruit and persuade constantly, and also have to understand your numbers and, in software, your technology.

pay.label: Compensation (approximate)
pay.md: Founder pay is usually low until a financing. Kruze Consulting's payroll data (reported secondarily, 2026) puts median startup CEO salary at US$147k at seed in 2025 and US$153k in its 2026 benchmark; US$203k at Series A; US$216k at Series B. A much lower Pilot survey of 1,844 founders reported an average of US$75k, down 43% (2025; includes bootstrapped founders). For Europe, Creandum's 2025 data cites a median CEO salary near €115k, though the stage is unclear. *US/UK/Italy at the earliest stage:* often zero or a living stipend; EF pays £6,000 (London, equity-free) to join; YC invests US$500k per company but does not pay a salary. *Honest outcome distribution:* most seed-funded companies do not raise a Series A (Carta: about 10% within 12 months, another 15.6% within 12-24 months; Carta's analysis found graduation rates between stages barely improving, February-March 2026, secondary); startup shutdowns are rising (Carta 966 in 2024, +25.6%); returns to founders are extremely concentrated in a handful of companies. *Italy:* founders raise less and exits are scarcer (Growth Capital observatory, 2026). For a typical student founder, expected cash income in the first three years is below an employed graduate's.

path.label: Career path
path.md: Idea/prototype (months) → pre-seed/accelerator (6-12 months) → seed (1-2 years) → Series A (about 2-3 years; Carta's median seed-to-Series A interval was 616 days in Q2 2025) → scale or shut down. Most founders' first company does not reach Series A; many go back into employment with strong operator credentials.

exits.label: Exit opportunities
exits.md: After 2-3 years (company folded or sold): senior PM or product/strategy roles, chief of staff, founder's associate, VC platform or associate roles, "acqui-hire" employment at a larger firm (the buyer hires the team, not the product), or a second venture. After 7-10 years: continued CEO, operating partner or investor roles, serial founder, or angel investing.

tiers.label: Tier list of employers
tiers.md:
*(Tier groupings reflect industry consensus and practitioner perception, not objective fact; for founders: accelerators and investors.)*
- *Tier 1 accelerators/talent investors:* Y Combinator (US$500k for 7% plus MFN SAFE), Entrepreneur First (£6k talent investment then US$125k for 8%; majority-technical cohorts; takes few non-technical people, per EF FAQ, 2025-26).
- *Tier 2:* Techstars (US$220k, reported), Antler, Station F-type campus programmes and top regional programmes such as Hub71 (Abu Dhabi) and CDP Venture Capital's Italian accelerator network (17 hubs counted in 2024), plus Seedcamp (Europe; from general knowledge, not verified here).
- *Tier 3:* university incubators, corporate accelerators, local/regional programmes and bootstrapped paths.
- *Investors (seed/Series A, perception):* in Europe Atomico, Index, Balderton, Accel, Creandum and Speedinvest are widely cited; in Italy CDP Venture Capital, United Ventures and P101 are widely named (not verified for current status).

enter.label: How to enter
enter.md: *How first-time founders realistically start:* (1) work on a problem you know from a job or university; (2) find a co-founder (EF says 80% of participants find one within 8 weeks, employer-stated); (3) build the smallest working version, increasingly with AI tools, and get ten paying or committed users before raising; (4) apply to an accelerator or angels only with traction; (5) keep personal runway for 12-18 months. *Backgrounds:* computer science, data science and AI graduates have the easiest route (EF explicitly prefers technical founders); business graduates should pair with a technical co-founder. *Calendar:* YC runs batches throughout the year (Fall 2026 applications closed 27 July); Techstars and EF cohorts have set dates; no gatekeepers for bootstrapping. *Interviews:* founder pitches and investor interviews, not exam-style. *Visas:* see 2.6 (UK Innovator Founder endorsement £1,000 and fee £1,357; Italia Startup Visa with €50,000 funds; Singapore EntrePass; Japan Startup Visa; UAE and Saudi programmes). *Certifications:* none matter. *Skills and portfolio:* shipped product, customer discovery notes, early revenue, fluent writing and selling. *Common mistakes:* building without customer contact; raising too early; giving away equity in unequal splits or without vesting; running out of runway; accepting terms without legal advice. *Alternative routes:* join an early-stage startup first (3.4), a venture studio, or a corporate innovation unit. Entry difficulty: **2/5** to start a company (no gatekeeper) but **5/5** to reach YC-level funding or a funded outcome.

downsides.label: Honest downsides and who it is NOT a good fit for
downsides.md: Most companies fail; you may earn less than a graduate job for years, carry personal financial risk, and lose co-founder friendships; stress can be extreme. Dilution means even successful founders can own a small percentage. Not for you if you need income stability or have large debts, dislike selling, or want work-life balance in the first years.

index.intro:
Researched 9 October 2026 for the Admetia career-orientation site. Thirteen branch reports explain, for students and early-career readers, which areas, roles and sectors each branch opens, what the work is like day to day, what it pays, and how to get in. Every report uses the same six-section template and the same rating scales, so roles can be compared across branches. All figures are dated and approximate; check the source lists before publishing a number.

Files: `reports/<branch>.md` (one per branch); Finance, Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence were researched in parts (`reports/<branch>-part-N.md`) and assembled into the single branch file. `reports/italy-pay-addendum.md` fills Italian pay gaps across all branches. `progress.md` is the run log.
index.scales:
- **Stress 1-5:** 1 = low, predictable deadlines; 2 = occasional crunch; 3 = regular deadlines and steady pressure; 4 = frequent high-stakes pressure driven by clients, markets or incidents; 5 = sustained extreme pressure (e.g. junior M&A on live deals, trading through volatile markets).
- **People/communication 1-5:** 1 = mostly solo work; 3 = regular team and stakeholder communication; 5 = the job is mainly relationships, persuasion and client work.
- **Quantitative/technical 1-5:** 1 = basic numeracy; 3 = solid spreadsheets, modelling or statistics, some scripting; 5 = advanced maths, statistics or programming is the core of the job.
- **Entry difficulty 1-5:** 1 = many openings, open to most graduates; 3 = competitive, needs a relevant internship or demonstrable skills; 5 = extremely selective (low single-digit acceptance rates, target schools or elite credentials).
- **Background fit:** strong (standard feeder) / possible (hired regularly with extra preparation) / stretch (rare, needs a deliberate route).
- **Tier lists:** Tier 1/2/3 or the industry's own labels (bulge bracket / elite boutique / middle market, MBB / tier-2, Big 4 / mid-tier). Every tier list carries the line "Tier groupings reflect industry consensus and practitioner perception, not objective fact."
- **Pay:** local currency, with base or total stated, city, year and source; no currency conversion, because rates move. "No reliable data found" is used instead of guesses.
index.matrixIntro: S = strong, P = possible, X = stretch. Columns are the 11 base backgrounds: Mgmt = Management, Log = Logistics & Supply Chain, Fin = Finance, Acc = Accounting, Mkt = Marketing, DA = Data Analytics, Econ = Economics, CS = Computer Science, Cyber = Cybersecurity, DS = Data Science, AI = Artificial Intelligence. Ratings come from section 5 of each report; "strong" means the background is a standard feeder, not that entry is easy (check entry difficulty in section 4).

index.compareIntro: Hours are typical (peak) per week; stress, people, quant and entry difficulty use the 1-5 scales in section 2. Entry pay is approximate, copied from each report's summary table, with currency and base/total as stated there; "n/a" or "no reliable data found" means the researcher found no reliable figure (for Italy see [the Italy pay addendum](reports/italy-pay-addendum.md)). Ranges such as "3-4" or "4 (5 at top boutiques)" are kept as the reports give them.
index.assumptions:
1. **Location.** The reports sit in `research/branches/`, separate from the existing `research/careers/` library. That library was written for Europe-focused master's graduates, and sub-agents could use it only as leads to verify.
2. **Template wording.** The heading "4. Banks vs. other employer types" is kept word for word in every report, including non-finance branches. There, the section compares the employer types relevant to the branch (for example FMCG vs agency vs tech in Marketing).
3. **Additions to the template.** Each report has an "Entry difficulty: X/5" line per role family and a role-family summary table, which the index comparison needed. The tier caveat sentence was made mandatory.
4. **Multi-part branches.** Finance (4 parts), Computer Science (2) and AI (2) were assembled by script (`tools/assemble.py`). Each part's numbering is kept with a prefix (P2-3.1 = part 2, section 3.1), so cross-references inside a part still work. The orchestrator wrote these sections of the assembled files: section 1, the overview table in section 2, the cross-part table in section 4 and the overall ratings in section 5(a).
5. **Depth.** "Deep" branches give every role family the full template at length. "Medium" branches give the full template more briefly.
6. **Backgrounds.** The 11 base backgrounds are read as a degree or early-career background with that name, not as the job itself.
7. **Overall branch ratings** (section 3.1 above) are judgements that summarise the role-family matrix. A background rated "stretch" overall can still be "strong" for one role family (e.g. Logistics for commodity trading houses).
8. **Dates.** All work is dated 9 October 2026. Sources from before October 2024 are used only when nothing newer was found, and are flagged in the reports.
9. **Model use.** All 20 sub-agents ran on Sonnet: 18 research tasks plus 2 gap fixes, an AI part 2 rebalance and an Italy pay addendum. No Haiku agent was used, because format and consistency checks were done by script (`tools/collect.py`: 124 role families, no out-of-range ratings, all matrices complete). A Haiku agent would have spent budget on the same check.
index.branchesNote: **No fourteenth branch was added.** The two branches newcomers ask about most that the brief did not list are **Sales & Business Development** and **Human Resources**. Rather than spend a sub-agent on a separate report, sales and BD were added as a full role family in Marketing (3.8: SDR/BDR → account executive, key account management, with OTE pay), and HR as a full role family in Management (3.4). Sales is the larger entry door for business graduates and is the one to promote to its own report if the site needs it.

italy.preface: Compiled 9 October 2026. Fills the "no reliable data found" gaps on Italian pay across the 13 career-branch reports. Every figure is dated and sourced; where it rests on a weak source, the row says so.
italy.howToRead:
**RAL (retribuzione annua lorda)** is gross annual salary before income tax and employee social contributions. It is the figure Italian job ads and recruiter guides quote. It normally includes the 13th month (and the 14th where the contract has one) but excludes bonus unless stated. Always compare RAL with RAL, never with a US/UK "total compensation" number.

**Net pay (netto)** is what reaches the bank account. At typical graduate levels, roughly 75-80% of RAL survives at about EUR 30k, roughly 68-71% at EUR 40k, and about 64% at EUR 50k. These ratios come from calculator estimates for 2026 (13 monthly payments, employee INPS contribution 9.19%, IRPEF brackets 23% up to 28k, 33% to 50k, 43% above, plus local surcharges that vary by town): Gi Group puts EUR 30k RAL at about EUR 1,730-1,770 net per month, and QualcheRisposta gives EUR 1,882 (30k), EUR 2,103 (40k) and EUR 2,478 (50k). Treat these as approximate; the sources differ by up to about EUR 150 per month at 30k.

**13th/14th month (tredicesima, quattordicesima).** The 13th is paid in December by law. The 14th (usually July) exists only in some contracts, notably Commercio/Terziario. A "RAL of 36k" can be 12, 13 or 14 payments, so the monthly net differs.

**CCNL (contratto collettivo nazionale di lavoro)** is the national collective agreement for an industry. It sets minimum pay by level (livello/area), the number of monthly payments, seniority steps (scatti di anzianità) and leave rules. Companies can and often do pay above the minimum ("superminimo"). Three examples:
- **Credito/ABI (banks).** Under the November 2023 renewal, the minimum for the 3rd professional area, 1st level reaches EUR 2,742.34 gross per month from 1 March 2026 (FirstCisl table via QuiFinanza). Over 13 payments that is about EUR 35.65k a year, before seniority steps and bank-specific pay. This matches the bottom of a Deutsche Bank Milan M&A analyst ad (EUR 35,650-45,000, June 2026) that cites the credit CCNL, so a bank's entry salary can simply be the contract minimum. The contract expired on 31 March 2026; unions asked for about EUR 518 per month more and a 35-hour week, and I did not confirm an outcome.
- **Metalmeccanico (engineering industry, Federmeccanica).** Minimum gross monthly pay from 1 June 2026: D1 EUR 1,784.94, D2 EUR 1,979.37, C3 EUR 2,211.43 (13 payments, so about EUR 23.2k, 25.7k and 28.7k a year before superminimi and bonuses).
- **Commercio/Terziario (Confcommercio).** 14 payments, levels from 7 up to Quadri. The tables I found conflict with each other on amounts and dates, so I quote no figure here; use the contract text.

**Variable pay.** Bonus is usually "MBO" (management by objectives) or "premio di risultato", expressed as a percentage of RAL. Recruiter guides give bonus ranges separately from RAL; I note them where useful. Banks and finance firms pay far more of their total package as bonus than industrial firms.

**Benefits and welfare aziendale.** Italian employers add meal vouchers, supplementary health insurance, pension contributions and tax-advantaged "flexible benefits". These are not in RAL and are worth a few hundred to a few thousand euro a year. The tax rules on them change often, so check the offer letter.

**Milan premium.** JobPricing's Salary Outlook 2026 (data for 2025) gives average private-sector RAL of EUR 32,991 nationally, EUR 35,137 in Lombardy (first among regions), EUR 34,119 in the North, EUR 32,746 in the Centre and EUR 29,777 in the South and Islands. For tech and product roles, Levels.fyi's self-reported data shows a bigger Milan gap (software engineer median EUR 50.5k in Milan vs EUR 39.3k for Italy overall; product manager EUR 62.7k vs EUR 51.2k), but with small samples.

**Why Italian graduates compare with Milan offices of foreign firms.** Foreign banks, consultancies and tech firms in Milan set pay against group or European grids, work in English and offer a path to London, Paris or Frankfurt, while many Italian employers pay close to contract minimums. AlmaLaurea finds that, all else equal, Italian master's graduates working abroad earn about EUR 673 net more per month than those in the South (see section 3). Recruiter guides such as Michael Page do not split by city, so national ranges blur the Milan/foreign-firm premium.

**Scope notes:** All figures are gross RAL in EUR thousands (k), base pay unless a bonus is stated. "Entry" is the recruiter's under-5-years band, "~5 years" is the 5-10 years band, and "Senior" is over 10 years; Michael Page bands are wide, so the low end suits 0-2 years and the high end 4-5 years. Confidence: **high** = official contract table, gazette or public-sector notice; **medium** = recruiter survey or a real job ad; **low** = aggregator, forum, undated page or a proxy role. Where no source exists I write "no reliable data found". Currency amounts of other countries are not converted.

italy.benchmarks:
**AlmaLaurea Rapporto 2026** (XXVIII survey of outcomes, presented 11 June 2026; interviews in 2025 with graduates of 2024 at one year and graduates of 2020 at five years). Net monthly pay:

| Level | 1 year | 3 years | 5 years |
|---|---|---|---|
| First-level (bachelor's) | EUR 1,491 | EUR 1,684 | EUR 1,796 |
| Second-level (master's) | EUR 1,495 | EUR 1,695 | EUR 1,903 |

- Real (inflation-adjusted) entry pay fell slightly: about -1.4% for first-level and -0.9% for second-level graduates (as reported by PMI.it).
- Master's graduates working in Italy earned EUR 1,452 at one year against EUR 2,290 abroad, and EUR 1,840 at five years against EUR 2,941 abroad (Open, 12 June 2026). Living costs abroad are higher.
- By degree group, AlmaLaurea's regression (equal conditions, one year after graduation) says, against the politics/social and communication group: medical-pharmaceutical +EUR 310 net per month, industrial and information engineering +256, computing and ICT +222, economics +128, science +105, law -117. Working in the North pays +68 and the Centre +50 versus the South; working abroad +673. A job in the credit sector adds +287 compared with the social-services branch, and ICT sector jobs add +184.
- Group averages for master's graduates one year out (survey 2024, as summarised by Il Sole 24 Ore Infodata on 24 May 2026 from AlmaLaurea): industrial and information engineering EUR 1,783; computing and ICT EUR 1,777; medical-pharmaceutical EUR 1,660. I did not find a clean 2026 figure for the economics/statistics group (the AlmaLaurea page lists "economico" without a number in the text I could read). For first-level graduates in the same survey: engineering EUR 1,703, ICT EUR 1,653.
- The 2026 report also gives five-year employment rates of about 96% (engineering), 94.8% (ICT) and 91.6% (economics/statistics) according to a secondary site (tesify.it); these are not pay.

**JobPricing (Salary Outlook 2026, University Report July 2026).** Average RAL of graduates across all ages is EUR 42,378, versus EUR 30,999 for those with only a diploma; bachelor's EUR 34,640, master's EUR 45,877. Average RAL for all private-sector workers in 2025 is EUR 32,991.

**ISTAT.** One summary cites an average gross annual pay of EUR 31,856 for 2025 (secondary source; I did not open ISTAT's own table).

**How these compare with the role tables.** A master's graduate five years out earns EUR 1,903 net a month; at 13 payments that is about EUR 24.7k net, or very roughly EUR 31-33k RAL at the typical net share. That sits at the low-to-middle end of the "<5 years" bands for finance, data and software roles (35-55k), and well below the MBB and bank-M&A ranges. The gap has three likely causes: AlmaLaurea is an average across all degrees and employers, including public sector, part-time and small firms; recruiter guides sample roles placed through recruiters, which skew to Milan, large firms and multinationals; and MP26 bands are for under 5 years of experience, so the upper end is not reachable at 1-2 years. Bocconi and Polimi graduates (JobPricing EUR 41.4k and 38.2k average starting RAL) sit near the middle of the MP26 entry bands. In short: use the MP26 low end as a realistic starting figure outside Milan and the high end as a Milan, multinational or specialist-skills outcome.
